DOUBLE BICISTKSICE. Two lives are lived by many a living soul, An outer and an inner life: the one, In sympathy with friends, in open tone Express'd, and frankly patent to the whole Community 'midst whom our days do roll Their course. The other, secret, mute, alone With God and our own thoughts, laid bare and prone Before His eye—their judge and witness sole. A crowd of musings, hopes, high aspirations. Of penitential tears, sharp agonies, Of earnest strivings, conscious aberrations, We pass among and through without surmise By those who, from our cradle to our grave Can mark how staidly, admly, we behave.— MARY COWDEN CLANKS.

GOOD OLD DOG. Dash knows his master wears a hat, To keep him warm, or cool; He goes without, does Dash, but that Is just as much the rule. • His master's hat is part of master, As his own bushy tail Is part of Dash—a sad disaster Were that fine brush to fail Dash saw the March wind lift the tile
—As master drove weapaee A marketing. ant I s mile

As if it ran a race, And Dash flew after; but the thing Had got the start, and rolled • Fast as the chariot of a king. While master's head grew cold. And master's heart got anxious, for The bowling hat was bent (A stupid thing), he plainly SaW, On plunging in the T Anrendt,:saying so, "Aye, so I thought r" He saw it disappear Over a bank, which bounds the flow Of Trent, to anglers dear. A river iastsa place, efiots d you see, F that; But never, surely, meant to be A hat-box for a hat.

"There goes a hat !" cried Saucy Sail; Said Peter, "What a joke! Food for the fish! It never shall. While Dash can swim a stroke! It never shall, you laughing girl, While Dash has legs enough, Although the Trent's an ungly swirl, And his broad bosom's rough." A hat's a sacred thing to Dash, It may be master's life, Worth more than all his cows and cash, Dearer than child or wife. So reasons Dash, as Dashes can; Then in the flood he bounds; Good dog! a deed like that in man Were worth a thousand pounds `. He buffets with the angry Trent, Its tricks and awkward ways; A hundred eyes on Dash are bent, A score of tongues give praise! "He's got the hat !" "Good dog !" "Well done Some fifty voices cry; May we be there to see such fun When next the wind is high!

A lady, joking about her nose, said, "I had nothing to do in shaping it. It was a birthday present." "It is rather hard to die in abject poverty," said one. "It is harder still to live in it," was the rejoinder. "Mother," said a little girl, who was engaged in making an apron for her doll, "I believe I will be a duchess when I grow up." "Row do you expect to become a duchess, my daughter ?" "Why, by marrying a Dutchman, to be sure,'" replied the little girl. An American lady corning from Canada assured the cue. toms officer that she had nothing but wearing apparel in her trunk; but he went to the bottom of the articles and found a dozen bottles of brandy stowed away. "Madam," demanded he sternly," do you call these wearing apparel?" "Yes," the lady demurely replied; "they are my husband's nightcaps." Horne Tooke, when at Eton, was one day asked by the master the reason why a certain verb governed a particular case. He answered, " I don't know." "That is impos- sible," said the master ; "I know you are not ignorant, but obstinate." "Rome, however, persisted, and the master flogged. After the punishment the master quoted the rule of grammar which bore on the subject ; and Home instantly replied, "I know that very well, but you did not ask for the rule—you demanded the reason. Thai NEW TESTAMENT REVISION. —An esteemed and careful correspondent has shown us a copy of the Revised New Testament of 1881 in which every alteration made in the Authorised Version is marked and numbered. The changes amount on the whole to 36,191! This is a prodi- gious number, and far exceeds any estimate and calculation hitherto brought under our notice. It will be remembered that Bishop Ellicott reckoned the number of corrections to be about three in every five verses ot the Gospels and Acts. This would give a total, according to our correspondent, of 2,250. In fact, the alterations made in this group of five books amount to 14.610! The Book of Revelations is altered in no less than 2,467 places in its 407 verses. The miscal- culation which Bishop Ellicott and his colleagues appear to have made as to the number of the alterations is curious enough.—Guardian. A Wosnaaarra Caocs.—The most astonishing thing ever heard of in the way of a timepiece is a clock described by a Hindoo rajah as belonging to a native prince of Upper India, and jealously guarded as the rarest treasure of his luxurious palace. In front of the clock's disc was a gong, swung upon poles, and near it was a pile of artificial human limbs. The pile was made up of the fall number of parts of twelve perfect bodies, but all lay heaped up together in seeming confusion. Whenever the bands of the clock indi- cated the hour of one, out from the pile crawled just the number of parts needed to form the frame of one man, part joining itself to part with quick metallic click; and when completed, the figure sprang up, seized a mallet, and, walk- ing up to the gong, struck one blow that sent the sound pealing through every room and corridor of that stately palace. This done, he returned to the pile and fell to pieces again. When two o'clock came, the two men arose and did likewise; and so through all the hours, the number of figures being the same as the number of the hour, till at noon and midnight the entire heap sprung up, and, march- ing to the gong, struck one after another each his blow, and then fell to pieces. Tiis BURNING OF THE ORIENT AT THE BATTLE OF THE NILE.—Tne mighty glare she shed on all sides, as she be- came a pyramid of flames, enabled the men on board the two fleets to see each other distinctly. Their different colours were distinguishable; the dismasted hulks of France, and the shot-riven sails of the British. At ten o'clock the fire reached the magazine, and she ohm up with a dreadful shock, that made every ship in the bay vibrate to her keel. Her officers and men sprang into the sea in hundreds, and were seen, some helplessly drowning, others clinging thick as bees to spars and pieces of floating wreck. Many were picked up by our boats, and many even dragged in at the lower-deck ports of our ships, at the very moment the guns were run back to be reloaded. Many of her crew stood the danger to the last, and continued to fire from her lower tier of guns while the ship was a mass of flame overhead. A silence that seemed awful followed this tremendous explo- sion. The firing, as if by mutual consent, instantly ceased on both sides, and no sounds were heard but the wild cries of the drowning and wounded, and the splash of the burning brands as they fell hissing into the bay from the vast height to which they had been blown. Seventy of her crew were saved by our boats: but among the many who perished (she entered the action with 1,010 officers and men) were her captain, Casa Bianca, and his son, a boy only ten years old. She had on board the ,plunder of Malta, amounting to £600,000 sterling.—Prom 6' British .73altles on Land and Sec." SEVEN TIMES MARRIED.—It is announced ia,the columns of the Anglo-Indian press that his Highness the Nawab of Gondal contemplates entering the holy state of matrimony no fewer than seven several and distinct times in the purse of the present month. He has chosen several youthful and lovely brides from among the daughters of the Gondal aristocracy, and has made arrangements to lead them to thel altar, one after another, in seven successive days. It will be the pleasing duty of each bride, progressively and in regular rotation, to attend the weddings celebrated subse- quently to her own, so that the first lady of the series will enjoy the unusual privilege of witnessing seven nuptial ceremonies, in all of which she will be more or less directly rested, within the limits of a single week. The seven- raal aralegroom, however, obviously a student of feminine necaliarities, and wisely desirous to avert future domestic ta elates such as well might arise from jealousies founded upon any unequal distribution of his favours among the memars of ibis conjugal heptagon, has bestowed upon all his hr i les wedding dresses and ornaments of identical mate' vial, ~esign, and value. The rooms they are destined to accuny in his palace are all furnished exactly alike, and the accident of seniority, as regards the mere date of their re- spectlve marriage ceremonies, is not to carry with it any nrecedence at Court. It appears not to have been as yet lnally decided whether the Nawab, at the expiration of his wedding week, shall attempt to spend seven honeymoons at once, or take them successively. This is the only official detail of his prospective bliss that has not been definitely settled to the satisfaction, as we understand, of himself, his seven brides, and the Gondal public in general.—TeleoraP h. e rrTHE TEMPLE or DIANA.—At Ephesus, was 435 f high' and its erection required the labour of 200 years! SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CITCTURE, &c.

~..------.-.._ pliigdahurust a number of thSeoetnxceafvraestihondi of ancient statues. of thveeriteheas altstrerehpourtbedroufrsohmt toE A discovery of bronze weapons and other articles has been made near Oberode, in Hanover, by some labourers. Among other things there is a sickle-shaped tool, a knife for skin- ning animals, a bracelet, and some rings. M. Jacques Blocks has published an explanation of his process for the use of dissolved yellow amber in oil painting. He claims that by its aid the colours assume a brilliant and durable appearance, and that it obviates any need of further varnishing. Certain crystallised bodies such as tourmaline and quartz have the property, of disengaging electricity when subjected to pressure. The MM. Curie have been eirperimenting on the conditions of these phenomena, and have succeeded in a,eertaining the quantitative relations of the electricity di.engaged by various degrees of pressure. The inquiry \ promises to be interesting, and to increase our knowledge of the mysterious force in question. The discovery of additional links in the Darwinian chain is reported. At the last meeting of the Bonn Natural History Society of the Lower Rhine, Professor Schaaff- haus= exhibited the femur of a horse of colossal size found in the valley of the Wupper, near Elberfeld. Fossil bones of the horse found near Vallendar were also exhibited. Professor Schaaffhausen stated that these remains repre- sented predecessors of the existing species, but not the hippotherium. More fragments of Hittite sculptures from Carchemish have arrived at the British Museum some of which have hieroglyphs upon them. The sculptures, which are of no great size, are thoroughly Assyrian in character, one bas- relief, which represents the lower part of the body of a god, or hero, being perhaps of Assyrian workmanship. Another fragtnent contains the head of the goddess Astarte, without the star-like moon above the head represented as upon Babylonian gems. The Journal of Applied Science states that a German has discovered a method by which dyeing matter can be com- pletely extracted from woollen goods so as to make the latter quite white. The process is, however, not applicable for indigo vat-dyed materials, but it is said to answer well for all other colours. The fibre is said not to suffer in the I least by the treatment. It is also stated that the inventor has sold his process to a society of French manufacturers for 70,000 francs, who intend to take out patents in dif- ferent countries. M. T. Coquillon some time since published an account of an instrument for the detection of fire-damp. A spiral of platinum or palladium is made hot by an electric current, I and this by catalytic power produces the combination of the I mixed gases. A modification of this lamp has been em- ployed to produce the slow combustion of fire-damp. Platinise asbestos is used as wicks for a lamp fed by some I hydro-carbon; by this flame a layer of platinum wire gauze I is heated to red heat, and it is kept glowing by consuming any fire-damp which may be in the atmosphere. It is stated that one lamp with five burners will consume in a day 4,000 cubic metres of an explosive mixture of gases. In Caroline , Colliery, near Langendreer, in Westphalia, where some ex- I periments have been tried, nine cubic metres of explosive ' gases were consumed by one lamp in seven minutes. I M. Gautier, of the Paris Ecole de Pharmacie, has been ' experimenting on the physiological and chemical action of , the venom of serpents. Amongst the result of his inquiries there is one which is especially curious. He finds that venom—that of the cobra, for instance, contains alkaloids in addition to fatty matter. The analogy between the venom glands of serpents and the salivary glands of man led him to inquire whether the latter also secrete alkaloids, and to his surprise he has discovered that this is so. Human saliva contains a very feeble quantity of an alkaloid which, if isolated and accumulated, is capable of acting as a venom. Human saliva is, however, seven or eight thousand times less venomous than the secretion of the cobra. M. Gautier has haza-ded a conjecture that this discovery may help to . explain the "new disease" which it will be remembered was manifested in the rabbit which M. Pasteur inoculated with saliva taken from a ckild which had died of hydro- phobia. GIPSY LIFE.—From the Athenceum we hear of the death, in the neighbourhood of IlharkOf, of M. I. Banavin, who, though a member of the medical profession, had devoted 35 years of his life and most of his substance to journeys to; gipsy encampments in various parts of Europe, Asia, and Africa, and to the collection of a vast mass of materials con- cerning the gipsies. He reckoned the gipsy dialects at twenty, many of which he had learned, as well as Sanskrit, Zend, and other Asiatic tongues. The materials thus as- siduously collected run some risk, it is said, of being lost, as M. Kunavin's old servant is resolved to burn the papers I unless he is able to give them into the hands of M. Bass &ND Vault LABOTIRERS.—I reside in a purely agn- emit-mai parish, and my family for many generations past, on both my parents' side, have been tenant-farmers, so that I naturally cling tenaciously to everything connected with farm life. My mother was proud of ,her large apiary, and from early life I took a deep interest in the welfare of my mother's farming stock, the bees. Mother did her utmost to help the married labourers; four men with families lived from boyhood with my father until his death—one of the men resided in a village two miles away from the farm, the rest lived in our own village; mother furnished an apiary for each labourer, and for some years undertook their super- intendence. Great indeed was her delight when they cleared sufficipnt to pay the rent of their cottages by the bees and honey. From bees they began feeding pigs, then they ob- tained each, one or more cows, and rented the pasture from her father. One of these labourers is now doing well as a small farmer, and attributes all his success to the influence of the bees in teaching him valuable lessons on cottage economy. Imagine my surprise, therefore, when I was in- formed that cottage bee keeping is becoming a thing of the past. During a ramble on two successive evenings I called upon seventeen cottagers who, I knew, kept bees a few years since, for I had aided most of them in driving and uniting their stocks to avoid the brimstone pit in the autumn. I was glad to find that fourteen still kept good thriving apiaries ; some of them had several stocks in the old- fashioned skeps, several only two, but in every case the cottages were clean and neat; generally the flagged floor was sanded with a ring of bright red (raddle) underneath the chairs, and there were many tokens that the inmates were doing well. The contrast betwixt these families, who were in every instance farm labourers, with some of the other neighbours, often in the same lane would be notice- able to the most casual observer. I have heard the remark, "Whoever is fond of his bees is fond of his home." Beekeeping, although an humble pursuit. undoubtedly has this happy influence. I never yet knew a farm labourer who kept bees and took an interest in their welfare who was not a respectable, well-conducted member of society. Two of the families had given up beekeeping; the bench still clung to the wall, but it was forlorn and going to decay; the cottage home also bore traces of neglect if not careless- ness. Upon inquiring why they had given up keeping bees: "Oh! they did not pay for the trouble." "Did you pay much attention to them ?" "No, sir, we have no time," was the reply I obtained. "How could you expect them to succeed and pay you if you never looked after them ?" The lesson I should like to teach—not alone to those who take an intelligent interest in Our working population, such as the parish clergy, magistrates and retired tradesmen, but to farmers especially—try to help those who are willing to help themselves. Try our plan—give your labourer a swarm of bees, and watch the result. Of course a few hints about their history and management would be acceptable along with the gift, and would be received gladly. We have a widespread superstition in this country that a hive of bees, if purchased, cannot prosper; they must be borrowed to be successful. The plan generally adopted is to give the first swarm to start the apiary, on condition that it must be re- turned' any time during two years. I should also like to see a few prizes given at all our local flower shows, as well as at every county agricultural show, for the best honey and wax; also for neat hives made by farm labourers. The prizes ought not to be money prizes, but books—if on any rural subject or natural history, so much the better. We have many excellent and skilled apiarians who would deem it a pleasure to attend our local shows to give instruction in the keeping of bees. One other point must not be over- looked—the simpler the method the better. I always re- commend cottagers to begin with a single hive or stock, and to use the ordinary straw skep ; then to gradually increase their stocks when they have mastered the first simple rules. There is no "royal road" to successful beekeeping, but the difficulties are trivial, and none but what a little thought and care can banish entirely. I have ever found our fitful and changeable climate was the worst foe I had to contend against. For example, a continuously wet summer, is very unproductive; at the close of such a season the stocks, in- stead of having a rich store laid by for winter consumption, are generally in a starving condition, and without a little care in feeding they may be destroyed. Wet summers are rich in swarms, because a strong, fertile queen, finding most of the cells empty, fills them with brood; this usually—as it is not unlikely to do during the present season—ends in disaster and loss, for every second and third swarm is hived separate'y, and left to care of itself, instead of being again returned to the parent stock, to strengthen it, and enable it to take advantage of every fine hour in honey collecting. I hope I have said enough to cause the kind-hearted far- mer's wife to try to improve the minds and habits of their home labouring population. A rich reward awaits all efforts for their improvement.—J. F. R. in Agricultural Gazette. PROFESSOR TANNER'S PRINCIPLES OF AGRICULTURE.— Professor Tanner, Examiner of Agriculture under the Go- vernment Department of• Science, is in favour of the system of imparting information in dialogue form, and he is ap- parently of opinion that for beginners an easy and familiar style is best. Thus, in a little book on the principles of riculture, written by him and just published by Messrs. lmillan and Co., "Lesson No. 10" as fol- :--" Do plants ever get sickly and ill, Tom?" said Bill; "they want food as we do, but do they ever get ill ?" To this.TOra replies, "They look sickly and ill very much too often; but, as they cannot speak, this is the only way they can show us there is something wrong." “ What makes them ill? Is it taking too much good stuff ?" asked Bill. "Oh, no, no," said Tom, "the plants set you a good ex- ample." And so on. "Bill," we may observe, is repre- sented EL, exhibiting an almost unquenchable thirst for agri- cultural knowledge, though occasionally a sceptical spirit breaks forth, as shown in the passage," You don't mean to say that plants can faint away as Jemmy Ford did in the Assembly Rooms the other day ?" said Bill; but he is as- Sured by his instructor that the cases are analogous, for, as the latter observes, "both want fresh air, and if they do get it they look very queer."—Daily News. TRIAL OF SHEAF BiwnEns an DERBY.—The trials of sheaf binders at Thulston, near Derby, which commenced on Monday, was resumed on Wednesday morning in fine but threatening weather. In the early part of the day the machines which failed to accomplish their task on Monday evening resumed, and completed their several allotments in a satisfactory manner, viz., Johnston's, Howard's, and Messrs. King and Bomford's. The lots consisted of oats and barley, the number of acres in each instance being fixed at two. A Samuelson machine took the field at 12 47 p:m., making no less than nine or ten stoppages during the three hours and three-quarters it took to complete its task, which was accomplished, however, in a very creditable manner. A Wood's machine did not start work until eight minutes past one, and was so far successful that only three stoppages were necessary, the whole of the two acres being cut in eight minutes less than two hours. One of M'Cormick's machines got into the field at nineteen minutes past one, and made but four stoppages, the time occupied being seven minutes short of two hours. It will be seen that the binders and reapers are capable, when in good working order, of cutting and binding an acre of oats or barley in au hour; but it may be stated that the judges will not, when giving their awards, take into consideration the time occupied so much as the excellent manner in which the work is accom- plished. Aultman's machine cut well. BIRDS AND INSECTS.—One of the prettiest of the poems in the "Tales of a Wayside Inn" is that which tells the fate of the "Birds of Killingworth." The farmers, it will be remembered, decided to exterminate the :singers of the woods and fields on account of their supposed damage to the crops. A " ceaseless fusillade' begins, and is not slackened until the birds have all been slaughtered or frightened away. The only advocate they have is the poet-schoolmaster, who vainly warns the agriculturists of the greater dangers they are encountering. The natural enemies of the insects hav- ing been got rid of, all manner of creeping pests increase and multiply until the ruined crops convince the villagers that the birds are real "farmers' friends." Finally the poet has the satisfaction of seeing a waggonload of singing birds brought to the village, and turned into the mute woods, which once more become vocal. It will be pleasant to many of Longfellow's readers to know that although the details are the poet's own invention they;have a substantial founda- tion in fact. In a letter addressed to a correspondent in Manchester, the veteran poet states that Killingworth is a farming town on Long Island Sound, in the State of Con- necticut. Some years ago there was an animated debate in the State Legislature, and as a result the birds were doomed to destruction as stated in the poem. The experience of the New England farmers is the same as that of the Old World. The yearly damage by insects in France is estimated at forty millions sterling. At Baden, where the sparrows had been stamped out, they were re-imported in order to contend against the cockchafer. The fecundity of the insect tribes can only be effectively kept in check by the provision which Nature herself has made for preserving the balance of power the different forms of life.

livered. , Mr. Terrien de Lacouperie is believed to have solved a considerable philological problem. In an essay on the " Early History of the Chinese Civilisation," which is a development of a paper read before the Society of Arts, he s, has exposed the fallacy of the ordinary opinion which would agricm,.... regard China as a world by itself, with a distinct language Nlacmill*o aryl a peculiar way of writing which it has invented for lows The linguistic facts and suggestions already put " forward by Mr. de Laconperie point to an affinity between the languages and traditions of ancient China and of Baby- lonia. With the establishment of the common origin of the Accadian and Chinese writings the barrier falls to the ground which has been supposed to separate the people and the language of China from the rest of the world. Some previous speculations on this subject are associated with the names of the Rev. John Chalmers and the Rev. J, Edkins. ' ANCIENT torntsx Toots.—Mr. W. M. F. Petrie writes from Bromley, Kent, to the Academy In the course of examining the methods of working the most ancient remaine in Egypt, I have found indubitable proofs of the regular use " of saws and tube drills for cutting quartz, granite, basalt, &lc. Now, as bits of such tools would be unexplainable without knowing the examples of their use, it is very pro- bable that they may. exist, in collections, among the heaps of little things that lie in unlabelled obscurity. What, then, need to be looked for are—first,tronze or other metal blades (smooth-edged) about an eighth or a sixth of VI inch thick, and two inches or more in width; and second, bronze or other metal tubes about an eighth of an inch thick, and from three-eighths up to four inches in diameter. If any should be found, a portion of the edge should be dissolved in acid, and the 'residue examined microscopically to de- termine what power—emery, beryl, garnet, Ac—has been used with the tool for cutting. There are indications in the svorking which can hardly have been made by any tool ex- cept a crown drill of the modern pattern, with cutting stones set in the edge of it." LOCAusitigi A BuLLET.—The determina' tion Of the exact situation of the bullet in the body of President Garfield has an interest which not only is international; but which, will also be historical, for it has now been proved to be possible to detect the exact position of a bullet in the human body without even touching the flesh. Professor Hughes, who is now occupied as one of our English Commissioners at the Electrical Exhibition at Paris, has for many years been engaged in examining a special property of electricity. Without going very minutely into the theory of the instru- ment which he has invented, and which is called an induc- tion balance, it may be stated that he has discovered a means of detecting the presence in the neighbourhood of his small instrument of any mass of metal, and of estimating its direction with respect to the instrument. On July 16, in the present year, the following telegram was received by Mr. Preece, of the Telegraph Office in London, from Mr. Graham Bell, at New York, whose invention of the tele- phone was really a primary step towards Professor Hughes' invention :—" Can Hughes suggest form of induction balance to locate leaden bullet in President? If so, cable at my expense.—Graham Bell." Mr. Preece immediately corresponded with Professor Hughes, and the latter gentle- man, after a few experiments, replied on the same day to explain in what way his instrument must be modified to do what was required. The result of this correspondence was that Mr. Graham Bell applied the instrument to the Presi- dent's body at different parts, and so he found different lines of directions, which must all pass through the bullet. The intersection of these must, of course, show the exact point where the bullet is situated. EXHIBITION OF ELECTRICITY IN Pents.—A Paris corre- spondent says :—Great things are expected from this Con- gress and Exhibition. More than sixty miles of wire and cable will conduct the electricity in all directions from the lamps to the different apparatus exhibited over an area of 50,000 square yards. Everything will be in movement from morn till eve. The force produced will be sent tele- graphically, so to speak, into all the corners of the Palace. A wire extended to the apparatus, with the pressure of a knob, will set the machine working as if it were directly attached to a motive force of great power. And yet nothing will be heard around it, neither noise nor fire, although this wire may represent a force of ten or twenty horses, or more. The magic of this magnetic thread has all the properties of Orpheus's lute. Not ouly will it draw sounds as well as trees, but its next achievements are announced to be the traction of omnibuses and railway trains, the distribution of water power hundreds and thousands of miles distant, and; in general, the gradual supplanting of coal and steam for heating and transport purposes. This may be a dream of the far future, but a brief foretaste of the happy reality is promised on a small scale to visitors to Paris during the next three months. All the principal countries of Europe and the United States will be represented at the Congress and Exhibition. On the ground floor of the Palace the beautiful Pavilion de la Ville de Paris has been transported ' from its site on the Champ de Mars. In it will be placed the electric clocks of the municipality and fire alarums. The centre of the nave is being filled up by a lighthouse in the midst of a large basin, with artificial cascades, to be lighted in the evening with parti-coloured electric fires. On the first floor pictures and objects of art are being arranged to be illuminated by a sun lamp, called Clere's system. In one room there is to be a miniature theatre, to show the ap- plication of the electric light on the stage. In another all immaginable uses to which electricity can be put for domes- tic purposes, from safes guarded by electric bells to electric pianos and billiard tables, are to be on view. A gentleman having put out a candle by accident one night, ordered his waiting man (who was a simple being) to light it again in the kitchen, adding, "But take care, James, that yow do not hit yourself against anything in the dark." Mindful of the caution, James stretched out both arms at full length before him, but unluckily a door that stood half open passed between his hands and struck him a woeful blow upon the nose. "Golly gracious!" muttered he, when he recovered his senses a little, "I always heard that Phad a very long nose, but I vow I never thought it was longer than my arm!" Three brothers, bearing a remarkable resemblance to one another, are in the habit of shaving at a barber's shop in New Orleans. A few days since one of the brothers entered the shop early in the morning, and was duly shaved by a German who had been at work in the establishment for one or two days. About twelve o'clock another brother came in, and underwent a similar operation at the hands of another person. In the evening the third brother made his appear- ance, when the German dropped his razor in astonishment, and exclaimed, "Veil, mine goodness! dat man hash the fastest beard I ever saw; I shaves him in dis mornin', anoder shave him at dinner-times, and he gomes back now mit his beard so long as it never vas." PRECAUTION.—A troupe of wandering musicians were once playing before an hotel. At the end of the piece one of the members left the group, approached the leader of the band, and pulled out a little paper box which he emptied into his left hand while the eyes of the leader followed every movement. He then took a plate in his right hand and passed it around. There was a large collection, but every one wondered what he held in his left hand. "Why, it's very simple," said the chief when questioned; "we are all subject to temptation, and to be sure of the fidelity of our enfiertor we c.1.,1 ire him tn hold five Meg in hie left hand. and ue count those :,:st wlien he returns, ts,) as tv make sure vf the money."

IVI tSCELLANEOUS.
Mr. Whalley, M.P., contradicts a report that he intends to resign his seat. Another Liberal seat has become vacant, Colonel Joicey, one of the members for North Durham having died on

Monday. The wife of the Mayor of Liverpool on Saturday gave birth to a daughter. The happy event will be signalised by the presentation of a silver cradle. At Nottingham, on Monday, a man. named Brown was hanged for the murder of Elizabeth Caldwell, a woman with whom he had lived. Both were drundards. I The horses which have been running with the Liverpool
and York coach (now discontinued) were sold on Saturday. Mr. Lightoller, of Chorley, was the purchaser of one of the
A youth named Cooper, son of a London auctioneer, shot himself dead at Littlehampton, on Monday. He was about to return to lowa with a woman he had been living with for

a fortnight. In Dublin, on Monday. Colelough, late distributor of stamps in the Irish Queen's Bench Division, who had been convickd of. forging stamps, was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude. Sit John Anderson presented on Saturday to the inhabi- tants of his native place of Woodside, a borough within the ; Parliamentary boundary of Aberdeen, a free library, corn- posed of more than 5,009 volumes.
At a meeting of the Cobden Club, held on Monday, Mr. Joseph Arch and Mr. George Howell were elected honorary members of the club. _ _ _

The Birmingham Watch Committee has called on Major Bond, the Chief Constable, to resign. The Major has for some time acted in opposition to the committee. Mr. Balfour, Solicitor-General for Scotland, has been ap- pointed Lord Advocate, and Mr. Asher, M.P., Solicitor- , General. Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., has been appointed I a Lord of the Treasury, unpaid. Alex nder Bruce, labourer, was arrested at Perth on Mon- day night, on suspicion of being concerned in the blowing lupof a vessel in the Tay. He has' lately been working in I conneciion with a sand vessel running in opposition to the ' one exploded. At Margate, on Tuesday, John Slate, a chief engineer at Hammersmith, drank a quantity of cyanide of potassium, and also gave some to a man and child. They did not take sufficient to harm them but Slate died in two hours. He was married, and was about to return to London with his wife. It is stated that during the course of Monday the Premier received about 100 telegrams and messages from various parts of the country, forwarded by Liberal clubs and associa- tions, calling upon the Government not to yield to the Lords' amendments to the Irish Land Bill. It is estimated in the _Aquarium Gazette that our wheat

crop this year will not yield what we call an average crop. Barley is largely over average, oats are disappointing, beans and peas are better than at one time they promised to be, and that too may be said of our green crops. Hay is one of the shortest crops ever known. A Berlin correspondent states that Jew-baiting still continues in Germany. Disturbances took place in Stettin on Monday night, where a demonstration was made against the Jews, though the police interfered in time to prevent damage to property and arrested forty of the par- ticipants. A marriage with a deceased wife's sister lately took place at Neuchatel. The remarkable feature of the ceremony was that the officiating clergy included two ex-Chairman of the Congregational Union, the Rev. Dr. Stoughton and the Rev. J. C. Harrison. Mr. Colman, M. P., was also present. The total receipts into the Exchequer from the let of April to August 13th were £28,658,000, ygainst £28,418,000 last yea'; customs, £6,736,000, against £6,614,000 ; excise, £8,772,000, against £9,217,000' stamps, £4,513,000, against £4,386,000; post-office, £2,512,000, against £2,091,000. The balance in the Bank of England on Saturday last was £844,299; Bank of Ireland, £801,685. AFGHAN WAR ESTIMATES.—An estimate was issued on Tuesday for £500,000 as an instalment of the grant in aid of the Afghan war. A note states that the Imperial grant will amount altogether to £5,000,000, of which part will be met by the remission of a debt of £2,000,000 incurred by the Indian Government in 1879, and the remainder will consist of six annual payments of £500,000 each. Two burglars were caught at Sheffield on Tuesday morn- ing under remarkable circumstances. They had made their way into a house in the suburbs by opening a window. They I then unfastened a door, and a policeman passing by soon looked in. " It's all right," said they, and closed the door. The policeman, however, had a suspicion that all was not right, and he insisted upon entering. It was then found that they were burglars. The agricultural returns issued on Monday by the Board of Trade show that the extent of land under wheat in Great Britain, as compared with 1880, has decreased by 3.6 per cent and barley 1 per cent, while that under oats has in- creased 37 and potatoes by 5.2 per cent. The number of sheep and lambs in Great Britain has diminished by 71 per cent, and that of pigs 2.4 per cent, that of cattle remaining almost stationary. A DOONLE EVENT.—Two gentlemen were fishing a few days ago in a lake at Llantrissant, when one hooked a pike weighing over two pounds. Before the fish could be landed it WAS swallowed, hook and all, by an enormous creature of its own species, and both were safely landed. As soon as the big pike found himself out of the water he opened his capacious mouth with a gasp, and the smaller fish shot out of his gills a distance of several yards. The pike whose voracity thus hastened his untimely death weighed 181 b. At the half-yearly meeting of the Midland Railway Com- pany, held on Tuesday at Derby, the chairman (Mr. W. Thompson) stated that the number of first-class passengers I carried during the half-year had diminished by 15,138, the receipts being £8,066 less, while the third-clam passengers had increased 214,341 and the receipts £21,028, the total in- come from coaching traffic having increased £15,955. The receipts from merchandise showed a falling-off of £37,986. A dividend was declared on the ordinary stock of the com- pany at the rate of 51 per cent, per annum. Sir Walter Nugent, Bart., Was placed on trial in Dublin on Saturday on the charge of having forged a bill of exchange for £1,600, and thereby defrauded the Royal Bank of Ire- land. The case was remarkable by reasons of the defence— that Lady Nugent was the delinquent, and that Sir Walter was perfectly innocent in the matter. The jury consulted for three-quarters of an hour without coming to a verdict, and they were then discharged. The defendant was admitted to bail till the next commission. . A BISHOP ON THE SALE OF Ltvpsas.—The Bishop of Bangor, in the course of his triennial charge on Monday, said he could not disguise his feelings of shame and indig- nation at the manner in which lay ecclesiastical patronage was exercised. Most unfit and incompetent men were pre- ferred for livings owing to political sympathy or family ties, and when inducted they alienated Churchmen, owing to their indifference and negligence. He hoped the time would come when the parishioners would at least have a negative voice in the selection of the man to whom their spiritual welfare was entrusted. The advertisements of sales of livings in ecclesiastical journals were scandalous. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.—Lord Lymington intends next session to call attention in the House of Commons to the condition of friendly societies, especially of those which are unregistered, and move resolutions. A return which was moved for by Lord Lymington and obtained early in the session gives the number of persons who were in the work- house on March 31, and who had belonged to friendly societies which had broken. This displays the evils of some of the small village clubs, almost all of which are insolvent, and whose condition acts as the strongest incentive against thrift. This return, it is hoped, will shortly be published.— Daily News. LOST AND MISSING IN LONDON.—Lost and missing per- sons are on the increase in the metropolis. The commis- sioner of police, in his report for 1880 (just issued), states that the total for thy year was 10,860 children under ten years, and 3,338 adults, being 2,350 more than in 1879. Out of the number, 6,509 children and 655 adults were found by the police; 4,336 children and 2,484 adults were found by their friends or returned home; 84 adults committed suicide, and one is reported "drowned." This leaves 15 children and 114 adults who have never been found. In a note to the statistics, the commissioners state that "many missing persons are found by friends and no communication made to the police." He also ventures the opinion that "the disappearance of adults is almost invariably voluntary, and temporary only." Still many people will continue to think it very distressing that 129 persons, 15 of them being child- ren, should suddenly disappear in the metropolis, and be altogether lost, despite the most anxious and persevering in- quiries of their friends. THE PRESIDENT OF THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE ON METRODISM.—Dr. Osborn, president of the Wesleyan Con- ference, was entertained by the Wesleyan Methodists of Devosport on Monday. It reply to addresses of welcome, he complained of the charge laid against Methodists that they indulged in jargon, that they were not friendly to culture, that they were behind the age, and that the increas- ing wealth of the people would prove the destruction of the Methodist Connexion. These assertions he dealt with seriatutn, urging that the language used by the ministry was educational English, and that they were not opposed to culture; that whilst fashions came and went, and difficulties' arose in the Church respecting vestments,Methodisrn enjoyed perfect liberty of dress, and had no need of casting about to seek means of avoiding regulation. He maintained that Methodism was in advance of the age, and that its creed was more complete than that of most other sects; and urged that sanctified riches in the Connexion would do what sanc- tified poverty could never do. The future of Methodism he looked forward to with the greatest possible assurance of its prosperity and success. A CRUEL DECEPTION.—A young Irish peasant girl, named Catherine Hodge, was charged at the Liverpool Police Court, on Wednesday, with travelling from New York to Liverpool in the Inman steamer," City of Berlin," without having paid her fare. In reply to the charge, the accused said she made the acquaintance of a young man while she was living in New York, and on leaping that she was desirous of returning to her parents in Ireland, he pro- mised to accompany her and marry her on her arrival in the old country. He went with her on board the steamer, but when the hour of departure arrived she could not find him, and thus, without money or friends, she was obliged to go with the steamer. She further informed the magistrates that she had no intention of going by the ship if she had not been misled by the young man.—Mr. Mansfield. the demo-, r•Tperz.iry m 1;(1 he , , to ~ L ..ty iyo Ia lie

A police-court is a very accommodating place to transact business in. If you haven't the money to pay cash, the judge generally gives you time. A youth was heard to remark to a jolly and fat Tentonian, 1 as the circus pageant passed the city hall this morning: "Haven't I seen you before? Your face looks familiar." 1" Is dot so ?" said Hans. "When you get so old as me your face will look familiar, too."

A citizen went into a Norwich hardware store the other day and inquired," How much do you ask for a bathtub for a child ?" "Three dollars and seventy-five cents," was the reply. " W-h.e-w !" whistled the customer, "Guess we'll have to keep on washing the baby in the coal-scuttle till prices come down." A GOOD DRATJGHT ANIMAL—As two young men were passing a farmhouse they saw the farmer trying to harness a mule, and, thinking to quiz him, one of them gravely asked, "Will that creature draw ?" to which the farmer curtly responded, "Of course he will. He will draw the attention of every fool that passes along the road."

In a primary school, not very long ago;the teacher under- took to convey to her pupils an idea as to the use of the hyphen. She wrote on the black-board, "Bird's-nest." and pointing to the hyphen asked the school, "What is that for ?" After a short pause, a young son of the Emerald Isle piped out—" Plaze, ma'am, for the bird to roosht on !" _ . _ _

The cashier of a French bank enters the private office of the president, nervous and agitated. "Sir," he says, "I have something on my mind which I feel myself compelled to disclose to you, though for months I have striven to con- ceal it." The president turns pale. "The fact is, I—l love your daughter!" The president breathes more freely. "Ah, you, love my daughter! Do you ever make any errors in your books or in counting your cash—find yourself ab- stracted, eh?" "Never, sir !"—with pride. "Then, sir, I must decline to encourage your suit. You are not really in , love."

THE BARLEY AND WHEAT HARVEST.—As the harvest progresses, and the grain crops mature, and become ready to fall before the reaping machine, it becomes evident that this is a barley • more than a wheat year, the fields of the former being almost everywhere of uniform high character, good in quality, no less than in bulk of produce; while those of the latter are, as a rule, so difficult in the latter characteristic that, despite the excellent kern which was produced by the weather in July, the yields in a large num- ber of districts are expected to be under an average, and whether the total crop throughout the country will come to an average seems a matter of doubt. That it is an all- prevailing characteristic of the present season in barley being much better than wheat, Is distinctly proved by the appearance of Mr. Prout'a crops at Sawbridgeworth, which, although far heavier aid better than the crops surrounding, and a very large proportion of other districts' certainly are distinctly marked in the superiority of his barley fields over those of the chief cereal. Mr. Lawes remarked last year that his experimental plots, where wheat had been grown after wheat, exhibited in 1879 almost identical results to those realised generally throughout the kingdom. Mr. Prout's peculiar system of management in a similar way has not wholly overcome the natural influences of the sea- son. His wheat crops are good, and will perhaps average from 4 to 4i quarters per acre; but his barley is far better, and while the yield of the latter appears to indicate all over his farm between 5 and 6 quarters to the acre, the quality is very first•class.—Farmers' Chronicle.

MEASUREMENT OF INTENSITY OF SOUND WITH THE MI• CROPHONE.—It would appear from recent experiments by Herr Oberbeck described in the Annalen der Physik, that the microphone is a very delicate means of measuring the intensity of sound. The use of it is based on the fact that the elec- tric resistance of the small carbon contacts increases during the sound excitation, and this increase (in a suitably ad- justed microphone) is a measure of the intensity of sound. The microphone Herr Oberbeck uses is of the hammer and anvil type. It is placed in one branch of what is well known as a Wheatstone's bridge, which receives the current of a thermopile. An equal resistance being inserted in the other branch, the mirror galvanometer of the bridge is at rest. When a sound occurs, however, the balance is dis- turbed through increase of the microphone's resistance, and the galvanometer is deflected accordingly. The instrument does not act with all sounds—thus, the sound produced by the fall of a lead ball on a piece of slate did not affect it; but the same ball falling on a piece of wood gave a sound which did. The tones of a piano gave a great variety of effects, according to the note and the way it was struck. With less force, the deflection as less. The pizzicato tones of a violin and the tones of a dosed wooden pipe gave simi- lar effects. The human voice at a moderate distance gave con- siderable action, and very different deflections were got with the vowels spoken strongly in the same tone. Herr Ober- beck used the apparatus to investigate the relation between intensity of a Boutin and the energy expended in producing it. Dropping various balls on a wooden plate from various heights, he proved that the intensity varies much more slowly than the height (proportionally to about the square root) ; it is, however, within certain limits proportional to the weight. Some curious effects were got with sounding pipes, the pitch of which was altered by means of a piston, and their intensity by varying the blast. In the caseof certain tones, an increase of blast (to nearly double) gave a considerable increase of deflection in the galvaaometer, while, ' with other tones the same increase gave no st,-;11 effect, but even sometimes a diminution. LETTER FROM NEW ZEALAND.

I may, I think, assume that your readers are not so deeply and painfully engrossed in the grave events taking place in the Sister Isle, as to feel no interest in the political affairs of a young but lusty colony like New Zealand. I confess that colonial political strife sometimes looks very small, and would truly be almost insignificant but for the fact that it is waged over the question, "What shall be the foundations of a great future empire." I desire, without party bias or enthusiasm (for I feel neither), but with the intention of acknowledging whatever appears wise and good in either Party, to give you my first impressions upon Colonial Poli- tics.

One of the most prominent figures on the political stage of this colony has been, and still is, that of the veteran Sir George Grey. Few men have seen so much of official ser- vice, and few men have retained at threescore years and ten so much physical energy, so much elasticity of spirit and enterprise, or so lively an interest in all human affairs. Mili- tary duty in early manhood, explorations in Australia, the responsibilities of Governorship in South Australia at the Cape of Good Hope, and in New Zealand, the labour of book- writing and of speech-making in and out of office, have exhausted neither the splendid constitution nor the mental vivacity and vigour inherited from his Irish ancestry. Like every man who has made himself a political power, Sir George has friends and foes equally ardent and faithful. He is, on the one hand, stigmatised as an unpractical dreamer who trades upon imaginary woes, whilst for real ones he is incapable of providing any remedy, and whose supreme object is official power and historical fame.SirGeorge's friends, whilst not agreeing with all his proposals, maintain that he is a man of noble and patriotic aims that he is deeply. _

imbued with sympathy for the masses, and seeks the genirk welfare by securing equal political rights and an equal share in material prosperity; that for these ends he advocates the abolition of the Legislative Council and the election of the Colonial Governor by the voice of the people, so that whilst still remaining part and parcel of the British Empire, New Zealand would ipso facto become a Republic. Moreover, it is claimed that the chief liberal measures enjoyed by the Colony—such as a democratic suffrage, vote by ballot, and triennial parliaments—are due to Sir George Grey. In short, Sir George is regarded as the Colonial "Gladstone," and his name is the sign and signal for party conflict; " Greyites " and "anti-Greyites " charging each other with a bitter enthusiasm worthy of those good old English con- flicts before the ballot came and put a quietus upon them all. Sir George recently emerged from his island retreat, and has delivered a succession of speeches (one of which I had the pleasure of hearing), vigorously assailing what he regards as the evils of the present political position. In particular Sir George denounced the system which gives (in all county affairs) to a man of wealth 45 votes, and to a poor ' man only one, which lays a property tax upon even the im- provements in land, yet allows absentee landholders to go scot free; which permits vast estates to be owned, as in the United Kingdom, by a few individuals; which offers no check to Chinese immigration; and by which the govern- mental affairs of the Colony are confined to a few governing families, a political clique bound to conserve each others' in. ; in a word, Sir George broadly declares that the present Government has converted one of the best into one of the worst of constitutions. Like a true Irishman, Sir George is unable to renress his national sympathies, and proposes that the House of Representatives should discuss and pass a resolution upon the situation in Ireland, to be for- warded to the Home Government. In accord with outside criticism in general, Sir George deprecates violence, and in- sists upon peasant proprietorship as the best and the essen- tial remedy for Irish grievances. Following Sir George Grey, the Premier, Mr. Hall has delivered a practical and in some respects a satisfactory reply. The most important part of Mr. Hall's speech refers to the Legislative Council. Mr. Hall combats Sir George's proposal to abolish the Council by showing that it had never resisted any measure upon which public opinion was thoroughly decided, and that it had repeatedly done good service by saving the Colony from dangerous proposals which had never been renewed, such for instance as those for wholesale provincial borrowing, and for giving Maoris greater electoral privileges than Europeans. Moreover, it is never wise, Mr. Hall justly argues, to give any body of men unrestricted power as Sir George Grey's plan involves. Mr. Hall proposes, therefore, not to abolish but to reform the Upper Chamber. At present the Council consists of members nominated for life by the Governor-General, and it is possible, Mr. Hall admits, fora headstrong Minister and a pliant Government so to increase the number of the mem- bers of the Council as to destroy its moderating in- fluence at a time when most needed. Mr. Hall, there- fore, proposes that the Council should be one-half that of the House of Representatives, and that whenever a vacancy occurs it should be filled up by the vote of the House; also, that if upon any measure there should be a prolonged difference of opinion, the two Chambers should sit as one and vote decisively upon it. This appears an important and a Constitutional reform. At present the Council is in no degree representative; by the proposed change it would be so at least indirectly, and would also embrace a wider class, including men who had rendered im- portant service to the country and others eminent for talent and character. En passant, Mr. Hall rebuts the charges made by Mr. Bradlaugh in re the Maori prisoners as false and impertinent, and boldly avows that as the burden and responsibilities of government have been thrown upon the Colony, no outside interference will be tolerated. I may add that the,last batch of the native prisoners was liberated a few days ago, so that Mr. Bradlaugh will no longer have a Maori grievance to air in the House of Commons. Rumour has it that the Maori clients have paid their advo- cate a handsome fee in the form of a gift of goodly land; but this must be received cum grano salis. The last session of the present Parliament opened on the 7th inst. with an address from the Governor-General in lien of Queen's Speech, but similar in character. The Govern- ment and the colony are congratulated upon the present state of affairs; commercial depression is passing away, population rapidly increasing, the Maori difficulty on the West Coast amicably settled, revenue returns are satisfac- tory, thanks to rigid economy and to judicious taxation; the address is, in fact, self-complacent and sanguine. Among various measures to be introduced during the session besides that relating to the Legislative Council, are bills for the regulation and restriction of Chinese immigration, a new licensing bill, and also a bill for the redistribution of seats. This last will probably be hotly contested, as it pro- poses to abolish a few secure seats on both sides of the House. It is notable that instead of adopting the advice of that astute financier, Sir Julius Vagel, and launching into a new course of extravagant expenditure by constructing new railways and subsidising immigration, the Government cautiously promises to assist companies prepared to con- struct main lines, and leaves the progress of immigration to the influence of natural causes. Now, let me add a few items not directly political. Dur- ing the month of April a census was taken of the whole Colony, the returns of which have not yet been published save for one or two districts. It is expected that the total population will be over half a million. In the provincial district of Auckland there has been an increase since 1878, when the census was last taken, of 26,329. The numbers, According to the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, are as follow :-1878, 118,671; 1881, 145,000, including 40,000 natives. The population of the city of Auckland, including its suburbs, has increased since 1878 about 13,000, and is said to number between thirty-nine and forty thousand. The exports of this province show an increase upon the year of £260,000. The question of a direct Mail:Service between this Colony land England is exciting considerable attention here; its establishment is but a question of time, and must come with, if not before, the opening of the Panama Canal. But which first shall be the Colonial terminus? Dunedin has Rut in the first claim, and urges the Government to subsi- dise the Union S.S. Co. ; but it is objected that Dunedin has no suitable harbour and not sufficient depth of-water for large steamers. Auckland insists upon her natural advant- ages of geographical position of capacious harbour and deep waters, and the near prospect of a new and spacious dock, capable of taking the largest vessels. To improve the harbour Dunedin has just floated a loan of £lOO,OOO, and will doubtless press her claim with Scotch pertinacity, but the probability is that the position of Auckland will give her the palm. I have more than once referred to the Te Puke settlement it is now made into a township, in connection with which I give in the following discussion, which took place at the last meeting of the Tauranga County Council. The chair- man said he had been asked by one of the Te Puke settlers to obtain the Council's sanction to having the four roads in Te Puke named as follows :—No. 1, Spencer-road; No. 2, Huxley-road; No. 3, Darwen-road ' • No. 4, Tyndall-road. Mr. Brown: Darwin! That's the missing link man (Laughter). Captain Turner (to Mr. Brown) : The road beetween your place and Darwen-road is called the "Missing Link-road." (Laughter). Mr. Wrigley: I should have thought they would have called the road after the name of the vessel they came out in, the " Lady Jocelyn." Captain Turner: There is " Jocelyn-street in Stewart's Town." Mr. Brown: Is that " Spencer " the Rev. Mr. Spencer, of Maketn ? (Laughter). Chairman: Oh, no! It is Herbert Spencer the great scient- ist—.(laughter). A Member: It will do for both of them. (Laughter). On the motion of Mr. Wrigley, seconded by Mr. Brown, the required permission was granted. I close with a weather note' This winter month has been so far an alternation of blustary wet days, and remarkably fine ones. Sunday, the 12th for instance was bright and lovely as a May day, the atmosphere clear and exhilirating, and the prospect from the summit of Mt, meno,sttoyhiu with my family, I took my afternoons ou walk beauti- ful; but the days are short and ere I could descend, the golden sun had set • the west glowed with living amber, the eastern horizon reflected masses of purple and green; the air grew cooler and the dark green foliage of the blue- gum tree (the famed Encalyytns, and one .of the most common here) grew darker, whilst slowly and m confusion rose the which inclynseereißoluYslnlyosopnr,saind vaacrinosrseshisetringelhue som, bre shadow short hour totally eclipsed her beauty. f t res and in one Iho • Pe in my next letter to send you a brief account of the Maoris or natives of New Zealand. EDWIN Cox. Auckland, June 20th, 1881.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMEN T.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMEN T.
HOUSE OF LORDS.,--MoNnAy.

ECCLFSTASTICAL SUBSIDIES.—LOrd STANLEY of ALDERLEY asked the Colonial Secret lry a question respecting eccle- siastical sul,idics in Ceylon, and the Earl of KIMBERLEY replied that, looking at the number of religions in Ceylon and the influence of some of them, the Government had corne to the conclusion eget the subsidy granted to the 10,00 t) Anglicans and 5,000 Presbyterians in the island was not to be justified. The endowments being indefensible in Principle and opposed to the wishes of the majority of the inhabitants, it had seemed to him desirable that they should be put an end to. TUNISIAN AFFAIRS—The Earl of DUNRAVEN called attention to the state of affairs in Tunis, and moved "That in the opinion of this House any interference with the integrity of the Ottoman Empire in North Africa is likely to prove dangerous to the peace of Europe." His Lordship expressed a hope that the Government would now give the House the explanation they promised on a former occasion. —Earl GRANVILLE, in the course of a reply in which he vindicated the conduct of the Government, said he could not deny that difficulties might arise with regard to the state of affairs in Tunis, but at present they had not arisen, and the Government were not aware that our treaty rights had been broken. The motion was eventually withdrawn. Their lordships at 25 minutes to eight o'clock adjourned to half- past 11 o'clock, when several peers returned. It was, how- ever, 25 minutes to 3 o'clock before the Land Law (Ireland) Bill was again received from the Commons. Their further amendments were ordered to be considered on Tuesday.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

THE LAND BILL.—CONSIDERATION OF THE LORDS' AMENDTIEN'TS.—Both sides of the House were well-filled, and the galleries, especially the Peers', were crowded to overflowing, and Mr. Gladstone, who arrived towards the close of "question time," was loudly cheered from the benches below the gangway on his own side. Before the Orders of the Day were reached, Mr. MACDONALD, amid much laughter and ironical cheers, asked whether it would be competent for any Member to save the House further trouble by moving the rejection of the Lords' amendments en masse.—The SPEAKER replied:that, of course, any Mem- ber could move that the amendments be considered this day three months; but he added that, if successful, it would lead to the loss of the bill.—Mr. GLADSTONE having ' moved that the reasons for the Lords' amendments be con- sidered, Mr. PARNELL urged that a statement should be I made with regard to them—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that it would be unsatisfactory if he were to make a selection of 'what he considered the most material a mendments ; he therefore proposed to take them seriatim, and he asked the House to follow patiently in a task which was now•one of diminished scope and labour.—Mr. Dan-FYN expressed a hope that no concessions on material points would be made to an irresponsible body, for if they were the Goverrment would not continue to receive the support which had hitherto been accorded to them.—Mr. HEALY declared that the course taken by the Government inspired distrust, and the Irish members.saw in it only the beginning of a policy of surrender—Mr GLADSTONE then stated that the amend- ments had been gone through and considered on their merits, and " compromise " was a word he should not wish to have applied to their proceedings upon this bill. He thought the House, having trusted them so far, would be inclined to trust them to the end, and would not refuse to enter on the detailed consideration of the subject. The motion of the right hon. gentleman was then agreed to, and the House proceeded to consider the Lords' amendments and reasons, each of which that touched the principle of the bill was rejected. • HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. _ _

-- -- Lord Redesdale, in the absence of the Lord Chancellor, took his seat on the woolsack at five o'clock. The Marquis of Bath presented a petition praying for the release from Lancaster gaol of the Rev. S. F. Green, rector of Miles Platting. The Commons' amendments to the University of Scotland Registration Bill were agreed to. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—THE MEASURE PASSED.

• The Marquis of SALISBURY made a statement on the motion for the consideration of the Commons' amendments to the Lords' last amendments, explaining the motives of his party in their conduct with respect to the Land Bill. The noble Marquis contended that they were directed by a consistent principle. His opinions were unaltered as to the injustice in many cases of the provisions of the bill, but he was not prepared to wreck it, and his party would not take any action which would return the bill to the House of Commons. He urged that their Lordships had only removed excrescences and guarded against dangerous pro- visions, and said for the principle of the bill and the results it might produce the Government alone would lie respon- sible, and not the House of Lords. He parted with the bill with the hope that it might be a great benefit to the Irish tenants, and not much harm to the landlords.—The Mar- quis of Lansdowne withdrew the amendment touching leases which stood in his name.—Lord CARLINGFORD ex- pressed an opinion that if the bill passed in the form it had now been returned by the Commons not one of the essential principles it contained would be sacrificed, and it would not have failed as far as Parliament was concerned to attain the objects it had in view. He thought it had been distinctly improved by the action of the majorities of the two Houses of Parliament. Speaking as a landlord, he believed the bill would do that class essential good by placing the rights of property, which were not at this moment in Ireland in a satisfactory condition, upon a firmer and a safer founda- tion—Earl GRANVILLE remarked that the Government felt that the effect of this bill would be to prevent agitation, but if any should unfortunately continue they would not relax in vigour and energy in maintaining the majesty of the law. —The amendments having been agreed to without opposi- tion, Lord SALISBURY confirmed the Prime Minister's state- ment of the previous evening that there had been no arrangement in the matter between the two political parties. —The bill then passed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIJESDAY. THE ALKALI Acv.—Mr. Donsox gave an assurance that I no time should be lost in bringing the Alkali Act into opera- tion. .

THE JUDICATURE AMENDMENT BILL.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL stated that it was absolutely necessary to pass the Supreme Court of Judicature Bill in some shape or other. The clause dealing with patronage had been struck out, and the question of circuits was under the consideration of the HOME SECRETARY. The decision of the Lord Chancellor on this point would be ascertained._

_ THE DECORATION OF THE HOUSES OF PARLIAMRNT.— There was a brief debate on the long interruption of the decorations in the central hall of the Houses of Parliament, in the course of which it was explained that the delay was chiefly attributable to the present unsatisfactory state of mosaic art. THE NAVY ESTIMATES.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates.—Mr. TREVELYAN made an interesting statement on the condition of our navy. The prevailing opinion was, he said, in favour of small ships, and upon that policy the Admiralty was proceeding. It was important in these days of torpedoes and steam rams that we should not hive too many of our eggs in one basket, and the Admiralty was further influenced by the difficulty in getting officers to undertake the responsibility of working the gigantic machinery of large ships. He added that at the present moment we might be said tobe ahead of all other navies in the character of the guns mounted in our sea- going ships, and that there was not the slightest cause for alarm in that respect. He admitted that the building of war ships was below the mark, but stated that in 1881, for the first time for four years, the performances of the Admiralty had exceeded its promises. 7,948 tons of ironclad ships were promised, and 9,325 were actually completed by the year's end. The Admiralty bad undertaken this year to build 10,816.t0n5. Mr. Trevelyan also explained, with re- gard to the heaviest class of iron ships, that it had been determined, instead of one vessel of 14,000 tons, to lay down two vessels of 9,000 each ; and instead of one vessel costing £1,000,000, it had been arranged to lay down two vessels at a little over £500,000 each. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

- -- THE WORRING OF THE COERCION ACT.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. BIGGAR called attention to the action of the Irish Executive in the admini- stration of the Protection AA. He contended that a great number of peaceable and respectable persons were arrested i under the Act who did not at all come within the description of the classes against whom the Government, when the Act I was before tne House, said that it was solely intended to be ' used. Even if they had been guilty of the charges of which the Government only suspected them, they could easily have been dealt with by the ordinary law, but, be argued, ' the Government had used the Act for political intrposes to get rid of prominent members of the Land League.—Mr. PARNELL submitted a resolution declaring that, in the opinion of the House, the Act had not been administered in accordance with the declarations or the pledges given by Ministers when the assent of the House was being obtained for the suspension of the Constitution of Ireland. He con- tended that the Act had failed for the ostensible purpose for which it was asked; but it had not failed in so far as it had been used for putting down public opinion in Ireland, stop- ping peaceful and constitutional agitation, and establishing a reign of terrorism in the minds of every peaceably- deeisposed. citizen of the country. If trod for any advantage that Government at the com- mencement of the session had proceeded with such a measure of land reform its reception heT wash The m mixedo most stebcardetaubper ieienn different from what the reception f- would have been this bill was likely to be.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL recited some statistics in reply to these observations. i,h very telling gen- tleman declared that of the 192 imprisoned e learned under the Act, 31 were arrested on reasonable suspicions for shooting at persons, and inciting others to murder; murder der.3 and attacking dwelling-houses, and making raids for ar2ms6- for f 1 for intimidation, 5 for treasonable practices, 8 for arson and attempt to set on fire, and inciting others to arson; 7 for ' maiming cattle and inciting others to do so, and 54 for riot and assault and inciting to riot and assault. These figures the Solicitor-General said, left 25 cases to cover all the' other matters affecting threatening notices, and so on.
