LONDON CORRESPONDENCE. The House of Lords played their part in the little comedy of conflict between the two Houses more el umsily than the House of Commons. After the statement Mr. Gladstone made at an early hour on Tuesday morning, confirmed at night by Lord Salisbury, that the Opposition were not in- formed of the course the Government were prepared to take on the various amendments, it is indeed doubtful to what extent the proceedings of Tuesday night in the House of Commons were arranged. But there is no doubt of the per- fect state of preparation in which noble lords came together on Tuesday night to carry out the last scene of the comedy. If there had been any, it would have been removed by an in- cident which took place early in the sitting. ThG peers be- gan to gather punctually at five o'clock, amongst the earliest comers being Earl Granville and the Marquis of Salisbury. The two leaders sat looking at each other across the table for the space of ten minutes, Lord Granville wearing his ac- customed smile, and the Marquis of Salisbury indicating some condition of repressed excitement by the incessant nervous beating of his foot on the floor. Just before the business of the sitting commenced, Earl Granville walked across, and seating himself by the real head of the House, conversed with him for several moments, The Lord Chan- cellor was not present, and Lord Redesdale more or less adequately represented the dignity that should attach to the woolsack. Promptly at the stroke of the quarter, Lord Salisbury approached the table, being received by a cheer from his own side, which was now fairly crowded. A few ladies sat in the galleries, but the season being over, there was no probability of those displays of grace and millinery which marked the earlier stages of the bill in its passage through the Lords. Lord Salisbury made a very graceful and adroit retreat. He showed that wherein the Commons had accepted the Lords' amendments they had improved the bill. He ad- mitted that wherein they had resisted no questions of prin- ciple were touched, nor was it consonant with the position of the Lords to insist upon the amendments affecting prin- ciples, seeing that they had agreed to the second reading of the bill. For his own part and his own side he declared that no opposition would be offered to the Commons' amendments, though he announced with a pleasing return of the truculence of Friday, that if the Duke of Argyll or the Marquis of Lansdowne insisted upon their amendments which had been rejected by the Commons, he should cer- tainly divide with them. All this-Was very adroit. It made out in fact that the amendments moved by the Conserve- tives and rejected by the Commons were not of great im- portance or were for other reasons undesirable; those moved by the ordinary supporters of the Ministry were so excellent and desirable that if their authors desire to move them, Lord Salisbury would support them, the disgrace of retreat was on their heads. The Duke of Argyll was not present, being more pleasingly occupied in the full enjoyment of his honeymoon. The Marquis of Lansdowne was in his place, and announced with great gravity that, whilst he held the same opinion of his amendment, he was not prepared to press it; and so, after a few words from Lord Carlin ford the performers retired, the curtain dropped, and the crowded audience departed, having witnessed the last scene in the long and varied drama of "The Irish Landlord." Whatever may have been the cause of Lord Salisbury's submission, it was complete. To the very last the Tory organs declared that he could hold out upon something. There was an amendment to the seventh clause about which he was very anxious. He was also very solicitous about Lord Lansdowne's amendment. He wanted, at all events, to show that he was not frightened at the House cf Commons. When the hour came, it is true that he very considerately effered Lord Lansdowne his support for one single amendment, knowing very well that Lord Lans- downe would not proceed with it. But for the rest, he simply cried "off." His tone was so subdued and quiet that he bad not even a sneer left in him. He let the bill through without so much as explaining what had caused his change of front. He tried to make out that he was satisfied; but if satisfaction produces such 'a depression of spirit as Lord Salisbury exhibited, and tones the temper of a high-spirited man to the point of utter placidity, Lord Salisbury may pray to be preserved from a disappointment. His depression was not, I am told, caused by what happened at the meeting of the peers. The hundred of his political disciples who met him in Arlington-street were very kindly towards their leader, assumed fully the responsibility with him for the step that had been taken, and were only decided in refusing to go any further. The House of Commons was the scene on Monday night of considerable movement, in consequence of a report, re- garded by many people as accurate, that the President of the United States had succumbed to his wounds. The rumour was circulated by the press with all reserve. A New York Herald cablegram received by the Central News shortly before three disposed of the report as one without founda- tion, but this was received at an hour too late for some papers to make use of. The only justification for the state- ment seems to have been a telegram posted at the Reform Club. The rumour probably owed its origin to the admitted critical condition of the President. There is a widespread belief among Americans in London that the President will succumb to his wounds, his recovery having been too long delayed. Mr. Gladstone's domestics and some members of his family were on Monday the victims of a fright which con- siderably disturbed the usual equanimity of life at No. 10, Downing-street. There arrived at the door a large box ac- companied by a note, which on being opened proved to be from a chimney sweep, who professed to have discovered a new method of removing what he called "soot kinkers." These "kinkers" are pieces of consolidated soot, which defy the usual efforts of the unscientific chimney sweep to re- move them, and lead to smoky chimneys. In order that Mr. Gladstone, to whom the note anti box was addressed, might, have an opportunity of seeing for himself the sort of "obstruction " contained in his flues, the entertaining sweep intimated that in the box would be found a few specimens of "kinkers" removed from Earl Granville's chimneys. The box was opened with trepidation oy the servants, who re- garded the whole affair as a Fenian device for leading them unconsciously into peril. The chest contained a number of pieces of black substance, which were promptly subjected to copious douches of cold water to destroy any latent mischief which might be lurking in them, and the whole was removed by a couple of policemen. Upon inquiry, the sweep turned ont to be all he described himself. On learning what had been done with his samples of " kinkers," he said he had thought Mr. Gladstone was "not the kinder bloke to do a thing like that to a fellow-creetur." The collapse over the Irish Land Bill is complete. If it were not for the fight over the Irish estimates, there would be nothing to talk about in Parliament or out of it except the holidays; and the holidays have already been 90 fully discussed that there is little to say about them. In political circles the only question is as to whether Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury has surrendered over the dispute between the Commons and the Lords, and even that excites but a languid interest. To make it appear that the surrender is Mr. Gladstone's, most circumstantial, though confessedly imaginary, descriptions of interviews between the leaders are putlished. One account tells us how Lord Cairns and Granville made up the quarrel. As a matter of fact, Lord Cairns did not see Lord Granville. Another story tells how Mr. Gibson got over Sir Farrar Herschell. As a matter of the plainest truth, Sir Farrar Herschell had no commission to surrender anything, and did not explain to Mr. Gibson what the Government intended to do on Monday night. Mr. Gladstone has said most unequivocally that there had been no bargain, nothing ot the nature of a compromise, no ar- rangement which was prefigured. That settles the question. The Tory whips are indignant at the persistent rumours to the contrary. Not only was there no bargain, but the Op- position leaders did not knew what the Government intended to do nor the Government what the Opposition leaders in- tended to do. Yet we shall probably hear quoted as hietory in the future what Lord Cairns said to Lord Gran ville, and what Sir Farrar Herschell offered Mr. Gibson. One effect of "the crisis" is surprising even to Radicals, and rather alarming to more sober•minded constitutional minds. It has shown that the House of Lords has lost its hold over the minds of the democracy. It is so in London no doubt. There was a prevalent idea that as compared with the Commons the hereditary branch of the Legislature bad rather risen in popular regard. Its business-like habits, the amount of statesmanship and oratory stored among its members, the fact that Parnellism had "deteriorated and even degraded" the elected chamber, the fear lest democracy should go too fast—all these had been quoted as a proof of the new hold which the Peers had gained over the hearts of their countrymen. But the contrary has now been mani- fested beyond a doubt. It is very difficult to get from a genuine working man one word in favour of hereditary legislators, after the events of the week. People do not pro- fess to understand the Land Bill, but they regard it as "Gladstone's bill to settle Ireland," and they have been I angry beyond a doubt. Your 'busman tells you that he doesn't see "what them chaps is good for save to make a row." I found the waiters in a Westminster restaurant gathered together on Monday night debating the situation. They were applauding unanimously the suegestion of one of their number, that the best use to which the gilded saloon could be put would be to turn it into a refreshment room for the Lower House ; and this idea was gravely pressed on the ground that it was likely to settle not only the dispute about the Land Bill, but also the vexatious kitchen difficulty. The same spirit is generally manifested in all directions. Of late the idea of abolishing the House of Lords has been uni- versally ridiculed, but the mere manifestation of its power to destroy the legislation of a session has changed the cur- rent of popular feeling, and the opponents of the hereditary chamber have determined forthwith to push on with their agitation.

IHE REV. S. F. GREEN. —The Church of Enoland Working Men's Society have just issued the following peti- tion for Mr. Green's release, which is being very largely signed, by men only. When completed the document will be presented to the Queen, to the Houses of Parliament, and to Mr. Gladstone. "The humble petition of the under- signed shows that the Rev. Sydney Faithorne Green, mourn-. bent of St. John's, Miles Platting, has been imprisoned since March 19, 1881, in the gaol at Lancaster, for refusal to obey the judgment of Lord Penzance in spiritual matters, and that inasmuch as a Royal Commission has been appointed to consider the constitution and working of the very court to which Mr. Green, on conscientious grounds, , declined to render obedience, thus practically recognising the fact that there is some tangible pounds for the objec- tions of the rev, gentleman and, other like-minded clergy- men, we your petitioners humbly pray that Mr. Green may, pending the sitting of the said Commission, at least, be re- leased from custody." The various branches of the Society throughout the country have received instructions from headquarters to convene meetings for the promotion of t.,.e rev. gentleman's release.
STATE OF IRELAND.

T:le contributions through the _Trish Trorb/ to the Lam: Leue for last week are I,6Godollars. Through the Poston (U.S.) Pilot, from July 10th to the 31st, they have Sent 8,842 dollars. Mr. Dillon, M.P., wrote on Saturday, stating that he does not intend being present in Parliament during the present session. He feels unable to undergo much exertion, but will in the course of a fortnight come over to England on a visit to some friends. Several farm labourers who have been getting in hay from same meadow land on a farm in the neighbourhood of Car- rick-on-Shannon, from which a tenant had been recently evicted have received a series of letters threatening them with death if the should continue to work on the land, and fearing that the threat would be carried out, they have given op their work. At Tuesday's meeting of the Land League, Mr. Sexton, M.P., who presided, referred to some criticism offered at a previous meeting on the spending of the funds of the League. He said it was necessary that there should be some secrecy when they had to fight an infuriated class of relentless land- lords and a hostile Government, but the time would come when every penny expended by tbe League would be ac- counted for. He deprecated hasty fault-finding with the well-considered policy of the League, and suggested that any malcontents should bring forward their complaints on the platform of the National Convention a month hence, "when the supreme authority of the Irish people would meet." The Rev. Mr. Rylett said he was afraid the Land Bill would produce a situation which would require the League to take up a more determined position than hereto- fore. They would have to consider whether they would say plainly to the tenants, "Regard this bill as naught, and come to the conclusion yourself what you think is a fair rent after providing for your families."

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDSY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDSY.

MUN ICIPAL CORPORATIONS CONSOLIDATION BILL.—Earl SPENCER introduced a Municipal Corporations Consolida- tion Bill, which will not be proceeded with this Session, but will be circulated and considered during the recess.— The Bill was read a first time.

THE TREATY NEGOCIATIONS.—EarI GRANVILLE mode an announcement respecting the treaty negociations of pre- cisely the same nature as the one made in the House of Commons by Sir Charles Dilke. MR. PARNELL.—In reply to Earl Fortescue, Lord CAR- LINGFORD stated that Mr. Parnell had been on the Commis- sion of the Peace for nearly ten years past, and he was still on the Commission. Before their Lordships adjourned they had a brief discus- sion as to the details of future legislation on the subject of the maintenance of highways. HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY. THE FRENCH TARIFF—Sir CHARLES DILKE made an important statement respecting the state of the negotiations for a renewal of the commercial treaty with France. The right hon, baronet said that some time ago the French Go- vernment proposed that the negotiations should be resumed at Paris, on the 22nd instant. After examining certain of the French proposals for the duties on iron and on cotton and woollen yarns and goods, Her Majesty's Government considered that, although still unsatisfactory, they offered a basis for further discussion. Consent was there- fore given to the reassembling of the Commission, on the condition that the existing treaty was prolonged for three months in order to give ample time for the examina- tion of the latest proposals. The French Government de- clined to accede to this prolongation, and Her Majesty's Government consequently did not feel justified in accepting the invitation for the Commission to reassemble. NEW WRIT.—A new writ was ordered to be issued, amidst cheers, for the election of a member for the borough of Leeds. in the room of Mr. Herbert John Gladstone, now a Junior Lord of the Treasury. THE COERCION Acs.—ln the resumed demte upon the administration of the Coercion Acts, Mr. FORSTER, in a long speech, defended the action of the Irish Executive. He said the enormous majority of the arrests had been made on the ground of intimidation, and he maintained that they proved that intimidation existed ; that men were afraid to pursue their daily business; that witnesses could not be got to give evidence and juries to convict; and that the ex- ceptional legislation desired was the only means of pre- venting the unwritten law taking the place of the written. He denied that the Act had been made use of for putting down constitutional or legal agitation. It had not been, as alleged, used against a leader of the Land League because he was a leader. The greater number of those arrested were engaged in carrying out a system of organised intimidation. The question was—Could they well safely let these men go free? He was sorry to say that, with a regard to the safety of the country, he believed they could not. With regard to the demand for the release of the prisoners under the Act, Mr. Forster referred to the threat of continued agitation on the part of Irish members, and said that before opening the prison door the Government must see wbat power Mr. Healy and those who acted with him possessed to keep up the intimidation.—A number of Irish members joined in the appeal for an amnesty.—Mr. WairroN contributed to the debate a personal description of Mr. Forster, whom he de- scribed as "ever green and hopeful," and also as the wrong man in the wrong place.—The O'GORMAN MAHON ren- dered every tribute to the honesty of,Mr. Forster, but said he was the dupe of a clique in Dublin Castle.—The PRIME MINISTER complimented The O'Gorman Mahon for the geniality of his utterances, which he said, bore no trace of the spirit of mingled suspicion, defiance, and hostility towards the people of England and Scotland which was evinced by a small portion of the re- presentatives of Ireland. The right hon. gentleman then entered into an eloquent and feeling defence of the conduct of the Government in what was "a sacred," although "an odious duty." On a division, Mr. Parnell's motion was de- feated by a vote of 83, against 30.

div.head: PROPOSALS FOR THE REVISED EDUCATION CODE.
div.p: PROPOSALS FOR THE REVISED EDUCATION CODE.

Papers were issued on Tuesday showing the proposals made by Mr. Mundella for a revision of the Educational Code. In the first place, it is proposed to adopt the average attendance in each school as the basis of the grants which have hitherto been made on account of individual scholars —whether infants (under seven) or children above seven, presented for examination in reading, writing, and arith- metic. Secondly, 250 attendances will be no longer required as a condition of examination, but all scholars who have been on the register for six months will have to be presented to the inspector. The rate at which each item of the grant will be assessed cannot yet be stated, but it is desirable that for the present attention should be directed to the educa- tional rather than to the financial effects of the proposals. The full grant will be paid if singing is satisfactorily taught from notes, or according to the tonic sol-fa system. Sewing is to be compulsory for all girls and for boys below seven years of age. Under the heading of special merit the in- spector shall have regard to the organisation of discipline, the employment of intelligent methods of instruction, and the general quality of the work in each school, and have power to recommend an additional grant on the average attendance. When the attendance in an infants' school amounts to 40, a separate adult teacher is to be employed. With regard to the arrangements for class schools, the stan- dard in the lower division is to be I. to IV., in the upper divisions V, and upwards. Domestic economy is no longer to be required tabs taken up by girls ass condition of their being examined in specific subjects. Grants will no longer be confined to reading, writing, and arithmetic, but will be made for proficiency in class subjects. Not more than three pupil teachers will be allowed in any school or department, and stipendiary monitors will no longer be recognised. In calculating the staff of a school, an assistant teacher will count as sufficient for 60 scholars, instead of SO as hereto- fore. Certificates to assistant teachers will no longer be given without examination under 59 of the Code. No cer- tificate is to be cancelled, suspended, or reduced until the Department has informed the teacher of the charges against him, and has given him an opportunity of explanation. Honour certificates for the payment of the fees of children who hold such certificates will be discontinued.
—.— Colton tells us what once in a while applies to the matri- monial speculations of modern times, that "Marriage is a banquet where the grace is sometimes better than the feast." '

div.head: WIFE 111URDER7AT SALE.
div.p: WIFE 111URDER7AT SALE.

At Sale, on Saturday, a man named James Edwards mur- dered his wife with a clasp knife. Edwards, who is 42 years of age, lived with his wife (who was two years his junior), his two sons, youths, and a baby, in a cottage on the highway at Sale, where he carried on the business of greengrocer. Edwards went home between three and four o'clock, and on entering the house he said to his wife, "Let us be comfortable, and part comfortably," referring to a rumour which he had heard that she was about to leave him. One of the sons went up stairs, leaving Edwards and his wife together in the kitchen. He heard shrieks almost immediately, and on going into the kitchen he saw his father standing in the middle of the room with a blood- stained knife in his hand. It seems that as soon as the son left the room Edwards and his wife had some words, and the man rashed at the woman, and before she could realise what he was about he had buried the blade of a new clasp- knife under her left ear, severing the jugular vein. The poor woman tried to defend herself, but only succeeded in diverting the direction of her husband's blows. Her left arm was seriously injured, her left cheek was gashed, and she received four other wounds about the head and body. Frightfully injured as she was, she managed to stagger into the next house, and having exclaimed "Oh, oh," she sank into the arms of a Mrs. Moore, by whom she was supported until her death, which took place within half an hour after she received the terrible injuries. When apprehended Edwards offered no resistance, and on being charged at the Police station with cutting his wife's throat, he said "Eh, I have done it." The prisoner had bought the knife the same afternoon at a Mrs. Hirst's, in School-road, Sale. The de- ceased was a fine, strong woman, whilst her husband is a man of small stature. Some four years ago Edwards was employed at the Liverpool-road (Manchester) goods ware- house, where he met with an accident, having some of his ribs fractured. He received from the railway company £2OO, and of this sum £9O is still in the bank. Jealousy is stated to be the cause of the crime, Edwards having heard that his wife was about to 20 to Australia with another man. Edwards was brought up at the Sale Petty Sessions, on Monday, and committed for trial to the Chester Assizes on the capital charge. The inquest on the body of Mrs. Edwards was held later on in the day, when a verdict of wilful murder was returned against her. husband. Dr. Ren- shaw, after giving the results of the post-mortem examina- tion of the body of the deceased, stated that he had attended Edwards fourteen months ago, and was of opinion that the prisoner was at that time in an unsound state of mind. He had on two occasions recommended the deceased to place her husband in a lunatic asylum, but she always stated that she would wait and "see bow he went on."

div.head: BLACKBURN RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE BLACKBURN RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

Colonel Yolland, the inspector sent down by the Board of Trade to inquire into the cause of the collision at the Black- burn railway station, was engaged on Saturday prior to commencing a similar inquiry at Shaw, in taking further evidence. The testimony of Wade, the guard of the express from Manchester to Hellifield, which was taken at his own residence in Higher Broughton, goes to confirm the story of the driver, for he stated that though the application of the Westinghouse brake by the driver can be felt in the guard's van he was not sensible of it being applied as the train approached Blackburn. After bearing the whistle from the engine he opened the valve of the Wegtinghbouse brake in I his van, but did not bear any rush of air or notice any reduction in the speed of the train. Mark Barker, the fire- man on the Manchester express, has also made a etatement affirming that the Westinghouse brake was applied before the train passed Bolton junction, but did not appear to act. Another death, making a total of six, occurred on Thursday, when Mrs. Mitchell, of Accrington, died in the infirmary. In her case recovery had from the time of the accident, been hopeless.

div.head: PEERS AND THE LAND BILL.
div.p: THE PEERS AND THE LAND BILL.
THE FEELING IN THE COUNTRY.

A great amount of excitement has been created in the country by the action taken in the House of Lords on Fri- day evening on the Land Bill—their adherence, under Lord Salisbury's guidance, to the amendments adopted by them in Committee. As will be seen from the paragraphs given below, hasty meetings were convened for Saturday and Monday, and Liberals generally urged the Government not to surrender a single principle of the measure. A meeting of the Cabinet was held on Saturday, at which, according to the Observer, it was decided to reject all the important amendments. What course was adopted by Mr. Gladstone when the bill came up for consideration in the House of Commons on Monday will be seen from our Parliamentary report. In the course of the morning service on Sunday at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, which was attended by a large congregation, Mr. Spurgeon referred, with his characteristic emphasis, to the conduct of the Tory peers, and prayed that God would "overrule the extraordinary folly of the great ones of this land, ared would, notwithstanding, prosper those measures designed to promote the well-being of the Sister Tale, now so torn and distracted, and thus would send her the balm she se much needed." The following notice has been sent out by the London and Counties Liberal Union to the members of the General Council and the members of the Union: "23, St. Swithln's-lane, London, August 12, 1881.—Dear Sir,—The Irish Land Bill—Urgent and Important.—At a special meeting of the Executive Committee held this day, it was unanimously resolved to convene a special meeting of the General Council and of the members of the Union, to be held at the City Liberal Club on Thursday next, the 18th instant, at three o!clock in the afternoon, for the purpose of passing resolutions with respect to the Irish Land Bill. Your attendance is earnestly requested.—l am, yours truly, JOLet NOBLE, Secretary. A meeting, which was attended by about 100 delegates from various Liberal Associations in London and through- out the country, was held on Monday at the Westminster Palace Hotel, to express disapprobation of the proceedings of the House of Lords. Mr. W. Harris, chairman of the National Liberal Federation, presided, and a number of members of Parliament were present. Resolutions were adopted emphatically endorsing Mr. Gladstone's policy. It was announced that, although the Premier would be un- able to receive a deputation, he would be willing to receive from the hands of Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., the resolutions arrived at. One of these resolutions was as follows : " That in the judgment of this meeting the action of the House of Lords with regard to the Irish Land Bill raises a question of the highest importance, and that the policy of the majority of the House tends to compel the country to consider the policy of maintaining a system which enables an irresponsible hereditary chamber to defeat the will of the nation as expressed by its representatives." Another reso- lution urged the Government to adhere to the Bill as it left the House of Commons, and offered her Majesty's Ministers hearty and unyielding support in their efforts to resist the dictation of a class majority in the House of Lords. Resolutions condemnatory of the action of the House of Lords, and upholding Mr. Gladstone's policy were also passed by meetings of Liberal Associations all over the country. It is stated that her Majesty signified her disinclination to seeing any appeal to the country in the present crisis. The Queen sent Sir Henry Ponsonby to the Premier to learn the latest particulars of the contest, in order that she might be fully advised of all that was taking place. Sir Henry remained in Downing-street several hours awaiting negotiations. Her Majesty, it is said, advised both sides to effect some kind of compromise, as she could not consent to any appeal to the country, in- volving a question between the people and the House of Lords.
PRESCOT SCITOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held on MondAv. There were present—Messrs. W. L. Evans (chair- man), John Wycherley, W. Goldsworth. and John J ,hnson Brown; with Mr. Henry Cross (clerk).—Mr. I'. div.head: ATTENDANCE OFFICERS' REPORT.
div.p: THE ATTENDANCE OFFICERS' REPORT.

The SCHOOL ArrRNDANcE OFFICER (Mr. W. Lloyd) reported that since the last meeting he had visited the several schools in his district, also the Huyton and Roby and Whiston schools. He had served 24 notices on the Parents of 30 children who had been irregular in their atten- dance at the board schools; also 44 notices for arrears of school fees. He had also visited the parents of 105 children whose attendance at school had been irregular, and in several of the cases the parents had been warned. The summonses (three) which stood for hearing on the 19th ult., as per last report, were adjourned to the 2nd instant, on which date they were heard; also two other summonses which he was instructed to take out on the 20th ult, la four of the cases the usual penalty was inflicted; the other case was adjourned to Tuesday, the 16th inst., to allow the defendant an oppor- tunity of producing a medical certificate.—The CHAIR- MAN observed that that was a very satisfactory report. ' THE INSUFFICIENCY OF TEACHING STAFF IN THE INFANT

SCHOOL.—REDtOTION OF THE FINE. The CLERK read the following letter which he wrote and forwarded to the Education Department, respecting the fine of £2O inflicted on the Board for deficiency of teaching staff in the infant school :—"The Board are in receipt of yours of the 2nd instant and enclosure. lam directed to inquire upon what grounds the reduction Of £2O in respect of the insufficiency of staff is made, and why the grant under article 19c for the two pupil teachers is withheld. The circumstances with reference to the infant school staff are as follow :—Miss Emma Lawler, pupil teacher, completed her engagement to the Board as pupil teacher in the infant school, and left on the 13th May, 1880. In consequence of the vacancy thus caused the Board at once advertised for another pupil teacher, and were only enabled to meet with one (Miss Fleetwood), who was appointed on the 4th August, 1880, and commenced her duties as pupil teacher in the infant school on the 23rd August (see my letter to the Department on the 11th September, 1880). At the end of the Midsummer holidays, which extended from the 23rd July to the 23rd August, Miss Fleetwood continued to serve as pupil teacher in the infant school until the 20th Decem- ber last. At that time Miss Webster, the assistant mistress at the girls' school, having resigned, left, and Mies Fleet- wood transferred to the girls' school; and after public advertisement the Board appointed Miss Guy (a ca adidate for ' pupil teachership) to take the place of Miss Fleetwood in the infant school. It is the experience of the Board that there is the greatest difficulty in obtaining transfer female pupil teachers. From the 20th December there were Miss Guy and another candidate for female pupil teacher- ship. Miss Jones engaged in the infant school. In the log-book (infants' school) staff entry, in consequence of the then recent vacancy in the pupil teachership in that school, caused by the termination of Miss Lawler 'a services, Miss Janes, the monitor's name, only was entered. Under these circumstances the Board beg that my lords will, if the fine or a part thereof is strictly incurred, reconsider the matter, and remit the whole or such part as my lords think fit. The School Board rate for the township is about 10d. to Is. in the pound, and the School Board have always thoroughly carried out the wishes of my lords with reference to the schools."—The CLERK stated that he had received the fol- lowing letter from the department:—" The detailed explana- tion given in your letter of the 20th ultimo enables my lords to remit nine-twelfths of the deduction under article 32c. For the first three months of the year the staff in the infant school was incomplete, Emma Lawler merely having stayed on until the inspection, and not having been formally engaged as assistant teacher. The pupil teacher Hall did not earn a grant under article 19c. Fleetwood has been allowed for."—The CHAIRMAN observed that £l5 would be returned, which was not so bad.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF TWO PUPIL TEACHERS.
div.p: THE APPOINTMENT OF TWO PUPIL TEACHERS.

The CLERK read applications for the offices of pupil teacher in the boys' and infants' school. For the latter there were two applications, and Miss Elizabeth Doke, of Warrington-road, Prescot, was selected. There were also two applications for the former, and Joseph Atherton, of Hall-lane, Huyton Quarry, was chosen. As it appeared that his father had made the application on behalf of his son, the Clerk was directed to write to the latter asking him to make a personal application. It Wag resolved that the Chairman and Clerk see the applicants selected, and if suitable, make the necessary arrangements and appoint- ment.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The CLERK stated that since the last meeting the over- seers had' paid £lOO into the bank. The amount .in hand was £294.—1n answer to Mr. Brown, the CHIIRMAN said that any member of the Board was at liberty to visit the schools at any time.

div.head: MR, GLADSTONE AND HIS FORMER CONSTITUENTS.
div.p: MR, GLADSTONE AND HIS FORMER CONSTITUENTS.

GREAT OVATION TO THE PREMI ER. Nothing could exceed the enthusiasm of the reception accorded to Mr. Gladstone at Greenwich on Wednesday. Upon leaving the Speaker's stairs at Westminster, in order to partake of the Whitebait Dinner, the Ministers were loudly cheered by a great crowd which had assembled in spite of the inclement weather. When the boat arrived at Green- wich, at least 4,000 persons had gathered together in front of the Trafalgar Hotel, at which the Whitebait Dinner is held. Along the avenue leading to the hotel were stationed 400 of the leading Liberals of Greenwich,svho formed them- selves into a guard of honour. Many of the ships in the river were gaily flagged, and Mr. Gladstone was greeted with prolonged cheering. Inside the hotel a most interesting ceremony took place. The Liberals of Greenwich presented Mr. Gladstone with a handsome ' chair of brown oak, with buff morocco covering, edged with the Westminster blue band and silvered nails. On the cushioned back Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone's arms, with the motto, "Fide et virtute," are embossed in gold. Above, let into a wreath in the wood work representing the rose, shamrock, and thistle, and a bundle of leeks, is a plaque of silver on which is engraved the following inscription :—" Preseated to the Right Honour. able William Ewart Gladstone, M.P., First Lord of the Treasury, together with an address, by the Liberals of the borough of Greenwich and the Liberal clubs of the neigh- bourhood, in testimony of their high appreciation of the priceless services rendered by him to the country, and in re- membrance of the proud 'distinction conferred upon the borough as their representative in Parliament from 18G8 to 1830. August, 1881." On either aide of the wreath is an axe, and underneath one side the .emblems of tyranny, a scourge, a birch rod and chains, and on the other side the emblems of liberty and prosperity, a wreath of palm leaves and various fruits. The chair which is a handsome piece of furniture of excellent workmanship throughout, runs on castors. Accompanying it is a footstool of the same mate- rials and style of workmanship. The presentation of the chair was accompanied by the following address, and by many enthusiastic expressions of personal devotion to Mr. Gladstone :—" Honoured Sir,—The representatives of the Liberal electors of the borough of Greenwich and the Liberal clubs of the neighbourhood, we desire to convey to you in permanent form our expression of the gratification it affords us to welcome you once again to the constituency with whom you were formerly so long and so honourably connected. We have watched, with have discharged the ryeisupisnotni csyei bo. luerTdhue eot inLedsanonefdt to(hlfar (Ireland)that the nei high lastßo ffii feelings of increasing admiration, the manner in which you greatee to which, by the Sovereign and the country, you have been ll will me l eecatseudr,e aonfdpeosapceocai anldl ever be remembered with heartfelt gratitude by the British nation. In the face of opposition and obstruction seldom witnessed in the British Parliament you have maintained a dignity of the highest character, reflecting the greatest glory on yourself as a British statesman. Your desire to promote the interests of peace, and to stay the progress of wars un- righteously commenced and cruelly prosecuted, has won the admiration of every true Philanthropist; and in days to come, when the history of the country during the years of your Premiership shall be read with a vision undimned by party obscurity you haveuntouchedritoyande .ord tin acf eby hostile thestilecclaomnvolue nthatshallrtioi t be en righteousness exalteth a nation. We trust that your invalu- able life may be prolonged for yet increasing usefulness and distinction; and if the chair—the token' of esteem and gratitude—which accompanies this address should be regarded as being worthy of your acceptance it will unspeak- ably enhance the pleasure with which, on behalf of the sub- scribers, it is now presented.—We remain, honoured sir, your faithful and attached admirers."—The Premier was evi- dently touched by the warmth of the feelings thus ex- pressed, and, in a singularly graceful speech, he heartily declared his gratitude for the kindnesses he had received from the electors of Greenwich. A reference in the address to the Parliamentary difficulties encountered by Ministers drew forth one or two significant sentences from Mr. Glad- stone. Those difficulties, the right hon, gentleman said, had brought into view a new and great necessity, a necessity in the feel HtheeuskeenestCommonsinterest; greater securities for the liberty of the nation, and for they twhhei enhe necessity —plveizof, for n advancing of legislation to its full efficiency. div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL

LIBRA.RY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting ~f this committee was held ort Wednesday, Mr. H. R. L•icey presiding. There were ,ilso Present Councillors Brook, Fisher, Dr. McNicol, and Mr. Sinclair, with Mr. Craik, Deputy Town Clerk.

div.head: Ltsautimes REPORT.
div.p: Ltsautimes REPORT.

- The Librarian reported that 2,019 books bad been borrowed from the Lending Library, clarilig the month from 17th July to 13th August, out of which 10 were banded out for reading in the reading room, the library being closed for repairs ctc., from 17th July to 9th August, 1881. He also begged to report that there were 2,335 members in the lending depart- ment. There had been presented during the past month, "The Course and Current of Architecture," by Samuel Hug- gins, one volume "By the Author." The 2,019 books were classified as follows :—History, 46; Biography, 49; Travels, 64; Natural History, 19; •Sciences, 40; Theology, 33; Poetry, 30; Fiction, 1,638; Political Economy, 1; Finer Arts, 4; General Literature, 95.

THE /INFERENCE LIBRARY. The Cnstitst,or : I think we ought to congratulate our- selves upon the transformation that has taken place in the library. We have got the two primary requisites, that is, light and ventilation. lam sure Dr. McNicol will agree with that.—Mr. %mow : And plenty of room.—Dr. Menem. : ' Yes; I suppose it arose out of the inconvenience to the Librarian.—The Castaway : According to the present arrangements we have the reference room, which we like to keep rather private, and then the public reading room. It has struck me whether persons coming here to study should not have some sort of form to deliver to the Librarian so as to keep them private.—Mr. SuicLata : I think the less of that we have, the better, so as to have no inconvenience. I do not like to give people too many forms.—Mr. BROOK: I scarcely think that is required.—The Cm:unsex' : Then I have been thinking of forms for the boys. The boys come here where the Librarian is, and ask for a book to read, not to take home. They fill up this form and the Librarian keeps the counterfoil.—Dr. McNicot : How would it be to have a book, and every time a boy comes in, to record his name 2-Mr. SINCLAIR : But what have we to ga:n by it 2-The CHAIRMAN : If the boys are perniitted to read books without making application, we must put the books in a different place to where they now Btand.--31r. SINCLAIR : I thought it was the saving of a great deal of trouble to have them where they are. Now this form necessitates them to select a book which after they have got they don't like. As it is at present they can have what book they like.—The CRAm- aras: We have lost about 36 during four years. Of course there is no great loss in it.—Mr. SINCLAIR : What I feel is we should gets deal less reading. What I care about is to get the books used.—The CHAIRMAN: The only important thing on the other side of the question is that we shall pro- duce order and regularity On the part of the boys, and sub- ject them to some responsibility.—Dr. McNicor.: But have a book at the entrance to the Reference Department. —Mr. Stigmata: It will jest be the means of driving many a one away.—The CRantmew : Yes, I am afraid of that.—Mr. &scum: All I can say is I sometimes pick up a magazine, and if I had to write my name down to get a hook I should not take the trouble.—The CHAIRMAN: We shall have to select some other place then for the books in the Reference Library.—Mr. Bizoow: Why deprive them from coming in here ?—The CHAIR:maw: It will keep this more private.— Mr. &scram : Oh, not much ; and they can have this table. —The subject then dropped.

div.head: COMMITTEE.PAVI
div.p: COMMITTEE.PAVI
The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wedneslay, Alderman Johnson presiding. There were also present Aldermen Cook and Gamble; Cootie:llora McK .echni Baxter, Bishop, and Walks!.

THE ARCHING OF THE BROOK. The Stravavon reporting that the bricks being used in pursuance of the resolution of the Council in the archirg • over of the brook in the Gas Works yard were totally unfit for use, it was decided that the contractor (Mr. Middlehurst) be permitted to use bricks, at his own expense, other than those on the Gas Works land, providing that they be to the entire satisfaction of the Surveyor, and no additional expense to the Corporation.

PLANS. The following plans were submitted and decided upon as follows :—Wash-house, Robin's-lane, for Mr. Wm. Rigby, disapproved,yard space insufficient; two houses, Park-road, for Mr. William Ball, approved ; two houses, Ellbess-lane, for Mr. Jesse Grundy, approved; wash-house, Atherton-st., for Mr. George Green, approved; alteration to cottage behind St. Mary's Church, for Dr. R. A. Gasket!, disap- proved : cattle sheds, &c., Cowley Hill-lane, for Mr. Joseph Birchall, approved; additional wing, Jzo., to Hillside Villa, for Mr. J. C. Bishop, approved; four houses, in road from Peasley Cross-lane to Thatto Heath, for Messrs. Green and . Hayes, disapproved, ashpit to be raised. Mr. Thos. Francis sent in a plan of a cottage, but he did not state where it was to be built, it was not accompanied by a block plan, and no elevation was shown. Some amusement was caused by the appearance of the plan, which was disapproved. I DISAGREEABLE FRONT VIEW. Mr. HART said that some time ago, when the Pavil Committee made their annual inspection they stopped to look at some houses in course of erection not far from Leach Hall, Sutton. When the plans for these houses came in at the following meeting on account of the situation of the ashpits and privies, the manager of the Sutton Glass Works,who lived near, raised an objection at the time to the man being allowed to erect those houses and stick a lot of ashpits in front of the windows of the houses, one of which he lived in. The committee at that time decided to send notice to Mr. Rimmer saying that the plans were disap- proved on account of the situation of the ashpits and privies. Mr. Rimmer asked what the objections were, and Mr. Hart wrote him pointing out wherein he was tyrong, and requiring the ashpits, to be erected in some other situation so as not to be in front of any house. He also stated that it was his duty to comply with the Act. Mr. Rimmer called at the office, but Mr. Hart being out he left the plan he new produced without any communication or message. What his object was he did not know. He had been told that Mr. Pemberton the owner of the land, had suggested to Mr. Rimmer the building of a wall so as to obstruct the view of the ashpits and privies from the front windows of the houses. He should ask for the committee's instructions that the premises should not be erected there unless a wall be put up. Mr. Rummer lead not sent another plan, and had made a great row about the objection that had, been raised to the ashpits.—The CHAIRMAN expressed his objec- tion to the buildings being erected with the ashpits in front of the houses.—The DEP= Twig aux read from the Act that every house should be provided with a privy and covered ashpit not in front of any houses, the situation to be subject to the approval of the Corporation.—Mr. HART asked if he might communicate to Mr. Rimmer that tie plan would be approved if a wall was built so ad to obstruct the view of the astopits.—This HU agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Rimmer bad perhaps built the houses in that fashion with the view of compelling the people who lived opposite to buy them. (Laughter).

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER COTTON, THURSDAY,—Ihings are coming to a very serious pass. There is no longer a possible chance to do any business owing to our helpless dependance on the wire- fullers behind cotton. There is much talk of organised oppo- sition in the form of stopping spindlrs, but it takes no practical shape, and even those most anxious for it do not pretend to believe it will be carried out. LIVERPOOL COTTON, THURSDAY.—Spot : There has again been a good demand at continually hardening prices, and the quotations for American are raised 1-16 d for low middling and upwards. Bales 14,000 bales. including 1,090 on speculation or for export. Import since Thursday 47,301 bales, including 32,452 American. Futures have been strong all day, and prices have gained 3-32 d for near and I-16d for distant positions. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, THURSDAY. Beef quiet at the quotations. Pork in steady consumptive demand. Bacon very firm and in good request. Hams quiet at previous figures. Shoulders firmer in value. Lard firm but quiet. Cheese strong. Butter dull of sale.

LIVERPOOL CORN, THIIRSDAY,—The market for wheat to-day opened very firm, but not much business has been transacted. Flour is very steady at yesterday's prices. Indian corn, which Is very fizm, is selling from 6s to Ss Oid per eental for new. Beans are unchanged in price from yesterday. Peas are steady at late rate.. Oats quiet. Oatmeal in fair demand at the quota. Lions of last Tuesday. LONDON DEAD MEAT, THULVIDAY.—Fair supplies on sale, and trade quiet at the following quotations :—Beef, 2s 8d to 4s 8d ; prime Scotch ditto, 4s 10d to 5s ; mutton, 3s 4d to 6s; lamb, 6s 4d to 7a; veal, 4s 8d to 58 4d; large p-ul, .1s 8d to 4s 8d ;small pork. 4s 8d to 5s per Sibs.

..- - CORK BUTTER, SHIYRSDAY.—FIrsts, 11s; seconds, 110 s ; thirds, 102 s; f surths. 925; fifths, 70s ; superfine, 1355 ; fine mild, 119 s; mild, 114.. Salt kegs : INirsts, 119 s; seconds, 114 s; thirds,lo3 ; fourths, 89s ; fifths, 735. Number of firkins in the market, 2,437.
There has been a considerable revival in the agitation among Liverpool sailors for increased wages, and the redress of other grievances.
Miss M"abel Wilberforce was on Thursday committed for trial at the Old Bailey for perjury. She maintained her self-possession to the last, declaring herself to be the victim of a conspiracy.

APPLES.—Frorn all quarters we have reports that this will be a tolerably good fruit year. Apples are ,p much better crop than they have been for some time, for although we hear of some failures, yet in the aggregate not only will the quantity be far in excess of that of any crop of recent years, but, what is of even more importance, the qu!ility will be good. Such sorts ns the Wellington, that in unkindly seasons are deformed and almost worthless, are this year beautifully clear in the akin, and promise to swell out to a large size. All the largest should be gathered first, and the small left for a late crop, for in abundant apple years the price sinks so low as not to be remunerative if they are all left until fully grown.—Farmers' Chronicle. _

process may be accompanied with the most pointed expressions of a resolution to insist upon fundamental amendments. We shall recollect that we have seen this sort of thing carried to great lengths before, with the upshot of a tame surrender the moment it was made manifest that the country was being roused, and would not suffer valuable legislation to be prevented or postponed by an irresponsible body of titled partizans. The Opposition Lords are not censured for giving way at the end in the way they did; but they are open to unflattering reflections for the perversity they displayed in inserting and re-inserting inad • missible alterations, in defiance of the House of Cora - mons, until the country had been wrought up into a condition of unwholesome excitement and anger. The rapid "movement to the rear" of the Peers, who had followed Lord Salisbury so obsequiously, when by standing their ground any longer they would have had to sustain the decisive charge of an adversary invin • cible in the political forces he wielded, betrayed the inherent pusillanimity of a monopolist class in the critical instant when that real courage, which shows itself in acts, not words, is most needed. The riddle of the House of Landlords' resistance to the Irish Land Bill is now easy to read. They made a point at fighting hard, and a movement as if they meant to clutch a great deal, just that they might finally lay hold of a little more than they could have done. if they had made no stand at all. In their way, these hereditary nobles, who profess to despise trade, and to be far above the huckstering habit, are as ready to do a bit of chaffering and bargaining where the
case is one of having to give up abused

powers and privileges for the benefit of the long-suffering masses of the people, as any plebian petty dealer could be. In the Land Act as it receives the royal assent, a small degree of con- sideration is given to landlord prescriptions and sus- ceptibilities than was afforded by the Bill as it first passed the House of Commons. But if the landlords are actually grateful for these slight concessions they
are indeed "thankful for small mercies." A good

typical example of the gains Lord Salisbury and the Duke of Argyll by their unholy alliance have secured for the Irish landlords, is the amendment in the clause relating to the access of the landlord to the court. The clause as drawn by the Government and sanctioned by the House of Commons, allowed a landlord to go to the court if he wished to have an increased rent of a holding judicially fixed, but for no other purpose. Lord Salisbury and his friends in the Upper House made a great point of insisting that the landlord should have unrestricted access to the court; and although it was not explained what a landlord would be likely to want from the court except an increase of rent, this free privilege of access was magnified so much, that the Government eventually allowed it to be inserted in the Bill, and that variation scores as a very momen- tous concession by Mr. Gladstone to the claims of the Lords. We do not say that in no part of the Land Act of 1881 will be discovered the marks of an un- friendly hand, contracting in some measure the scope of the advantages granted to the tenant-farmers of Ireland. The Act will bear upon its face as long as it remains on the statute-book some evidences of the ex- istence of an illiberal House of Lords, which was able in this clause and that to alternate somewhat the benefits bestowed upon the people of Ireland by those provisions. But we do say that, even as it stands, the Land Act is a wonderful measure to have ever passed through the ordeal of revision by a British House of Peers. The not remote ancestors of the present generation of Lords would have been aghast with horror if they bad witnessed such a transfer of sub- stantial interest in the soil of Ireland from Irish land- lord to Irish tenant. Now that the Bill is passed, and we glance back at all the obstruction it has met with, and all the malicious denunciations which have been poured ugon it by men so diametrically antagonistic in their sentiments and aims as the Tory oligarchy and the Irish Land League leaders, it is little less than a miracle that the measure has been carried at all. The country owes this marvellous achievement to the incomparable statesmanship of Mr. Gladssone ; and the fact that he has been capable, at his advanced age, of bearing the brunt of this tremendous battle for so many months, and of vanquishing;one deadly foe after another by the might of his single arm, until the last enemy lay prostrate before him, astounds the world, and forces tven the people of other great and self- ruling nations to confess that Mr. Gladstone stands solitary amongst the statesmen and national leaders of this generation, in the unique grandeur of his char- acter, in greatness of aim and purity of motive, and most of all in his unexampled capacity for the stupen- dous work of regenerative legislation which is the highest test of the fitness of a man to wield the destinies of a vast empire.

WILILE the House of Commons has had its time almost entirely occupied with the Irish Land Bill, the Education Department has not been idle. The speech delivered by Mr. Mundella the other even- ing must have led every one interested in education to expect very substantial reforms in the conduct of elementary schools. We now know what the De- partment propose to do. From the parliamentarypaper just issued we learn that it is intended to adopt the average attendance as the basis or the grants hitherto made on account of individual scholars, whether in- fants under seven or those presented in standards. The 250 attendances are to be abolished as a condition of examination, and all scholars on the registers for six months will have to be presented unless a reason- able excuse for absence be given. Due care is, however, to be taken not to inflict injustice on account of this ar- rangement, as the grants will be so assessed as to maintain the average rate of aid as far as it can be done. The Department is anxious at present to take into consideration the educational, rather than the financial effects of these proposals. It is therefore plain that teachers and school managers should con- sider their probable effect solely with reference to the education of the children, and not allow it to be inter- fered with bythe consideration as to how it will pay. Hay- I ing made up their minds on this point they may then with perfect propriety look at the proposals from a financial point of view. Among the grants com- mon to all schools it is worthy of notice that in the case of music the full grant will be paid if singing be satisfactorily taught from the notes, tonic sol-fa or otherwise, but only half the grantif taught by the ear only. We consider this a satisfactory arrangement. If our schools would only send out large numbers of pupils able to sing at sight, they would community. Sewing, the musical portion of the nity not only for girls,ibnugt'fotroall boys under en compulsoryyear of age, and a special grant will be given for it. As seven to special merit the inspector is to have regard to yof the m e work,t hods the organisation and discipline, the employment of theu a ligeneralt especially instruction,eciayin th e sandtan standards; s; generalan and, q in order to encourage teachers to aim at excellence, he is empowered to recommend an additional ant on the average attendance varying The introduction of a seventh standard eoridsi school is "in these respects f • air, good, or excellent." which we hail with satisfaction, as it pointnaggrfaesatuthree s upwards giving fair promise on the part of the elementary school to something considerably beyond the three R's, which many people regarded 10 years ago as a sort of national luxury. With respect to class sub- jects the school will be divided into two divisions— standards I to 4 being the lower, and standard 5 and upwards the higher. Class subjects are assigned to these, the grants for which will be made as now on the average attendance, but an increased grant will be paid if 20 per cent. of the scholars examined are presented in standard 4 and upwards. Not more than three pupil teachers will be allowed in any school or department whatever number of certificated teachers may be employed in it; stipendiary monitors will no longer be recognised, and an assistant teacher will only count as sufficient for 60 and not 80 scholars as in the past. Honour certificates are to be abolished.

These proposals will no doubt be keenly criticised, but it is quite evident that they are the result of much careful deliberation. There is one feature in them which suggests an invaluable improvement looming in the not far distant future—the reward of real ex- cellence. The teacher who is faithful and thorough- going has good reason to expect that the more perfect his work the more profitable will it become to him in its financial results, whilst the benefits of a higher eduCation for the masses cannot be over-estimated.

div.head: LOC A L NOTES.
div.p: LOC A L NOTES.

The Catholics of Widnes are without doubt the most in. fluential of the religious denominations in that town in regard to members. This is, probably, owing to the fact that the Hibernian population greatly preponderates. It is gratifying to see that the priests who have charge of the Catholic congregations are determined that the children of their flocks shall not be behind their Protestant fellows in point of school accommodation, for a beautiful school is now in course of erection for them in Newtown. The build- ing is estimated to cost £1,300; it will accommodate GOO children, and stands on about 270 yards of ground at the corner of Margaret and George-streets. The architect is Mr. Edmutul Kirby, of Cook-street, Liverpool, and the structure is expected to be ready for occupation some time during the '1 autumn. Jadging by the contribution of the Vicar of Widnes to the Parish Messenger, that gentleman does not appear to be very much entranced by the neighbours who pour into his " territory " like the Goths and Huns who at one time swarmed over Europe. Let me hope that the matter in dis- pute as to the wall will in a short time be amicably settled. After the pretty warm discussion which has been elicited by Mr. Higginson, surveyor to the Widnes Local Board, submitting to that body a scheme of sewerage which was alleged to be much superior to that of Major Cross, the Chairman, who is a practical engineer of same eminence, the members have given their verdict decidedly against the surveyor, and in favour of the chairman. Mr. Kershaw, the chairman of the joint Highway and Health Committee, who were appointed to consider the subject, when speaking at the special meeting held on Tuesday, told the members that though at first he was prepossessed in favour of Mr. Hig- ginson's plans, he found the route suggested by the Chair- man to be 200 yards shorter and not beset by such engineer- ing difficulties. During the course of the discussion the Surveyor has displayed some want of tact, for when asked questions by the committee upon his rival's scheme (if I may be permitted to use such a word) he pretended utter ignorance of its proposals. This looks a little like envy either of the Chairman or Mr. Copland, the sewerage sur- veyor, and such a course of proceeding has certainly irritated several of the members somewhat against him. I am at a loss to know what there was to hinder Mr. Higginson being thoroughly posted in both schemes, and ready to answer any question that might be put to him upon their respective merits. A public man should by all means cultivate suavity of manner and a polite method of dealing with opponents. On reading your report of the Local Board meeting at Widnes the other week, I was somewhat at a loss to know what was meant by the statement that the railway com- panies had been requested to cause their bridges to "drop dry." However, I happened to be in the main street of Widnes on Wednesday afternoon during a thunderstorm, and as I was called upon to pass under the London and North-Western Railway Company's bridge, I had light thrown upon what dropping dry meant, for I suddenly dis- covered the water coming through one part of the structure on to my poor self as if from a spout.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday the presiding magistrate (Mr. Bibby) gave a marine store dealer a casti- gation which he will not be liable to forget, at least for a short time to come. It appears that the worthy in question had bought several hundredweights of good scrap iron belonging to the L. and N. W. Railway Company from two girls within a period of a few weeks, and he professed to have believed the tale they told him that they had picked it up on some waste ground. The chairman said he had grave doubts whether the dealer ought not to be placed where the girls were standing, and he censured his disgraceful conduct in most withering terms. There are few towns of the same size where juvenile thieving is so prevalent as in Widnes, notwithstanding the numerous arrests during the last two years and the many committals to industrial schools; and I hope that Mr. Barker, the new superintendent of police, will continue the work so well begun of trying to rid the town of the many young scamps who prowl about seeing what they can lay their hands on.
The returns in connection with the Widnes Science and Art classes have just been received, and I believe they are of a favourable character.

The dispute between Mr. Annett, master of Trinity boys school, Runcorn, and the School Board of that town, has gone in favour of the former, a letter having been received from the Education Department to that effect by the Board. Under these circumstances it seems that Mr. Kynnersley, Her Majesty's inspector, was not correct when he told Mr. John Simpson, the vice-chairman of the Board, that Mr. Annett would lose his certificate if he declined to furnish the returns. In future Mr. Kynnersley had better follow the advice of the Yankee humorist and never prophesy until he knows! The Rev. Canon Barclay, the chairman of the School Board, was not led away by this statement on the part of the in- spector, for he characterised it as absurd, and warned Mr. Simpson that if he were a wise man he would always take wbat an inspector said cunt grano sails. --

The Gods-acre attached to the Frodsham Parish Church will no doubt occupy the attention of the earnest and hard- working Restoration Committee, now that the funds for the fabric and a new organ are in a fairly satisfactory condition, for although it is important that the accommodation for public worship should have some attractions yet we must not forget that "The slender debt to nature's quickly paid, Discharged, perchance, with greater ease, than made." and if we individually may not like to look forward to the time when we shall shuffle off this mortal coil it would be some slight consolation to know that decent provision is made. The present accommodation is very limited indeed, and whether the responsibility of providing additional ground be undertaken by the aid of private subscriptions, the Rural Sanitary Authority, or a burial board, it must be borne in mind that it is a pressing necessity, if the burial of the dead is to be done decently and in order • the latter pro- vision it is alleged would doubtless be the best, as it would secure the direct supervision of interested persons, whereas if the matter was taken in band by the Rural Sanitary Authority, a large majority of the members would have no interest in the matter.

The Frodsham Cricket Club Fete, advertised for the firs proximo, will no doubt be well patronised, judging from the attractions offered. The club includes amongst its members and supporters most of the aristocracy of the neighbourhood and is under distinguished patronage. The expenses during the current season have been very heavy consequent upon the outlay incurred in preparing the wicket, and erecting the pavilion, which new ornaments the ground, and I wish the fete every success.

Mr. Frank Dawson, the contractor for Frodsham sewerage has commenced the outfall works, an judging from the progress made, he will have the scheme far advanced before the winter weather sets in, a good length of piping having already been laid, in addition to extensive preparations for the settling tanks. The Frodsham Volunteers are to be congratulated on the interest taken in the corps by the local gentlemen, and I have reason to believe that next year will be more eventful for invitations than the present, as it has been whispered that Mr. James Reynolds, of Fox Hill, is disposed to offer facilities next year for the whole battalion camping out near his picturesque grounds. The Fenians having lately been on the rampage, creating all sorts of disagreeable feelings in the minds of peaceably disposed citizens, in various parts of the country, it is not to be wondered at that St. Helens should have been the victim of a plot emanating from the inner consciousness of a I woman. Who knows a woman who can't plot? Your humble servant knows two or three. This plot on the part of this St. Helens heroine may have been slightly founded upod fact, as in the case of some of our most sensational novels, but the story that has been circulated is considered to be a base fabrication, and the majority of the people give it but small credence. It is a fact that since the dastardly attempt to blow up the Town Hall of Liverpool, the mas- sive structure in Corporation-street, St. Helens, has been guarded every night by the police. On the eve of August the Ist. so the story runs, a woman, who was disturbed in her midnight slumbers by voices under her bedroom window, got up to see what the matter was, and she was rewarded by seeing the diabolical spectacle of three men, two of them being dressed as nightseil men, and the other one more res- pectably, engaged in conversation, the purport of which led her to believe that it was the intention of the trio to blow o'er public palace into smithereens. • SATURDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds (chairman) and
Mr. John Brandrit.

A SAD PAGE FROM A LIFE HISTORY.—EmiIy Holland, dressmaker, Liverpool, was charged with stealing a woollen shirt, value 4s. Gd., the property of Mr. Samuel Worrell, hatter, High-street.—Samuel Greaves, who is employed at Mr. Tonks's decorator, High-street, said that on the previous Tuesday night he saw the prisoner enter the door of the prosecutor's shop, take a shirt off a hook, and put it under her dress. She then went into Mr. Houghton's, shoemaker, and witness followed her and charged her with stealing the article. She afterwards handed the shirt to him, and he sent for Sergeant McMichael, who took her into custody.— The woman stated that she had not taken it with the inten- tion of stealing it, but simply to look at it. She should not have done so, but she was under the influence of drink, and if the magistrates would let her off she would sign the pledge. —Superintendent Williamson said that the prisoner be- longed to a highly respectable family. Some time ago she was divorced from her husband, and since that time she had led a very bad life, and When taken into custody had given fictitious names to the police.—The Chairman said the evidence against the prisoner was very conclusive, and as there were already 14 previous convictions recorded in her -case—though certainly they were not of a very serious nature—she would be committed to gaol three months, with bard labour.—The prisoner: Oh, dear me! Cannot you say less than that?—She was removed from the court, sobbing bitterly. CAUGHT IN THE Acr.—John Addison and George Heels, boatmen, Liverpool, were charged with having, early that morning. stolen 56Ibs. of coal, value 4d., the property of Mr. Edmund Finlay, salt and coal merchant, Top Locks.— Evidence was given by Mr. Edward Langshaw, clerk to the prosecutor, and P.C. Mutter, from which it appeared that about two o'clock that morning, the prisoners were caught by the officer taking the coal out of the yard.—Heelis pleaded guilty and Addison not guilty.—Each of the prisoners was fined 20s. and 18s. costs, and, in default of payment, ordered to be committed to gaol one month. Moma.—Before Messrs. Charles Reynolds (chairman) and _ .

div.head: John Brundrit.
div.p: John Brundrit.

ASSAULT CASES.—A young woman named Eliza Moores aged 18, was summoned for assaulting Selina Fryer, a married woman. Complainant said that on the 2nd inst. she had a quarrel with defendant's mother about permitting her husband to visit her house and remain there. On the following day defendant came to complainant's house and struck her. Defendant, in reply to the Bench, said that the row occurred owing to complainant making improper in- sinuations against her character. Fryer cut her elbow slightly with a knife which she used. Defendant was or- dered to enter into a surety to be of good behaviour six months, and pay lie. 6d. costs, or be imprisoned seven days. —Georger Fryer, husband of the complainant in the pre- vious case, was summoned for assaulting Mrs. Ann Fryer. Complainant said whilst her daughter and defendant's wife were quarrelling, she went up to get her own daughter away, as she saw her arm was bleeding. De'endant used very bad language, asd demanded that she should let the pair alone. He also hit her on both her temples and tried to kick her. He abused her so much that she was senseless for a short time. Defendant said the woman came into his house and caused a disturbance, and he thought he was jus- tified in using violence to put her out. The Chairman said defendant had no right to use violence, but as the case ap- peared to be a paltry one, and defendant had been much irri- tated by-complainant and her daughter, the summons would be dismissed.

I WEAK CASE.—A young woman named Ellen Ward, whose mother lives in Wolverhampton, was summoned for assaulting Harriet Barker alias Eaton, on the 6th inst.— Mr. Barton appeared for the defence.—The case was a paltry dispute, and complainant was proved to have used very filthy language.—The Bench dismissed the summons, and ordered complainant to pay 78.6 d. costs. AN INCORRIGIBLE DRAYMAN.— Frederick Sankey, a drayman in the employ of Sir Gilbert Greenall, was sum- moned for having been asleep whilst in charge of two horses and a dray at Sutton, on the sth instant.—The case having been proved by P.C. Egerton, the defendant said that when the officer spoke to him he at once told him that he was not asleep.—The Chairman said It was only on the Bth instant that defendant was fined 40s. and costs for a similar offence. He would now be fined 40s. and costs 12s. 6d., or, in default, one month's imprisonment. Defendant pald the money. AN OLD OFFENDEIL—Robart Moores, who had been con- victed a dozen times since 1876, was fined 40s. and costs 9s. Ed., or one month's imprisonment with 'hard labour, for I drunk and disorderly conduct in Bridge-street, on the 31st ultimo.

A BEERSELLER SITMIIONFD.-1.1)n Ogdm, of the Swan Inn beerhouw, was surnimm.d hy the police for Permitting drunkenne,;•l in his house, on the 10th lni t.—Mr. Lewin, who appe wed for defendant, asked the Beneh to adjourn the hearing of the case for a week, as tiersnd Int had been unable to summon a material witness.—Superintendent Williamson said be had no objection to offer to this course, and the hearing of the case was adjourned until next Monday.

YESTERDLY.—Bef ore Messrs. Alfred Thomas and 8. E. Chadwick. STEALING A Wersvcoar.—John Inglesfield, aged 19, was charged with stealing a waistcoot, the property of Martin Callighan, on the 30th ult.—Prosecutor is a labourer, of Cooper-street, and he bought the waistcoat at Mr. Imison's pawnshop for 6s. on the 23rd July, and left it in his bedroom on the morning of the 30th ult., and missed it on returning from his work at five in the afternoon. Prisoner lodged at the house, and slept in the same bedroom; and got a girl, aged ten years, named Mary Rafferty, of Zion-place, to pawn the article at Mrs. Smith's pawnshop for 3s.—PC. Noden apprehended the prisoner, who denied the charge, I and was sent to gaol one month with hard labour. Buyers of goods offer nothing better for any parcels of importance thin prices which it is impossible for manufacturers to accept present unless at a s trious loss to themselves. There is evidently an Increasing desire for orders on the part of producers, but such inducements as they can offer buyers are at present insufficient. Dr. Taylor, the medical officer for Scarborough, makes a statement which is anything but calculated to assure those who are responsible for the care and rearing of children. He states that fully 50,000 infants die annually in England alone through the administration of improper food. It is not that they do not receive enough nourishment, but that the nourishment is of the wrong sort. These figures are ratke startling even to those who have heard so much l• about infant mortality.
