A RITNCOEN WESLEYAN METHODIST SCHOOL Excuse. SION.—On Monday afternoon the scholars and friends be- longing to Nelson-street Sunday school, Runcorn, had their annual out, their destination being a field at Weston, which had been placed at their disposal by Mr. Wm. Bankes. Tea was provided at four o'clock, and at seven the return journey was commenced to the lively strains of the Mill Brow brass band.

HALTON PARISH TRIP.—The fifth annual trip. of this character took place on the 12th inst., when about 44 people left Runcorn station by the 2-52:train for Liverpool and New Brighton. The weather during the principal part of the day was not of a favourable character. CHILDREN'S SERVICE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN. On Sunday night, a children's service was held at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn. Appropriate passages of scripture were rad, and the Rev. J. D. Thomas gave three brief addresses. During the evening the children sang several hymns, accompanied by the choir. The proceeds will be devoted to defraying the cost of improving the seats used by the scholars. BRITANNIA BOWLING CLUB, CREWE v. RUNCORN BOWL. ING CLUB.—This match was completed at Halton, near Runcorn, on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the Runcorn Club. Mr. Welch, for the Britannia Club, played a good game both at Runcorn and Crewe, he being the only player that won at both places. Messrs. Wright and Lumb played very well for the Britannia Club at Crewe, but suffered a defeat at Halton. Mr. Price, of the Runcorn Club, proved too strong for Stone, of Crewe.

THE FLOWER QUEEN SERVICE AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Root's cantata, entitled "The Flower Queen, or the Coronation of the Rose," will be given in the Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, September 13th and 14th, and will be followed by Wass' s cantata, "The Foresters' Roundelay." Mr. W. Handley will act as conductor, and, judging from the success of "The Flower Queen" when last given In Runcorn, there is every prospect of a musical treat of no common order.

ACCIDENT AT A SAW MILL—On Thursday, a man named George Pugh (39), residing in Lord Nelson-street, was con- veyed to the Warrington Infirmary, suffering from a con- tused wound on the hip. The man, who works at Messrs. Collin and Son's, Academy-street, was in charge of the cir- cular saw, which was cutting a piece of timber. When it had cut half way through the wood, the saw jumped out and struck the man on the hip, wounding him as stated. His injuries are not serious and he is doing well.

MR. BEASLEY'S BANKRTIPTCI2.—Mr. Thomas Beasley, solicitor, bankrupt, of Runcorn and Widnes, and late clerk to the Local Board at that town, came up yesterday, at the 1 Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, for the purpose of passing his examination, which has already been so often adjourned. Mr. Hitchen, of Runcorn, and Mr. Gregory, of Liverpool, who appeared for various creditors, stated that the accounts of the bankrupt were still imperfect, and as the trustee (Mr. Bolland) was not thoroughly satisfied with the amount of information be had received, they must apply for another adjournment. The hearing was accordingly further adjourned to the 11th October, after the vacation.

H.armor Camas Cl:cont.—The yearly trip of the members connected with this choir took place on Saturday, when about 30 members and friends, accompanied by the Vicar, rent to Chester by train. The various " lions "of the rare old city were visited, and the !day's proceedings included the attendance at cathedral service, which we need :_carcely say was much enjoyed. A capital dinner was provided at the Blossoms Hotel, after which the com- pany were rowed up the river as far as Eaton Hall, to the grounds of which the Duke of Westminster, through Major Scotland, had supplied an order of admission. After par- taking of tea, the excursionists left Chester by the eight o'clock train for home.

ACCIDENT TO A RAILWAY GUARD AT FARNWORTIL—A luggage guard on the Cheshire Lines Committee, named George Ashurst (41), residing in Eldon-street, Warrington, met with an accident at Farnworth, near Widnes, on Wed- nesday. Whilst Ashurst was standing on a waggon, the driver started the train, the suddenness of the movement throwing him between the coupling of the waggons to the ground. A wheel passed over his hand and severely crushed it. He was also slightly wounded on the head. Asburst was at once taken to the Warrington Infirmary, and attended by Drs. Joseph and Richmond, who found it necessary to amputate the injured hand. He is progressing favourably. SUPPOSED LOSS OF A RUNCORN SCROONER AND THE CREW.--It is now about a month since any intelligence was received of the schooner Alma. which belongs to the port of Runcorn, and she is supposed to have been lost with her crew. She is a schooner of about 130 tons burthen, and be- longed to Brundrit and Co., ship builders. The vessel had recently undergone extensive repairs, and on the 22nd July left Penmaenmawr for Dublin, having a cargo of 132 tons of setts. There were on board six persons, including the cap- tain named Thomas Whitby, his wife, and a nephew about ten years old named Ward, two seamen, and a cook. Amougst these were Samuel Inglesfield and Matthew Edwards, both of Runcorn. It is supposed the vessel must have foundered during the heavy storm which occurred on Sunday the 24th July. Other vessels which left about the same time have put out two cargoes since then and no hopes are now enter- tained of the safety of the missing ship. Much sympathy is felt for the relatives of the persons on board the vessel.

EXPLOSION AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS—On Wed- nesday morning, about half-past five o'clock, an explosion took place at Messrs. Worth's chemical works, near Queen- street, which are used for the manufacture of bi-sulphate of sada. The explosion caused the windows in the neighbour- ing houses to rattle, and the inhabitants in some cases to rush from their beds. However, on enquiries being made, the matter did not turn out to be of so serious a nature as was at first anticipated. It appeared that the condenser in the condensing room had exploded, doing damage to the amount of about £5O. The cause of the explosion is said to be as follows :—The manager, on leaving the works at half- past eight on the previous evening, left a tap to the pipe which conveyed the gas to the condenser open. Next morn- ing, immediately after the explosion, the tap was found shut, and it was undoubtedly owing to this circumstance that the explosion occurred. The only person who was on the premises at the time of the explosion was the night watchman, and he does not appear able to throw any light en the matter. It would seem to be certain that seme time during the night some one must have gained access to the works and shut the tap, thus causing the explosion. The works are surrounded by wooden palings, over which it would be easy to climb. It is expected that the explosion has beea caused maliciously by some one. Tan VICAR OF WIDNES ON THE VICARAGE LAND. Writing to the Parish Messcnger, the Vicar of Widnes says: —" In 1875 the Easter Vestry, being informed that the por- tion of land, some 1,000 or 1,200 yards, adjoining the vicarage—and for years enclosed by the vicarage wall—did not actually belong thereto, resolved to rent the same from the legal owner. Strange so say the resolution appeared to be forgotten, for no rent was paid, and when the present ochupier of the vicarage took possession, he wasdisagreeably surprised to find five years' rent demanded, and the wall thrown down. From that time to the present the precints of the vicarage have witnessed a repetition in miniature of that period in early British history when the helpless natives could only gaze aghast at their fierce and northern neigh- bours, pouring into their own and peculiar territory, through and over the broken walls. This matter, like a few others handed down, have given to the churchwardens and council no small amount of auxiety. It was felt that although at this time the rent for back years could not be legally enforced, it was morally due, and the vestry of the present year determined to ask voluntary donations to pay it, and also decided to give up the land. A list was opened by Churchwarden Treacy, which shows that some residing out- side the parish have behaved very liberally. The same may be said of all the parishioners whose names appear; but money came In very slowly, ad the amount (140) has only now been completed.*

STAR OF TEMPERANCE BRASS BAND.—This band will, on Monday on the promenade, and on Friday on ttg.,anarket ground, play the following programme :—Over- tole, " Confidence," Hernnaerle ; fantasia, Rose d' Amour," 'Bleger • \raise, " Susette," E. Telford • ' selection, "Round ' the world," H. Round; quadrille, "Caledonians," R. Smith; polka, " Bijou," J. Harris; schottische, "The signal," M. Seaman; National Anthem. The performances of the band have been a decided • success during the summer ; and the public will regret to hear that owing to the fast shortening days they will only be continued or about three weeks.

BOWLS AT HALTUN.—The match between Mr. S. Yarwood and Mr. John Price, both of Runcorn, on the green of Mrs Ormson, the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton, was concluded the other night. The game was 51 up, and was of very even character up to 34, Mr. Yarwood having slightly the best of it. From this point, however, it could easily be seen that there was only one in it, as Mr. Yarwood, playing in splendid form, ran up 49 to Mr. Price's 38, and eventually won by six points, the game being—Mr. Yarwood 51, Mr. Price 45.

ATTEMPTED BHRGLARY AT RUNCORN.—ShortIy after two o'clock on Wednesday morning, as Sergeant Whalley was proceeding up High-street, Runcorn, he heard a cry of "Police," and on running back to the shop of Mr. E. Couset next to the Post Office, was told by the niece of Mr. Couse that someone had tried to enter the house at the back. The officer promptly went to the rear of the premises, and dis- tinctly heard a man making his escape across the roofs of some low cottages which run towards Mersey-street. He procured the assistance of two or three other officers, and began a close search in the houses of the neighbourhood, but uotwithstanding the strictest examination, no trace of the supposed burglar could be found. We are informed that Mr. Couse and his wife were away from home at the time. FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT DARESBURY. The Peaceful village of Daresbury was all animatioa on Thurs- day last, consequent upon the marriage of Miss Emily Jones youngest daughter of Mr. W. C. Jones, of The Elms, Dares- bury, to Mr. D. L. Wright, of Liverpool, which was celebrated in the quaint old church. The edifice had been elaborately and effectively decorated with flowers, plants, and ever- greens, and when the wedding party assembled the scene was most imposing. Long before half-past eleven, the time fixed for the performance of the ceremony, the church was crowded with spectators, and among those present were— Lady Brooke and family, Lady Greenall and party, Mr. Jones, Mrs. Jones, Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Quekett, Mrs. C. Jones, Mr. Kearsley, Mrs. Appleton and party, Miss Milner and party, Mrs. Wright and party, Mr. Crosfield and party, Mrs. Duck- worth, Mrs. Dodd, Mrs. Miller, Mrs. Wrigley, Mrs. Cobball, Mrs. G. Daglish, and others. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Canon Heron, of Moore, assisted by the Rev. W. H. Spencer, of Daresbury; and the bride was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were Miss Jones, Miss C. A. Jones, Miss Greenall, Miss E. Mil' ner Miss A. MacLaren, Miss F. Daglish, and Miss A. Miller. Mr. Wynne Jones, of Wilderspool, acted as best man. The bride was attired in cream satin, with a white veil, and the bridesmaids in cream-coloured silk dresses with hats to match. After the ceremony the Wedding March was played by Mr. Wright, and the newly-married pair left for The Elms, where the Adding breakfast had been prepared. From the church to The Elms numerous triumphal arches had been erected, bearing mottoes wishing "Health and Happine;s," "Peace and Prosperity," and "Success to the Happy Pair." Over 100 rescnts of s clstly description had been made to the bride, the servants presenting a handsome piece of crockery. About three o'clock the happy couple left for London, en route for Parrs and Switzerland. In the afternoon the school children from Daresbury and Moore were entertained to tea, and various games were engaged in on the lawn by the wedding guests, the weather being very favourable.

In reply to the Queen's telegram of inquiry and sympathy, Mrs. Garfield despatched the following message :—" To he Majesty Queen Victoria, Osborne, England. Your Majesty's kind inquiry finds the President's condition changed for the better. In the judgment of his medical advisers there is strong hope of his recovery. His mind is entirely clear, and. your Majesty's kind expressions of sympathy are most grateful to him, as they are gratefully acknowledged by me. —LUCRETIA R. GARFIELD.' —A Daily News New York telegram says: The papers comment feelingly on -the Queen's message to Mrs. Garfield.—The Times says: Be- neath all consideration of statecraft and national comity the sympathy of one woman who has known sorrow and be- reavement with another who stands in the shadow of widow- hood will awaken a responsive thrill throughout the homes of two great nations. WAsitmarox, August 19.—At 2-30 this morning the Pre- sident was resting quietly. He swallowed during yesterday nine ounces of liquid food, principally koumiss, all of which he retained and apparently digested. A more confident and hopeful feeling now prevails with regard to the President's condition. When the Executive Mansion was closed for the night, yesterday, Dr:Agnew went home, previously assuring Mrs. Garfield that he did not consider his presence necessary. The President was doing well. PROMOTIONS IN THE MARINES.—Lord NORTHBROOK, in reply to the Earl of Longford, explained the new system of promotion in the marines. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. ' The SPEAKER took the chair at four o'clock. Mr. Broome moved that the House be counted. The Smeasa counted 40 members present. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE BY A PRIEST.—MY. Fousraa said he could find no record of a report having been made by an Irish constable to his superior officer of his being struck by a Roman Catholic priest for not sainting him.

AFFIRMATION OF WITNESSES.—Tha ATromwEr-GEwEriAL, replying to Mr. Labouehere, said that if a magistrate refused to allow a witness to affirm, he having conscientions objec- tions to take • the oath, it was open by writ of mandamus to compel the magistrate to take the evidence tendered. THE RE-ARREST OF MR. MICHAEL DANITT.—Mr. PAR- NELL gave =doe that on going into Committee of Supply, if possible to-morrow, to call attention to the re-arrest of Mr. Michael Davitt.

THE COURSE OF PUBLIC Busnass.—Mr. GLLDSTONII gave notice that next week he should move that public business commence at three instead of four. He proposed to take the Regulation of Forces Bill and Irish Church Amendment Act Rill to-morrow.

NEW Warr.—A new writ was issued for the Elgin Burghs. THE IRISH Es'mu:rm.—The House then went into Com- mittee of Supply on the Irish estimates.—On the vote for the expenses of the chief secretary to the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland being proposed, Mr. BIGGAR moved that the vote be reduced by the sum of £2,000, the amount of the salary of the chief secretary. His motive for doing so was that he considered the right hon. gentleman now filling the office had been a thorough failure, and had shown general unfitness for the post. He had acted very unfairly as regarded the arrest of persons under the Coercion Act, and had shown a decided disposi- tion to give importance to reports of spies and informers.— Mr. PARNELL, while believing that Mr. Forster had broken down in his attempt to fulfil the multifarious duties of the office, admitted that he did not think one man existed who could satisfactorily discharge its many dnties. He thought a thorough reform was required in the Government of Ire/and as it was impossible to continue the present system. What was wanted in that country was local self Government.

BREACHES or THE PEACE.—EIIen Fearns and Julia Quinn were summoned for causing a breach of the peace. —P.C. Strickland said that on the 7th inst. be was going up Pleasant-street when he heard the two defendants quarrelling and using most disgusting language.—Each defendant was ordered to enter into their own recognizances of .£lo,and two sureties, to keep the peace for one month.—Annie Smith, Ellen Kearns, Julia Quinn, Mary Nolan, Mary Daley, Ann Duffy, Edwary Duffy, and Sarah Brown were charged with having been guilty of a similar offence in May-street, Moss Bank. Smith did not appear, and, on the application of Seperintendent Barker, a warrant was granted for her ap- prehension.—P.C. Strickland said that on the 9th inst. the defendants quarrelled and caused a crowd of about 200 people to assemble. Previous to his entering the street, some of the people had broken in the door of Duffy's house, and the windows. The defendants made use of very filthy language.—Each of them was bound over in £lO, and two sureties of £5, to keep the peace for two months; or, in de- fault, be sent to gaol for 14 days.--A like charge was pre- ferred against Sarah Brown.—P.C. 700 said that on the 9th inst. he saw the defendant going on Chapel-lane, Cronton, and using language of a very bad character to a man who was in her company. A great crowd followed.—Defendant said the only crowd upon the occasion was the policeman, who was standing at his own house door talking to his wife. In fact, there was not another soul about —The Bench ordered her to eater into her own recognizances of £lO to keep the peace for one month, or she must go to gaol for seven days.—Defendant (very excitedly) : I will not pay a blessed farthing. I will go to "quod for seven days.-- Elizabeth Bushell, who had been previously convicted, was, on the evidence of P.C. Pitt, ordered to find sureties in £lO, and two of £5, to keep the peace, for having‘made a dis- turbance in the street on the previous night, or go to prison for seven days. PHYSIOGNOMY AND A BOLD THlEF.—Bridget Fallon was brought up on remand charged with stealing a ham, the pro- perty of Mr. Samuel Sadler, grocer, Ann-street West. —Jas. Foster, an assistant to the prosecutor, said that about ten o'clock on Saturday night the prisoner entered the shop, and afterwards went outside for the purpose of examining several pieces of bacon. He kept his eye upon her, as she seemed to be a suspicious character, and a few minutes afterwards he saw her take the ham from a hook near the door, and walk off with it. He followed her and brought her back.—The magistrates sentenced her to one month's imprisonment, with hard labour. A COSTLY SPREE.—Anne Smith and Mary Daley were summoned for doing damage to the house of Ann Duffy by breaking the door and four panes.—Smith was fined 255. Gd. and Daley 155., and, in default, to go to gaol for 14 days.

BOARD AT Woßi.—Tie following were summoned by the Widnes School Board, who were repre- sented by their clerk, Mr. Danby, for not sending their children to school, and were each ordered to pay ss. includ- ing costs:—James Riley, Michael Kelly, Thomas Melia, Johanna Gerrity, Thomas Bate, John Tinkler, and John Whitfield. The cases were proved by school attendance officers Davies, Wood, and Joynson.

MALICIOUSLY INJURING A WOMAN'S CHARACTER.— James Mason was charged by Sarah Gerrard, a widow, who manages a shop in Irwell-lane, with having maliciously in- jured her character.—Mr. Beasley appeared for complain- ant, and said defendant was formerly a customer at com- plainant's shop, and, as ha would not pay what he owed, he was put into the County Court. On the 28th ult. he received a summons, and then went icto the shop to ask complainant why it had been sent. He next proceeded to say that "he would see her in a warm place" before he would pay the money, and charged her with being a thief and an immoral woman. He made such a disturbance that he raised the neighbourhood.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for two months, in the sum of £lO. A DRUMM Metes A DVENTURE.—Edward Walsh was charged on remand with having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap, and also with resisting and assaulting P.C. Robert Johnson.—Superintendent Barker said the case against the prisoner was a very serious one. On the 12th inst. Dr. O'Keeffe left his horse and trap opposite a house at Ditton. Walsh happened to be near the place, jumped into the trap, in which he drove for some short distance down Hale-road on to a piece of waste ground at the bottom of Harrison-street. He knocked down a little boy who was on the waste ground, and so injured his shoulder that he was not yet considered out of danger. Prisoner drove off without taking any notice of the lad, and he was afterwards followed to the Railway Hotel lw Mrs. Charlotte Evans, a woman who happened to witness he occurrence. On being taken into custody the prisoner assaulted the officer.—Mrs. Evans and P.C. Johnson gave evidence in support of this statement. Johnson added that he asked the prisoner for his name and address, but he would not give them. He then told him he must go to the Widnes Police Station, but he held firmly to a fence and refused to move. During the I struggle which followed, Walsh hit him in the face.— Prisoner, when formally charged by Mr. Lewin, deputy magistrates' clerk, said: I throw myself on the mercy of the court.—Mr. Lewin : If it were thought desirable you could be charged with stealing the horse and trap.—Mr. Evans (magistrate) said the Bench had been informed that the child's life is yet in danger.—The Chairman: The prisoner will be sent to gaol for one month for the assault on the police officer.

STEALING IRON.—WELL DESERVED CENSE RE ON A MA CLINE —Two girls named Elizabeth Bon- nen and Elizabeth Kincherley were charged with stealing a considerable amount of iron, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, who were represented by

TEE " SALVATION Am" AT PRESTON : RIOTOTS PitocxEnneos.—On Sanday several disgraceful scenes were enacted in the Theatre Royal and Skating Rink, Preston, which have been selected as the headquarters of a detach- ment of the "Salvation Army." Services are held here on the Sabbath, and are conducted in the style which has be- come so notorious among these enthusiasts, provoking the ribaldry of a section of the youth of Preston, who go to such places with no other object than that of promoting scenes of disorder. The interference of the police was re- quired on Sunday, both at the Theatre and the Skating Rink. At the former place some most disgraceful proceed- ings were witnessed, yells, cat calls, and every species of uproar being quite the order of the day. A large crowd col- lected in Fishergste on Sunday night, and at eight o'clock, when the "Salvation Army's" programme for the day was over, Inspector Keefe, with five other officers was obliged to escort the " HaPelujah Lasses" home in order to protect them from the possible violence of the roughs, whose de- light it is to pester these excitable people. - -

THE FRODSHAM BAZAAR CATASTROPHE. Sir,—After reading in your last issue the letter signed "A I Liberal," relative to the above heading, I could not help thinking what a pity it was the writer of it should not have bad something better in which to employ his time, and for which he is more fitted. It fails to do credit to either his head or heart. One cannot even say as much in its favour as the fox did in reference to the painted mask, when he said, on placing his paw on its brow, "What a beautiful face we have here; the pity is it should lack brains." Your I correspondent's letter not only lacks an indication of brains, but has not even the redeemable trait of a pretty face. Its composition, if composition it can be called, is a mere con- glomeration of words, most wretchedly put together. It is evidently the production of an erratic mind, unevenly balanced, and anxious to father on others the feelings he entertains himself. In spite of his professed grief at what he calls "bigotry and intolerance in the parish'," he is urA- doibtedly an enemy in disguise. He designates himself' Nonconformist of the parish, also one having nothinga.,, o hver to do with the bazaar or the church restoration fund , also as "a disinterested outsider, therefore is sure your readers will not charge him with interested motives.' Now, if by this vague tautological statement he wishes your readers to think he is altogether indifferent to the affairs of the Parish Church he will be disappointed. The fact of his having written at all on the subject plainly shows he has got an interest of some kind, though what that interest is is another thing; perhaps it is something analagous to the feeling of a cantankerous little dog that leads it to bark at everyone it sees. If, however, by the term "disinterested outsider," he means he is unconcerned about or not in- terested in the success of the restoration fund, then, no doubt the public will believe him. The fact of his "having nothing whatever to do with the bazaar," as well as the character of his letter, are quite sufficient to show his want of interest and sympathy, and that he is more an enemy to the parish than a friend, a sower of discord and strife, rather than an advocate of harmony and love. He then goes en to say, "directly after the sad accident, from the high wind blowing both tents down on Wednesday afternoon last, we heard on every side, so that I became astonished at the people's bigotry and overbearing manner. 'Oh! it just serves them right ; nothing better could be expected. The church will tumble down next. Anybody breaking the Sabbath, a retributive providence will follow. Sabbath breakers are worse than thieves, for they rob God of His own. It was the Lord's avenging wind to break down their idols.'" The above are but a few specimens of the harsh and bitter words heaped upon the vicar and working committee of the bazaar. Who were the people, I wonder, who were saying this on "every side ?" I myself talked with a great many respect- ing the accident, and must confess I never heard such ex- pressions come from the lips of anyone; but, on the contrary all seemed to be exceedingly sorry, and expressed their deepest regret at what had happened. I never even dreamt of the possibility of such malicious feelings existing in the mind of anyone, not even worldly people, to say nothing of I nonconformists, to whom they are attributed, until I teed your correspondent's letter. Nor do I believe in the exis- tence of such feelings even now, notwithstanding his revela- tions, except that they exist in his own heart, a matter concerning which I have little doubt. He next says, "According to my limited experience of such things it is merely an excuse for the nonconforming part of the parish to abstain from supporting the bazaar fund." What things does he mean? Certainly not the blowing down of bazaar tents., for that is a new experience in this neighbourhood. Nor can he even mean church bazaars without the tents it being about 40 years, I think, since the last was held: rather toe wide an interval, that, to base experience on Consequently the term "such things" cannot possibly refer to any previously observed attitude of Nonconformists to the Church, there having been nothing of a similar kind before to call such attitude forth. Then if there has been nothing of an outward character to give him this experience he must have got it from some things within; and the question is, what are those things? Undoubtedly they are little envious feelings of opposition and ill-will in the soul. And, if so, then I am glad he introduced that little word "limited experience of such things." It lets us see, though unin- tentionally, how narrow and circumscribed such feelings ars •' so narrow that I am inclined to think they are limited to his own experience only; or at the most, as in the case of the old extravagant story, instead of thou- sands of cats fighting on every side, there is, after all, only his and another. If his experience had been larger, and not so limited, he would have known that the excuse he frames for Nonconformists abstaining from supporting the bazaar fund is not applicable to them at ill, as a body ; for they did support it; they contributed in cash, gave goods for the stalls, and went in large numbers on the days of sale in order to purchase. It is really a great injustice to the Nonconformists to have such discreditable charges madee against them, all of whom, as far as my experience gees, which is not limited, not only wish well to the Parish Church, but have at the same time great respect for th vicar, Mr. Blogg, who is evidently a kind and courteous gentleman. It is to be hoped, however, the people of the parish will treat the jembled production according to its worth, and consign its ill-designed contents to everlasting forgetfulness. After the very serious advice your corre- spondent gave to some one respecting the affair, the wonder is, how the letter came to be written at all. He says, "When I heard a respectable resident:saying, I shall never give a penny towards the old church, for it cannot prosper now they have broken God's Day." I replied, 'My friend, if the wind had not accidentally turned over the canvas tents you would never have heard a word about the Sunday work of the men who put it up, and if you were wise you would never let it pass your lips again, for you may depend the committee has about as much to do with it as you have.' Now, one would have thought, Mr. Editor, after such earnest advice, your correspondent would himself have acted on it. Surely, if reticence was wise on the part of the respectable resident, it would have also been wise on his; but instead of this, he at once shouts out on the house- top what he advised not to be whispered in a corner; he immediately writes away to your much read paper, in order to give the hushed-up word all the publicity he possibly could. That inconsistent act itself, apart from all else, is quite sufficient to reveal his ignoble disposition. All real Nonconformists will know at once the true value to set upon this croaking scribe bearing, their name; but what the vicar and church committee may think about this anonymous friend of theirs, I know not, but can easily imagine their saying, "If this is how he shows his love, then save us from his spite." Being a friend then of neither one nor the other, but an enemy of both, it seems the only name we can designate him by is a kind of Ishmaelite, whose hand is against every one, and every one's band against him. In the interests of Nonconformists, whom at this time I wish to represent, I sincerely trust yen will give this a place in your nest issue.—l am, yours, etc., A NONCONFORMIST. Frodsham, Aug. 16th, 1881.

"MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE PEOPLE." "Distance lends enchantment to the view." Sir,—Your youthful correspondent, Master Arthur Ben- nett, has made a startling discovery. He finds that certain distant savages are dazzled by the regal splendour of monarchy as it exists in England. He speaks of this as "one of the strongest ties of the Empire ; and maintains that therefore we ought to keep up this system of splendid pauperage ! Now, it is all very wellfor outsiders like our colo- nists to enjoy the tinsel glitter of a monarchy, towardswhich they contribute nothing, leaving the British taxpayer to growl and pay the piper, while he wonders, and with reason, if the game be worth the candle. I have found this kind of cheap loyalty to prevail among the Canadians. They enjoy all the benefit (?) to be derived from this show equally with ourselves, and have their satisfaction heightened by its cheapness. They are the lilies of the Empire; they toil not, neither do they spin in its support; and yet are arrayed in the borrowed robes of regal splendour. It appears to me to be a very weak cause that needs to go so far afield for arguments in its support. If Master Bennett can find one argument in favour of monarchy on the other side of the world, we, who are sitting at the feet of the idol and have found it to be of clay, can see many more than one in favour of its abolition, and the substitution of a simpler and less expensive system. Englishmen, as a rule, like to get what they NY for. Now the millions annually spent directly or indirectly upon monarchy are ostensibly devoted to the go- vernment of this country. I say ostensilsly, for no man in his senses would maintain that the keeping of some dozen or so of people in a state of luxurions idleness has anything to do with the good government of this country. Royalty in England is neither more nor less than a regal incubus, John Bull's old man of the sea, sitting on his shoulders pre- tending to guide him, and being a burden and a hindersome encumberance to him. One very strong argument against the continuance of this system is this : that we are not justi- fied in placing any merely human being in such a position, and making demigods of them by offering them a kind of semi-worship. What wonder if in the midst of this foolish adulation they lose their beads and forget they are mortal, and their own intrinsic insignificance; forget also that they cwe their eminence to the fact of standing upon the loosely piled pennies of the people, which at any time by the will of the people may crumble beneath their feet. As it at present exists it is little better than the worship of the golden calf; it is the accumulated wealth gathered from the reluctant taxpayers of England that is bowed down to and spoken to as gracious Majesty. For, strip Gracious Majesty of the gilding of its income and other extrinsic attractions, and see what a poor show it would make in the world. This adoration of accumulated wealth, is it not mammon worship? Your correspondent, being fresh from school, will probably remember what caused the reduction of the English monarchy from absolute to limited. Not the virtues, but the arrogant blindness of Its members. The degradation of the sovereign from absolute to limited was merely the transition step to the entire abolition of the institution. Parliament must be the hhest and the ultimate governing authority in England,highestd the Premier its only and responsible bead. Self- government is a virtue individually and nationally: an it 13 time we as a nation cast away the regal leading strings which have been so long more of a hindrance than a guide to us. Time is working for us towards this end: mot is likenarhy in England is the shadow of a former substance. I the mud upon the wall; it is there because it is there, and because no one cares to be at the trouble of shifting it at present. The strongest prop to the throne is the sex of Bs present occupier. However open their eyes may be to the uselessness of the gilded sham, the people are disinclined to disturb one whose sex and associations appeal so strongly to their forbearance. John Bull is at present blinded by a petticoat; but when he gets his eyes free he will lower his head, make a charge, and. , 'weep away this effete old sham. The time is rapidly • •

approaching when Englishmen will have to ask themselves the question whether when, by the lapse of time, this post becomes vacant, another sinecurist shall be appointed at the nominal salary of three hundred and odd thousand pounds per annum, to live a life of luxurious idleness and play the role of non-ruling ruler. They will come to ask them- selves if the very existence of this institution is not a stand- ing disgrace to them, meaning, as it does, either the want of the ability to govern themselves or the good sense at once to abolish the fictitious rulership. That the good, practical sense of Englishmen will in the end prevail over antiquated and romantic notions of loyalty, I fully believe. The monarchy of England is as surely doomed as was Temple Bar, which, in some respects, it resembles. Both may have had their use, both become useless, and an obstruction to the business of life. Temple Bar was taken down; but some corporate idiots must needs erect a memorial of it, to be almost as great a nuisance as the Bar itself. So the absolute monarchy of England was taken down, but the men who did it were afraid of carrying out their work to its logical end, so they raised a memorial of the dead thing they had killed, in the shape of a limited monarchy. So we I have now the task before us of sending this regal travesty to seek its city similitudes among the pale shades of things that have been and are not. In concluding, sir, I would advise those who are casting about to find arguments to bolster up shakey institutions, not to do so; quiesence is their true policy. Ventilation is th 3 great enemy of these musty old structures, and the more we are led to discuss the them the sooner will be their fall. Well may they pray to be saved from their friends.—l am, sir, very truly yours, August 15th, 1881. JOHN PEERS.

RE THE RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD V. THE HEAD MASTER OF HOLY TRINITY SCHOOL. Sir,—l am directed to request you to 43 good enough to publish the following correspondence that has arisen out of the above case between the School Board, the Education Department, and the managers of these schools, in order that the public may judge of my right in refusing to supply certain returns to the local authority.-1 am, sir, yours respectfully, T. H. ANNETT. Holy Trinity Schools, Runcorn, 18th Aug., 1881. (1.) From the Runcorn School Board to the Education Department. "Runcorn School Board, Warrendale, Frod- sham Preston Brook, 6th July, 1881.—Sir,—I am directed to inform you that the Board have hitherto regularly received a weekly return (on forms supplied by the Board), from the various masters and mistresses of the public ele- mentary schools of the district of (1) the number of chil- dren on the roll, (2) the number of children in average attendance, and (3) a list of the irregulars and non-attenders; which returns have been of the greatest value to the Board in enabling them to carry out their bye-laws. Mr. T. H. Annett, the master of Holy Trinity Boys' School having refused in May last, and again in June, to supply the returns in question, I am to inquire whether my Lords are of opinion (sec. 22, Elementary Education Act, 1870,) that Mr. Annett is justified in refusing to give the Board the information they seek.—l have the honour to he," &c., dm. (2) From the Education Department to the managers of Holy Trinity Scheols. "Education Department, 21st July, 1881.—Rev. Sir,—l am directed to forward to you, for the observations ef the managers, the enclosed copy of a letter which my Lords have received from the clerk to the School Board of Runcorn.—l have the honour to be," dm., drc. (3) From the managers of Holy Trinity School to the Education Department. "Runcorn, August 9th, 1881.— Sir,—At a . meeting of the managers of Runcorn Holy Trinity National School, held this day, your favour of the 21st ult. to our chairman, the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., was taken into consideration. lam directed to inform you that the statements contained in the communication of the clerk to the School Board are not strictly accurate, inasmuch as the master of our school declined to supply a list of absentees only. That this is so, and, indeed, the position he has taken in this matter may be gleaned from the two newspaper cut- tings (appended), which give the officer's report of Mr. Annett's action. From a Runcorn paper of June 4th :—"May 26, 1881.—Mr. Rigby.—Sir,—l have paid my usual weekly visit to the Trinity boys' school to-day to consult with Mr. Annett respecting the Irregulars and non-attenders. He at once informed me that he should not have any more to say to me about them, and that he was exceedingly obliged to me for what I had done. So far as I was able I had always done my duty; but he told me that he had bees informed by the parents I had been inducing them to send their boys to Halton school on the ground that the walk would do them good. Mr. Annett said that taking this into consideration, and also that the cases reported had not been properly dealt with, he should decline to give me any more returns. The schoolmaster told me I was quite at liberty to come and copy the returns myself, and thus obtain any Infor- mation I might require. I told him that I had not made use of any such remarks as those attributed to me, and I requested that he would report the whole matter to the School Board. Mr. Annett said he should not do so, and heals° declined to give me the name of the parent who had told him so. I thought it advisable to inform you of what had taken place, and ask what course I had better adopt—whether I had better report to the Board, and also what course I ought to pursue in the future.— I am, yours obediently. THOMAS BOWYER." From the Runcorn Examiner of July 9th, 1881.—" Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, presented his document as to monthly returns, which was as follows :—The returns for the past month I have been unable to complete owing to Mr. An- nett, master of the Trinity boys' school, refusing to supply the necessary figures. Oa the 16th of June last I called at his school and asked him it he would supply the Board with the returns as usual. He declined to do so. and informed me that his books were at my service to copy from them what the Board might require. Since the last meeting," &c., &c. You will observe that every facility was offered to the officer for abstracting the information from the registers him- self. lam to say that Mr. Annett has been driven to this course of action for the following reasons :—Firstly. Be- cause. owing to injudicious remarks made by the School Board officer to certain :parents, boys have not been permitted to return to school after his visit. Secondly. Be- cause of the great loss of time incurred in writing out the , lists, and in subsequently listening to the excuses for ab- sence as ascertained by the officer (this is in accordance with the Board's rules). The attention that Mr. Annett has had to give to the officer on the occasion of his visit has often occupied the time devoted to two lessons, and of necessity interfered somewhat with the ordinary school routine. Thirdly. Because the excuses given by the officer were identical in some cases week after week, and after him- self visiting and finding great discrepancies between the visitor and parents' reasons, Mr. Annett concluded that the lists were not attended to satisfactorily (a duplicate copy of a list with the result of the officer's work enclosed). Fourthly. Because the teachers find that by sys- tematically visiting they do greater good than the School Board officer, and that their visits I are received in a more kindly spirit by the parents than his. In proof of this lam to point out that during the first four years of the Board's existence the percentage on the average attendance at our boys' school cud not exceed 70. Since the change of teachers, two years ago, it has gradually risen to 80 and 83, and during the past two months, i.e., since the School Board statistics were not sup- plied, the weekly average has gone up from 184 to 203. This visiting on the part of the teachers necessarily incurs much extra labour and trouble, but, as it is done out of school hours and with marked success, the managers feel convinced that, inasmuch as the average attendance has improved, and that Mr. Annett's sole object is the welfare of the school, he would not have taken the stand he has, neither, indeed would they have tolerated such action, had the school bemfited in the least by the School Board returns. —I have the honour to be; &c., dm." (4) From the Education Department to the Managers of Trinity School.—Education Department, 16th August, 1881. —" have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 9th inst. In reply, I am to furnish, for the information of the managers, a copy of a letter addressed by this department to the Clerk of the Runcorn School Board.—l have the honour to be, dm., dm." Education Department,' 16th August, 1881.—"Sir,—Ad- verting to your letter of the 6th ultimo, I am now directed to state that my Lords have communicated with the cor- respondent on account of the Holy Trinity Boys' School, and learn from him that the managers of the school have offered the visitor of your Board every facility for abstract- ing the information which he requires from the registers. Under these circumstances, the Education Department con- siders that no case for a reference to thein under section 22 of the Elementary Education Act of 1873 has arisen.-1 have the honour to be, &c., &c."

OUR POSTAL SERVICE. , The annual report of the Postmaster-General to the Lords Commissioners of her Majesty's Treasury 'illustrates, by many striking statistics, the fact that the department repre- sents the most colossal and probably the most efficiently managed business ever reared either by State or private en- terprise. There are now 47,000 post-office employes, and 14,549 post-offices. The number of letters delivered in the United Kingdom during the past twelve Months was 1,176,423,600, showing an increase of 43 per cent.; the nu mber of post-cards, 122,884,000, showing •an increase of 7.4 per cent.; the number of book packets and circulars, 248,881,600, showing an increase of 163 per cent.; and the number of newspapers 133,796,100, showing an increase of 25 per cent. Over 5,300,000 letters were dealt with in the Returned Letter Office, and of these it was found impossible to deliver 475,000. The number of cases in which letters , are posted without any direction whatever is often re- ferred to by medical men as a symptom of the growing absent-mindedness or confusion which is produced by life at high pressure, and which is thought to be shaping itself into a new type of mental disease. There were no fewer than 27,000 cases of the kind last year. One undelivered letter contained a bank note for £lOO, still unclaimed, and attached to the seal of another was a sovereign, which was returned to the owner, who had forgotten to remove it. The use of too fragile covers occasioned the escape of sow 30,000 articles, and the 11 escape of 30,000 articles no doubt occasioned in its turn, as the postmaster-General sententiously suggests, "much die- appointment"—a disappointment, however, for which the senders have only their own carelessness and stupidity to thank. The public have not yet overcome the playful habit of transmitting through the post-office animal and perishable matter, such as fish, sausages, birds to be stuffed, clotted cream, fruits, yeast, jellies, live kittens, and dead rats." All such dainties are stopped, out of consideration for the health of the officers; and persons addicted to making gifts to their friends of sausages, live kittens, or dead rats, will have to I select some other method of conveyance. There are now over 2,000 women in the employ of the post-office' and the I authorities speak very favourably of the success which has ' attended their efforts to utilise female industry. Mr. Paw- cett's admirable schemes for promoting thrift by making the post-office a huge savings bank, with branches in the smallest t highlyvillages and every facility for investment, havtheshme been lsuccessful. The telegraph business continues , to increase, the,messagee sent during the year. exceeding by 13 410,828 those dispatched Its 1879. , ,

TUESDAY.—Bo-fore is,,rs. F. W. Earle, A. B. Gladstone, and H. R. d'A Willis. DAMAGING RI,:-D•WSLEY PARK Wam,—William Barlow, of Thatto Heath, wa charged with wilfully and maliciously damaging a plantation belonging to the Earl of Derby, on the Ist August, to the extent of Id.; also with damaging a wall, owned by his lordship; to the extent of id.—lt ap- peared that on the Ist Augm; there was a festival in Knowsley Park, and to prevent p ,ople obtaining access to the park who did not choose to pkv the priceof admission his lordship's gamekeepers were located in various parts near the boundary wall, which ranges 'rom eight to ten feet in height. In Eceleston, for a distanco of one hundred yards, the upper portion of the wall was 'covered 'with cement and glass in order to debar persons gtAting ver. For many yards the top of the wall had been of this coating, and it being supposed that attempts tduaater would be made at this part, it was watched by two ga n - keepers (Messrs. James Thompson and Edward Smith.. About twelve o'clock the gamekeepers' attention was called to the fact that a man had got over the wall. The keepers emerged from their place of concealment, and the man see- ing he could not get back again before he would be caught, ran in the plantation, but was intercepted by a man connected with the sports, who handed him over to the keepers.—De- fendant was fined ss. and costs. ABSCONDING WITH WORKHOUSE CLormlNG.—Plicebe Fer- guson, a young woman, was charged that she being an inmate of the Prescot Union Workhouse, did desert and carry away certain clothes of the value of 175. 6d., belonging to the Guardians of the Poor, on the 16th November, 1880.— Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, prosecuted, and stated that the prisoner had had three or four illegitimate children in the house.—Mr. W. H. Bicknell, master, said the prisoner absconded from the Workhouse on the 16th Novem- ber, leaving a child aged twelve months behind her, which had become chargeable to the common fund. The child was in the house at the present time. When she absconded the prisoner had on a suit of Workhouse clothing, value 17s. 6d. Prisoner had been in service the last seven months, and had been in receipt of 5s per week. She never made any inqui- ries respecting the child.—ln answer to Mr. Earle, Mr. Har- tley stated the Guardians wished to press for a full penalty, because for some time past many women had deserted their children and gone away with Workhouse clothing.—Mr. Earle observed that the Bench considered it a bad case, and the prisoner must go to gaol for two months with hard labour. ALLEGED THEFT IT A SALE AT HUYTON.—James Mur- ray and Michael Moran were charged, on suspicion, with having stolen a mattress, the property of the executors of late Sir Thomas Birch, Bart., the Hazies, Huyton.—Mr. Superintendent Barker stated that there had been a sale of the late baronet's goods, and the mattress was missed, and it was found in possession of the prisoners. P.C. Morgan stated that he went to the residence of James Murry in Moss-street, Prescot, at half-past one o'clock that morning and found the mattress in the back yard. He afterwards apprehended the prisoners. On being charged with the offence, Moran said the mattress was given to him by a man in Liverpool for assisting him to load, and Murray helped him to carry it home. Murry said "not stealing it; it was given to us."—Remanded. ROBBING A TURNIP FIELD AT HUYTON.—George Fen- shaw, twelve years of age, was charged with stealing six turnips value 4d., from a field at Huyton, the property of John turnips, stated that in consequence of some 60 or 70 turnips having been pulled up and taken away from a turnip field, he, on the 4th inst., concealed him- self near to the road. After watching a short time he saw defendant enter the field and pull six turnips out of the ground. Since the summons had been taken out, turnips had been stolen from the field, but could not say that defen- dant had taken any of them. He did not wish to press the case against the defendant, who was the first he had caught. He simply brought the case to act as a warning to others. Defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined is. and costs, and ordered to pay the damage. COAL STEALING AT WHISTON.—Jane Smith, an elderly woman, was charged with stealing 601 b. of coal from the Carrs Colliery, Whiston, on the 12th August.—Joseph Storey, surface foreman at the colliery, said he saw the de- fendant picking coal from the "tip" heap. He had cautioned her on many previous occasions. The coal was worth Id.— Defendant stated that Storey had on more than one occasion given her permission to pick the coal. He had also given permission to other persons to take what coal they could from that heap. A witness swore to hearing Storey give defendant permission to pick coal from that heap.—Defen- dant was discharged with a caution.—Martha Titler, for stealing 401 b. of coal, value Id., from the same colliery, was fined ss. and costs. SLEEPING IN AN EMPTY HOUSE AT HUTTON.—John Jones and Charles Scriven were brought up on remand charged with unlawfully wandering abroad and sleeping in an empty house at Huyton, not having any visible means of subsis- tence.—Superintendent Barker said the prisoners were taken into custody at a quarter past twelve o'clock on Tuesday morning, for sleeping in an unoccupied house at Huyton. He asked the Bench to discharge the boy (Scriven) and put him into the box to give evidence against Jones. The boy met Jones in Liverpool a couple of days before they were apprehended, and they came on to Huyton. Jones sent Scriven and another boy, who had been discharged, round begging for the purpose of examining people's back doors, in order that he might commit a burglary.—The Bench dis- charged Scriven, who, on being sworn, said his home was in Liverpool. He met the prisoner near a brickfield, in Liverpool, on the previous Saturday week, and accompanied him to Kensington. Prisoner said he was going to break into a cottage on the Liverpool-road. He told him and the other boy to stop outside and watch, and if any one came to give him warning by a cough. They did not keep watch, nor did they pull their shoes aid stockings off as proposed by the prisoner. He was along with the prisoner when they were taken into custody in the empty house.—Mr. Supt. Barker said the ether boy was in very bad heelth and he had been dis- charged.—ln answer to Mr. Earle, Scriven said he was a baker and his father a dock labourer.—P.C. Hall deposed that he apprehended the prisoner and two boys on Tuesday morning, in an empty house at the Horn Smithies, Huyton. —Superintendent Barker said Jones gave the name of Ernest Melrose, and that he belonged to Goole. The authorities at that place had been written to and he had received a com- munication, which he handed to the Bench.—Mr. Earle (to the prisoner) : It appears that nothing good is known of you at Goole. You were in this house with two boys under rather suspicious circumstances. You have not given al good account of yourself, and you must be imprisoned for one month with hard labour. CHARGES UNDER THE POOR LAW—George Pope and Thomas Pope were summoned to show cause why they should not contribute towards the support of their mother, who was chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. Parkinson relieving officer, said defendants' mother had been charge- able to the Union since the 2nd June last. Both defendants had been applied to, but they had refused to pay anything. Defendants' mother was 74 years of age.—George Pope appeared in answer to the summons, but his brother was absent. The former stated that his mother resided at his house at Tarbock. She occupied the front portion of the house, and he occupied the back. He was a blacksmith.— The relieving officer said Gorge got good wages as he was a master blacksmith.—Defendant said he had only a boy working for him. Trade was bad, and he was only making just enough money to keep himself and family. Their worships were no doubt aware what could be made in an agricultural district like Tarbock. His brother was in business at Earlestown, and was in a very different position to him and could well afford to contribute.—Mr. Hartley (clerk to the Guardians) said he believed the brother was willing for an order to be made upon him.—The relieving officer said he was instructed to ask for an order for 3s. per week from each of them.—George was ordered to contribute 2s. and Thomas Sc. per week.--Richard Houghton was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute to , the support of his wife, who had become chaigeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. Swift prosecuted and Mr. Riley de- fended.—Mr. S. F. Wensley, relieving officer, was called to prove the case.—Mr. Riley asked for the production of the order, under the common seal of the Guardians, and signed by the chairman, authorizing the relieving officer to take those proceedings; but as it was not forthcoming the case was withdrawn.—Charles Clubb, St. Helens, was also summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his wife.—Mr. Swift prosecuted. Mr. Wensley, relieving officer, stated that on the 13th June defendant's wife applied to him for relief. She appeared before the Guardians, and they made an order for her admission to the workhouse, where she remained for a time. After coming out of the workhouse she again applied to him for relief, and on the 28th July she again appeared before the Guardians, and they allowed her 5s per week. He had paid her that amount weekly ever since. Defendant had told him he was willing to support his wife and children in the workhouse.—Defendant was ordered to pay 5s towards the support of his wife and children. SHOCKING STATE OF COTTAGES IT WHISTON.—Dorothy Thomas and Peter Mutch were summoned for neglecting to abate a nuisance on . their premises at Warrington-road, Whiston, which was injurious to health.—Mr. S. H. Hart- ley said he was instructed by the Guardians, who acted as the Rural Sanitary Authority where there was no other focal authority, to take proceedings against the occupiers of two cottages on Warrington-road. Whiston, with a view to get- ting the said cottages closed. The property originally be- longed to a man named Parkinson, who in the year 1831 bwyasthsee sent ut ao r Ld iaanncsa os tf e tr hLeupn Prescot si cc ot Asylum, Union. and The he emr ea mn a diedi n t ai n ei nd the asylum in 1874. In the meantime the Guardians col- lected the rent, and appropriated it towards the man's main- tenance, but after his death the rents had not been collected, and consequently the property bad got into a very dilapi- dated state, and was totally unfit for human habitation.— Dr. Hall, medical officer, said he had examined the cottages, and they were not fit to live in. One side of the building had tumbled down; a portion of the thatch was off, and what remained was decayed; the walls were damp ; there were no drains; no water supply, and no privy accommoda- tion. The cottages were unfit to reside in, and were in- jurious to health.—Mr. Twist, surveyor and nuisance in- spector,stated that he bad served notices upon the occupiers ordering them to leave the cottages.—ln answer to Mr. Willis, Mr. Hartley said the Guardians had tried to find an owner, but they could not do so. He believed the Duchy of Lancaster had taken the matter in hand.—Mr. Willis asked who the defendants paid rent to, and Mr. Hartley replied that they had not paid rent since 1874. The Authority did not wish to press the case against the defendants if they would leave the cottages.—lt was ultimately decided that Mulch should leave in a fortnight and Thomas in a, month.

TRANSFERS.—The following transfers were granted A beerhouse, Midwood-street, Widnes, from Robert Nickle to Jehn Moss; a beerhouse, Appleton-street, Widnes, front , Thomas Read to Robert Nickle; a beerhouse, Albert-road, Widnes, from Thomas reatman to James Hulme ; the Northwich Vaults, Waterloo-road, Widnes, from William Caton to Samuel Dagnell. A temporary authority to Bell at Clapgate Hotel, Halewood, until next transfer day was granted to James Martin.
NEWTON AND EARLESTO WN.

SCHOOL TREAT AT NEWTON—On Thursday, the annual treat to the scholars attending St. Peter's Day and Sunday schools, Newton, was held. The scholars met at the school about 2 o'clock, and marched in processional order, pre- ceded by the Reformatory band, to the church, where ser- vice was held. An excellent and appropriate address was delivered by the Rev. W. B. aesam. Returning to the „school the scholars, to the number of 500, partook of a good tea with evident enjoyment. Afterwards an adjournment was made to the Castle Hill field, and the weather being beautifully fine various games were entered into with con- siderable zest by the young folks.
MESSRS. IVICCORIZZODALE'S EMPLOYES' TRIP.—The work- people employed at Messrs. McCorquodale's printing works, Newton, and their friends, to the number of about 2,000, le-

Newton early on Saturday morning last by the London and North-Western Railway, for their annual excursion to Liverpool, where they spent an agreeable day in visiting the many " sights " of the city, and the varions attractions on the Cheshire side of the Mersey.

1.0.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN Lon.—On Monday last the members of the Temperance Mission Lodge, War- rington, to the number of 18 paid a fraternal visit to the above lodge. The visitors arrived soon after eight o'clock, and after the initiation of two candidates they were intro• duced and heartily welcomed. Business over, it was re- solved that the visitors be invited to occupy the officers positions and coduct the lodge; Bro. J. W. Hall, honorary deputy, presiding. Bro. Hall, in his opening remarks on the "good of the order," referred to the good feelings exist- ing between the members of both lodges whenever it had been their pleasure to meet one another; and he hoped the same kindly feelings would always characterise the members in the future. Such visits as the one they were now pay- ing the Earlestown Lodge tended to stimulate and strengthen the members in the good work in which they were engaged, there were always pleasant recollections to look back upon afterwards. He also spoke of the great advantages to be derived by members in reading Good Templar and temperance literature which would do much towards strengthening their members, especially the young ones, in the principles of the Order. There being so many and varied temptations surrounding them on every hand, it behoved them to prepare to meet the opposition to be encountered. He was very glad also to notice the very favourable reports of our meetings in The Examiner and other papers from time to time, it becoming evident that the press was becoming more and more on the side of temperance as time went on, and did very much to- wards the advance of the temperance cause in our country. He urged the members to be most determined in standing true to their temperance principles, and do all they could for the good of the Order, in reclaiming the fallen, and in preventing as much as possible others of their fellow crea- tures from falling. It was a grand work, for a grand object, the good of their fellow-men, and if they were faithful, they would meet with a glorious reward.—An excellent pro- gramme was then gone through in good style, songs being given by Bro. A. Thomley, L.Dy., Bro. Mason, &c.; recita- tions by Sister Bowden, Brothers T. Harrison, Alfred Mitchell, Bro. W. Gallop, of Walter Bonehill Lodge; and Brothers John Warburton and George Warburton, jun., of Earlestown Lodge. Bro. John Taylor, of Warrington, gave an excellent practical address on the character of Daniel, pointing out many useful lessons from his life and career, especially suited to the younger members. The visitors and a number of friends partook of supper before leaving for home, after a most enjoyable and pleasant evening.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans.

DESERTING FROM THE ARMY—Charles 07Dowd was charged with deserting from the 69th regiment of foot stationed at Sheffield.—The prisoner was met at Rainhill oh the previous evening by P.C. Thompson. As he could not produce. a pass he was taken into custody and locked up.— Prisoner was remanded to Walton to await an escort.

div.head: EDUCATION ACT, 1870.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT, 1870.

The following circular has just been issued by the Central Nonconformist Committee :—Birmingham, August 9, 1881. c'e have seen with great concern that an attempt is bein`g ,ade to induce the Government to restore the 25th clause 41 ,the Education Act, 1870. Under that clause, school boar le were empowered to pay out of the education rate the fees ,for poor children attending denominational schools. Again 4 this application of the rate the Noncon- formists of England and Wales offered in Parliament a strenuous resistance. The resistance was renewed in a large number of boroughs wfiera school boards had to be elected; and when the boards were constituted, the question whether the fees should be paid gave occasion to long and angry debates. The administration of the compulsory clauses of the Education Act were so rerionely embarrassed by this controversy that the late Confervative Government trans- ferred the payment of fees fron school boards to boards of 1 guardians, and made the payme t obligatory in all cases of I poverty. We have strong sympathy with those who object to this solution of the difficulty on the ground that, when 13-vents have applied to the guardians of the poor for the payment of school fees, the self-respect is diminished which prevents them from seeking parochial relief. To ourselves the solution was never satisfactory; but we are bound to say that in the present condition of public opinion no other im- mediate solution seems possible. To the payment of fees by school boards the objections urged in 1870 retain all their original force. There are large districts in which the whole of the Government grant for elementary education is ad- ministered through irresponsible persons, who maintain their schools for the sake of strengthening their denominational position. That public money should be employed at all for the support of such schools is a monstrous injustice; that such schools should be the only public elementary schools accessable to hundreds of thousands of children is an aggra- vation of the injustice. The laws which once compelled all Englishmen to attend the parish churches have been repealed. But in a considerable number of English parishes the children of Nonconformists are still compelled, under penalty,to attend the schools of the parish clergy. As a guarantee of religious liberty, the conscience clause is notoriously ineffective. If school boards were re-empowered to rtay the fees of children attending denominational schools, these schools, which are already largely supported from national taxation, would de- rive a considerable amount of additional support from the rates, and their existence would then be indefinitely per- petuated. It is probable that in many parishes school boards would be established with the sole purpose of securing fees for the parochial schools. It may be argued that it can make no difference whether the fees come from the poor rate or the school board rate; but experience shows that, while poor parents have very little objection to apply to the school boatd for assistance, their reluctance to apply to the guar- dians is very great. The amount paid ta denominational schools out of the poor rate is comparatively small. The amount they would obtain from the school board rate would in a very few years become very large. To re-enact the 25th clause, with whatever modifications, would be to add great strength to an educational system which, as long as it lasts, must continue to inflict on Nonconformists grievous injustice. We trust, therefore, that, should any movement in this direc- tion be made in your neighbourhood, you will offer it the most serious resistance.—We are, yours faithfully, W. Mid- dlemore, Chairman and Treasurer; R. W. Dale, H. W. Cross- key, J. Jenkyn Brown, Honorary Secretaries.

div.head: FRODSITAM.
div.p: FRODSITAM.

EVANGELISTIC SERVICE AT THE UNION CHURCH SUTTON WEAVER—Special services were held as above on Sunday last, and were continued on Monday evening, con- ducted by the Rev. John Burnham (the Rev. C. H. Spur- geon's singing Evangelist), and the Rev. J. Rigby, of Mal ton, Yorkshire.

_ A WRECK IN THE RIVER WEAVER.—A small screw vessel has been recovered in the river Weaver, which has excited much interest, and is secured near the Sure Hatches. It is a good model constructed of iron, and appears to have been provided with steam power, although the boiler, &c., has disappeared. It is stated that during a recent storm it drifted from its moorings at Warrington. VOLUNTEER MovEmENTs.—The Frodsham volunteer corps marched out on Saturday evening last, under the command of Captain R. Ashton, and visited the residence of James Reynolds, Esq., J.E., Fox Hill. A sham attack was made on the mansion, each man being provided with 20 rounds of blank cartridges, but the weather was very unfavourable for manceuvres of any extent. Refreshments were kindly pro- vided by Mr. Reynolds, which were served out to the men at the close of the movements.
THE FRODSHAM PARISH CIII7RCE BAZAAR—The bazaar which was held last week in aid of the Frodsham Parish

„- Church restoration was, notwithstanding the accident to the tents, an undoubted success, as the handsome sum of up- wards of £BOO was netted clear of all expenses, and goods to the value of about £2OO still remain in hand as a nucleus for another bazaar which it is intended to hold in the autumn. This result could not have been obtained without extraordinary efforts by the ladies and gentlemen connected with the management, and too much cannot be said in praise of the presence of mind displayed by all when the tents col- lapsed, as the sale of articles was resumed the same after- noon, first in the Church-street schoolroom and afterwards at Belle Mont, where the bazaar was continued to Friday evening. It must have been very gratifying to the vicar to notice the spontaneous feeling which prevailed; all con- cerned putting aside self, and working for one common object, namely, the success of the undertaking. It cannot be said that the Dissenters were conspicuous by their absence as many leading members supported the cause.

div.head: PRESCOT WINDOW GARDENING ASSOCIATION.
div.p: PRESCOT WINDOW GARDENING ASSOCIATION.

The first annual show in connection with the Prescot Vritadow Gardening Association was held on Thursday, in the Assembly-room, Derby-street, Prescot, the use of which was kindly granted for the occasion by Mr. W. L. Evans, IX. The exhibition was got up mainly through the instru- mentality and unremitting exertions of Mrs. W. L. Evans, assisted by Miss Moult and the Rev. F. R. Lee, curate of Prescot, and the society has for its chief object the encourage- ment of the working portion of the population of the town in the cultivation of a taste for plants and flowers, and the promotion of cleanliness as far as possible in their homes. The exhibitors numbered 35, and the plants shown amounted to over 300; in addition to which a number of fine green- house plants were contributed (not for competition) by Mr. James Beesley, Mr. Garratt, and Mr. Pratt, which relieved and added considerably to the effects of the exhibits. The staging was carried out by Mr. Beesley, and a word of praise is due to him for the excellent manner in which he performed the work. The prizes were awarded, according to the schedule, not necessarily for the largest plants or those which hap- pened to be in bloom at the time of the show, but for evi- dences of good management, cleanliness, dm., and members were invited to send as many plants as they chose for ex- hibition in addition to those entered for competition. The show was in all respects completely successful, in fact, the results far exceeded the most sanguine expectations of the promoters. The plants on the whole were tolerably good, some of them being a credit to their owners. Ihe judges were Mr. Norris' Halsnead Hall, Whiston ; and Mr. Peter Sherwood, Parkside, Prescot. The weather being fine there was a large attendance of townspeople, amongst those who visited the show being Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P. and Mrs. Evans, Miss Moult, Mrs. Spencely, the Rev. J. Barnacle (vicar of Rainford), Mr. W. Tyrer, Mr. J. T. Hall, Mr. F. Smith, the Rev. L. W. Sampson (vicar of Prescot), the Rev. F. R. Lee, Mr. and Miss Loekwood, Mr. Wm, Evans, Mr. and Miss Park, Mrs. Kendall, Mr. Jas. Berry, Mr. G. J. Paris, Mr. F. Green, Mrs. Driffield, and Miss Driffield, Mrs. H. Cross and the Misses Cross, Rev. H. Coates (curate at Moulton, Lincolnshire), Mrs. Coates, and the Misses Coates, Mrs. Johnson (Derby-street,) Mr. Joseph Garrett, Mr. James Mawdsley, &e. It was intended to have a miscellaneous concert to-night (Friday), but it was • unavoidably postponed for a week. The following is a list of the awards:

div.head: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

A public meeting, under the auspices of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars, was held, on the Market Ground, Earlestown, on Tuesday. After the singing of the hymn, "Dare to be a Daniel," Mr. James Linden,

Honorary Deputy of St. Helens, presided, and in opening the meeting said their object was to endeavour to persuade people to give up the use of intoxicating drinks, which were most dangerous to use, and which were doing harm to all who took them. He spoke of the opposition teetotallers met with some 25 or 30 years ago, the efforts to I obtain a hearing in any public place being very much neutralized by the great opposition the advocates met with from all classes of the community. It had been stated that education would cure drunkenness; but this was soon found to be a fallacy from the fact that no rank or station in life was exempt from its effects. It was a physical evil, and affected ape the moral nature of man, driving out of him in many cases all feelings of self-respect however enlightened he might have been. It was an unmistakeable fact, that whilst our nation had been becoming year by year more educated, they had also become more drunken; the drink bill was increasing every year out of all proportion to the increase of the population. They only knew of one safe and sound cure, the one they had come that night to recom- mend to those present, and he hoped the words of the lecturer would induce a good number of them to be determined to give up the use of drink, and come over on the right side.—The weather, which had become very dull, now inclined to wet, and a drizzly rain coming on it was decided to adjourn to the Distdet Infant School, which, by the kindness of the Vicar, the Rev.T. R. Matthews, had been placed at the disposal of the committee. There were about 150 persons outside who followed into the room, the number being afterwards augmented to about 300.—Mr. DUF- mu-, of Manchester, occasional lecturer for the United Kingdom Alliance, then delivered an address. He dealt very clearly with facts and figures, referring to the drink question in its different aspects, especially showing the injury done to the body by the use of intoxicating drinks. He quoted the opinions of such men as Sir Henry Thompson, physician to the King of the Belgians; Sir William Gull, Dr. B. W. Richardson, and Dr. Norman Kerr, of London ; showing clearly that science was on the side of the abstainer. He also referred to the greatly improved position of the Church of England, and of the various dis- senting bodies on the temperance question. The Archbishop of York, a number of bishops, a larger number of canons and other dignitaries, as well as about 5,000 of the rank and file of the clergy of the Church of England were now total abstainers, and many of them noble workers for the tem- perance cause. Every Christian sect had now its organised temperance society, and the great necessity fer great earnest- ness and activity in the cause of temperance by these different bodies was shown by the fact of such a large num- ber of members of various churches being suspended and struck off the.roll every year through drunkenness. It was robbing the churches of those who should have been its sup- porters, and prevented in a great measure the aggressive work so very necessary in our own and other countries. Trade was yet bad in various parts of the country, but it might well be so whilst so large an amount of money was spent every year in drink. Last year it amounted to 122 millions, a sum almost impossible to realise. Here the gentleman gave some very interesting illustrations to show what a million was. Laid flat one on another, they would reach a height of one mile, and if placed edge to edge a million would reach a distance of 12 or 14 miles, and the people of enlightened Christian England spent as much on drink in one year as would reach 122 times such distances. The lecturer referred to the case of the Caledonian Dis- tillery, Edinburgh, where 150 men produced in one year £1,500.000 of spirits; if the same amount of money was expended in wagons, or anything of that description in the same period, it would find employment for 1,200 or 1,500 hands. It was far better for our country and trade generally that the money should be spent in something that would be useful; whilst we spent on an average about £3 15s. per head on drink, the average for cotton goods was about 7s. od. per bead per year. If the amounts were only re- versed the change in the country would be revolutionary. As John Bright said, we should be hardly able to recognise it. In conclusion, he urged all present to adopt habits of sobriety, they would be able to work better, they would enjoy better health, it would be better for them all through life in every way; let them endeavour to do all they could to make their country better than they found it.—A hearty vote of thanks was moved by Mr. Geo. Warburton, senior, and seconded by Mr. T. O. Roberts, to the Chairman and Lecturer. NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
SATURDAY.—Before Messrs. J. H. Biaey, Houghton, and
Pearson.

THEFT OF MATTT•WG.—A man named Skelhorn was charged with stealing about.Ls yards of asphalte matting,the property of Mr. Pearson, at Golborne, on the 29th ult.; and another man named Boardman was charged with having received the same, knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. Moore appeared for the prisoners.—Thomas Thomson found Skelhorn in Mr. Pearson's garden on the day in question. After he went away the matting was missed, and informa- tion was given to the police. Late in the evening a man named Ashton saw Skelhorn putting the matting on the roof of Boardman's shippon, and Boardtnan was helping him.—P.C. Beardsworth found the matting on the roof of the shippon, and took Skelhorn into custody, and he then said that he had taken the matting, but when he did so he was in drink.—Skelhorn was fined £5, and Boardman was discharged. COAL PILFERERS.—Sarah Winstanley, Jane Helen Greenall, Dinah Evans, and Helen Glover were each charged with stealing a quantity of coal, on the let instant, the pro- perty of Messrs. Evans and Company, Ilaydock.—The prisoners were observed by a policeman going away from colliery carrying a bundle of coal each. On seeing the con- stable they at once dropped the bundles and ran. They were afterwards apprehended.
