were charged with assaulting a widow named Ruth Hindley, at Haydock, on the 4th inst.—Mr. Moore appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Swift for the defendants.—The defen- dant Greenell had been in the habit of calling at Hindley's house, but was told by her some time since not to do so any more. On the night of the 4th inst., about twelve o'clock, he went to her house again in company with Lawrenson. Both defendants were drunk. The woman was in bed, but they knocked violently at the door for admission. She got up and told them to go away, but they refused, and on per- sistently kicking at the door and making a disturbance she at length opened it. Greenall at once struck complainant on the face several violent blows with his fist, and so also did Lawrenson. In the scuffle the woman fell, and the de- fendants kicked her On the stomach and legs, and Green- all toolAold of her by the throat and said he would kill her, when she screamed for help. The woman was rescued by the neighbours. The defendants also damaged the furni- ture.—An arrangement was come to between the parties by which it was agreed the two defendants should each pay complainant the sum of £1 and all coots, they being also bound over to keep the peace for six months in their own recognizances of £2O.

div.head: CRONTON ATHLETIC SPORTS.
div.p: CRONTON ATHLETIC SPORTS.

The fifth annual Cronton athletic sports took place on Saturday afternoon in a field situated near Hough Green station, the use of which was granted by Mr. James Cook, Caxton Lodge. The patrons of the festival include among others Mr. Joseph Robinson, Mr. Edward Fleetwood, Mr. Edward Webster, Mr. james Mawdsley, Mr. R. C. Kaye, Mr. T. Lyon, and Mr. R. Durrill. Messrs. J. H. McMahon, Cook, and Cave (Preston) acted as judges; Mr. H. H. Tilley as starter; and Mr. D. M. Tilley as handicapper. Messrs. R. Burrill, W. Leather J. Ireland, J. Corns, J. Bustard, W. Tomlinson, and J. Leather, assisted in carrying out the general arrangements, but, as usual, the bulk of the work fell upon the hon. secretary, Mr. James Houghton, who per- formed the onerous duties of his office in an indefatigable and praiseworthy manner. The entries numbered 93, an increase on last year by 26, but, one or two exceptions none of the competitors were athletes of any note. As a rule the promoters of the sports have been favoured with fine weather—that indispensable auxiliary to the success of out- door amusements of every description—on the occasion of their annual festival, but on Saturday their luck seemed to have deserted them, as the weather was very unpropitious, rain falling almost without intermission nearly the whole of the time the proceedings were in progress. This of course seriously affected the attendance of spectators, of whom there were not more than 250 or 30ct present. The sports were timed to commence at 2-30 p.m. prompt, and no doubt the time fixed would have been rigidly adhered to, had not the arrangements been materially interfered with by the rain. The Dillon brass band was in attendance, the music of which tended, in some degree' to dispel the gloom which the bad weather had produced in the minds of many of those present. A refreshment tent, provided by Mr. Houghton, of the Unicorn Inn, Cronton, was located on the ground, and seemed to be well patronised. At the close of the proceedings the prizes were distributed to the successful competitors at the Unicorn Inn, by Mrs. H. Houghton. The following is a return of the events, prizes, and winners :- 220 YARDS FIAT RICE (FOR You=s).—First prize, handsome cruet with five bottles; second, pair of splendid vases; third, electro-plated butter cooler. McMahon, Widnes, scratch; 2, H. Connor, Warring- ton, 24. Seven ran. Final heat: 1, H. Connor, Warrington, 24; 2, J. Clarke, Widnes, 40 ; 3, B. Pierpoint, Liverpool, scratch. _ _ .

div.head: ST. HELENS MINERS AND WORKING HOURS.
div.p: ST. HELENS MINERS AND WORKING HOURS.

The dispute between the , colliers and their employers, which caused such great excitement in St. Helens the latter end of last year and the beginning or this, has been partly renewed within the last seven days. f;ctices having been posted at the pit brow of the St. Helens Collieries stating that the men were required to work every Saturday, and play on every alternate Monday, it was intimated to them on Friday that whoever did not work according to tho notice should carry away their tools, as the terms of the r,otice would be strictly adhered to. About 800 men are employed at these collieries, which belong to Messrs. Pilkington, and only about 160 of this number worked on Saturday. The remaining 640 declined to workon those terms, on the ground, that if they gave in on this question the next step would be a return to fortnightly payments. Another reason why they refused to work was that the change was a breach of agree- ment on the part of the masters, it having been agreed at the close of the strike that they should not work more than five days a week. This, they say, was one ef the reasons which induced them to terminate the strike. The statement of the masters is, however, in contradiction to the foregoing. They say that before the strike in March last the men em- ployed at their collieries worked eleven days in the fort- iltkhiinegteoenneseteastiee that a t but t b e n only a m average about 150 of them used every Monday as a play night, enjoying every alternate Monday as a holiday. On resuming work, the men were granted weekly pays, and an, arrangement " temporarily " granted that each Saturday did e outtbem ae men takeolay. advantage M esrs e. Pf day. The greater part of the workings being idl a three con-1 secutive days caused much loss and inconvenience to the masters, as the salaries of the officials were goi •ng on, the same number of ponies were being kept, and the pit generally was getting out of working order. The keeping open of the pits scarcely repaid them, as owing to the roof falling in it was necessary that they should be idle as short a time as possible. Under these circumstances they found it neces- sary. to adopt the system which • ' • the strike, in force prior to e strike, with the exception of weekly pays which they say they have no intention of discontinuing. The men pressed some dissatisfaction with the action of the masters, but the latter firmly declared that if they would not work under the terma stated in the notice they must find work elsewhere. On Saturday, about 160 of the colliers employed at the Ravenhead pit, and on Monday morning over 200 had commenced working. On Monday evening a meeting of about 200 was held on the Fair Ground, when Mr. Cross, the mi ners 'rules and declared agent, condemned the new his intention of appealing to the Home Secretary and the Government Inspector concerning their legality. He Con regretted that many had gone back to work. Arraenscoleu the hat was agreed to that a deputation visit Mw terms thor. F manager, on Tuesday morning, to ask upon men might resume work. On Tuesday night Mr. Cross advised the men to resume work, and there was a geneaal there understanding that they wenld do so. In the morning only remained about 200 out, and these were unwillingunder the circumstances to remain out any longer.

In view of the improvement in the engineering trade in Lancashire, an endeavour is being made to get the wages of the men advanced to the amount paid previousl,y to the re. dution of 2s per week 14 18,78,

£8 in June, 1879, by false pretences, and also by the use of a forged certificate, knowing at the time that the certificate was forged. He was further charged with obtaining a similar cheque for £8 in the month of January, 1880, by false pretences and by another forged certificate, knowing at the same time that that certificate also was forged, and with the intention in both cases to defraud.—Mr. Swift appeared to prosecute, and the prisoner was undefended.—Mr. Swift said: It appeared the prisoner was formerly secretary to a friendly society called the Shepherds' Return Lodge of the Ancient Order of Shepherds, Ashton Unity, and as Sefetary it was his practice when there was a death of a member to obtain a certificate of the death, and also himself to fill up a certificate, sign it, and get it signed by the Worthy Master and the Deputy Master of his lodge. After he had got it so signed and sealed with the seal of the lodge be would pre- sent it to the treasurer of the district, who would thereupon give him a cheque for the amount that was payable in respect of the death of a member or a member's wife. Upon the first of these occasions, in June, 1879, prisoner went to the treasurer of the district as secretary of the lodge, and presented to the treasurer a certificate in these terms : "Ancient Shepherds, St. Helens district, Ashton Unity, Shepherds' Return Lodge, No. 1,499. This is to certify that Brother John Roughley's wife died 19th April, 1879, aged 78, died of paralysis, and that he is good on the books of our lodge." This purported to be signed by Joseph Stirrup, Worshipful Master, Thomas Hill, Deputy Master, and was signed by Saxon himself. With that certificate in his hand, and with a certificate of death to support It, prisoner went to Mr. Peter Ball, Cooper-street treasurer of the society. and received from Mr. Ball a cheque for £B. Mr. Ball signed it himself and handed it to him. He afterwards went to the bank and got £8 which he applied to his own purposes thus robbing and defrauding the society. With regard to another case mentioned in the warrant he obtained by similar false and fraudulent methods a cheque in respect of the death of the widow of George French. He (Mr. Swift) did not propose to complete the case, because it was a case which could not be sum- marily dealt with. There were two charges—obtaining money by false pretences which was a misdemeanour, and then there was a charge of obtaining a cheque by means of a forged instrument, which was, if proved, a felony, and he believed (he was not prepared to say it was right) that this was only triable at the assizes, because it was under the Act of Parliament relating to a forgery; and although there was a warrant in the case he would give sufficient evidence to justify his worship in remanding the prisoner to Monday.— Peter Ball, painter, Cooper-street, said he issued a cheque for £8 to prisoner upon the presentation of the certificate produced. He should not have issued it except in the belief that the certificate was a true one. He had always had confidence in the prisoner.—Joseph Stirrup said he was worthy master of the lodge in June, 1879. He did not sign the certificate produced, because was not able to write. He did not authorise his name to be written, and it was not written with his sanction.—Thomas Hill said that in conse- quence of the discovery of irregularities he investigated the books and there was no such name as "John Roughley," to be found on the books at all.—Prisoner was remanded.

div.head: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTTIORITY.
div.p: PRESCOT RURAL SANITARY AUTTIORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, on Thursday, Mr. W. A. Meadows presiding. There were also present the Rev. Thos. Chambers, Messrs. J. H. Hall, E. Svder, and W. Tyrer ; with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk), Dr. Hall (medical officer), and Mr. J. Twist (sur- veyor.)

THE THATCHED COTTAGES AT WHISTON. The CLERK, in answer to the Chairman, said he had taken proceedings against the occupiers of the thatched cottages at Warrington-road, Whiston, and they had promised to leave the premises. The tenant who had been in the longest promised to go in a month, and the other, who had only been in the cottage six or seven months, in a fortnight. The cases were adjourned for a month.—The Surveyor was instructed, as soon as the tenants had left, to take off the roof and doors, and barricade the houses.

div.head: PERMANENT RE-APPOINTMENT OF DR. HALL AS MEDICAL OFFICER. _
div.p: THE PERMANENT RE-APPOINTMENT OF DR. HALL AS MEDICAL OFFICER. _

_ The CLERK read a letter from the Local Government Board, stating that they were in receipt of his letter for the 27th ult., and requesting that the particulars relating to the re-appointment of Dr. E. F. Hall, as medical officer of health for the rural sanitary district of the Prescot Union, might be communicated to them. With reference to the proposal of the Authority that Dr. Hall should hold office permanently, the Board informed the Authority that it was contrary to their usual practice at present to sanction the appointment of a district . medical officer of health for a longer period than . one year. The matter was left in the hands of the
clerk to explain the circumstances of the re-appointment permanently.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S. REPORT.

• The MEnicAL OFFICER (Dr. Hall) reported that the health of the district continued satisfactory. NO case of an infec- tious character bad been reported to him. ESTIMATt OF VlPENteft7ll.2 FOR NEET HALF YEAR. The et.ltax submitted estimate of expenditure for half year ending 25th March, 1881, as follows :—General ex- penses : salaries, £190; other expenses : printing, stationery, ifrc., £6O; total, £250; less (re-paid on account of salaries), £100; leaving £l4l. Whiston, interest and instalment, £lOB 15s. 01; water, £5O; Watkin (salary), £l3; sundries. £5B ss. Od ; total, £230. Rainhill, interest and instalment, £217 10s. Od ' • rent of sewage farm, £36; other expenses, £10; total, £263. Hale, interest and instalment, £3O. Total expenditure, £664.—The estimate was approved on the motion of the Rev. F. CHAMBERS, seconded by Mr. HALL. THE PROPOSED INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL AND THE OUT-

BREAK OF SMALLPDX A.T WIDNES. >, The CLERK said the Authority would no doubt remember the medical officer mentioning the desirability of a general ' infectious diseases hospital being erected for the use of the ! various local authorities' districts, and also the communica- tion forwarded to the authorities inviting them to join that • Authority in providing one. The Widnes Local Board did not think fit to join them, and at a previous meeting of the ! Guardians, Mr. Matthews reported that smallpox had made ' its appearance in Widnes. On the 10th August he wrote to the Clerk to the Widnes Local Board as follows :—" Dear Sir,—l am informed that smallpox has appeared in your district, and I should be glad to learn that steps have been ' taken to prevent the spread of the disease. I may point out to you that it is the duty of the local Authority to provide hospital accommodation if it is required." He received the following letter in answer :—" 12th August.—Dear Sir,—l have yours of the 10th inst., and it shall be placed before the next meeting of the Health Committee. In the mean- time I may inform you that there. have been two cases in one house. The man refused to go into the Union Hospi- tal. The medical officer and inspector were therefore in- structed to watch the eases closely. And I may say the patients are confined to their own house, where all possible precautions are being taken." He (Mr. Hartley) again wrote to the clerk to the Local Board as follows :—" 12th August.—Dear Sir,—l am in receipt of your letter of to-day, and am sorry to learn that there are two cases of smallpox in one house. You stated that the man refused to be removed to the Union Hospital. Again, I respectfully point out that it is the duty of the Local Board to provide an infectious hospital for their own district. If the disease spreads I fear for the consequences. Will you please bring the subject before the proper authority at the earliest possible moment, with a view of some provision being made for the reception and treatment of per- sons suffering from an infectious disease." To this letter he received the following letter from the clerk to the Board :—"l3th August.—Dear Sir,—l have yours of yesterday, and have sent copy on to tlie chairman of the Health Committee."—Mr. HARTLEY remarked that the Local Board were relying upon having the use of the work- house hospital, which was very wrong. Widnes had a population of 30,000, and the Local Board ought to make provision for themselves; the sanitary authority would require the workhouse hospital in case any infections dis- ease broke out in their own district.—No discussion took place, but the opinion of the members seemed to be in con- formity with that of the clerk. PLANS OF PROPOSED REFORM CLUB FOR RAINHILL. Mr. TWIST, the surveyor, submitted plans of proposed new Reform Club for Rainhill, and the same being in accor- dance with the bye-laws, they were passed.—The building, as represented on the plan, will be of a rather handsome structure, and will contain, hmong others, smoking-room, reading-room, billiard-room, committee-room, parlour, kitchen, bedroom, lavatory, &c. The size of billiard-room will be 241 t. 61n. by 201 t., and will be lighted by means of a skylight.

div.head: 8 TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: 8 TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTU-IVEST_LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN.
[SPECIAL.] No. XII. JAFFA TO JERUSALEM (continued).

Lydda was reached in two hours after we left our friends at Yazur. We found it a small, dirty village, composed of low, ill-built houses formed into narrow, muddy, unpaved, undrained streets, running at all kinds of angles. They say that St. George, the patron saint (save the mark!) of England was born here. So much the worse for him, I should say, if the town was no better than it is now. Of course, it is expected that Englishmen should get up a little enthusiasm in visiting the old church, recently restored, which bears his name. I fear our hearts were made of the wrong stuff to give a single throb for the memory of this mighty hero, whom I, in my young days, used to confound with George IV, the then reigning monarch, whosteimtahgaet and superscription figured on the obverse side o of St. George and the dragon on nearly every bit gold coin in circulation. Followed by fifteen to twenty children crying for " backsheesh," we rode up to the Arab door of the old church, but did not dismount. It was a little disap- pointment, I confess, that so few marks of antiquity remained cf the interesting spot. The ..guide bookinforms us that Led cr Lydda was burned down in the days of N. ero, but that it became, in early Christian times, the capital of a district in Judea. It was afterwards famed for its learned Rabbinical school, and in A.D. 445 was the scene of an ecclesiastical council, at which the heretic Pelagius had to defend himself. In 1191 it was entirely destroyed by Saladin, and in 1271, after its re-erection, it was sacked by the Mongols. What, then, we ask ourselves, can be left of the ancient town in which Peter sojourned and wrought with miraculous power? All that we can assume is that some of these old looking stones, built with clay into their rude, uneven walls, may have formed part of the streets through which he passed. Not easy to get up much enthusiasm on a sup- position like that! But as we rode outside the village, along the old, old ways, we said to ourselves, Here wetravel on sure historic ground. The Apostle most surely trod these time- wom tracks; his eyes most surely rested on these widely spreading fields and yonder purple hills; and from this place he went forth, with his face Joppa-ward, to raise the dead, and to receive the wonderful message from God, in virtue of which we, as Gentiles, stand here in adoring grati- tude to-day. Even these sacred associations clinging to the place, we were glad to escape. The Arab children followed US on the way, running in front of our horses and wailing behind. Then, as we came nigh to Ramleh, we were beset by three or four lepers, one of whom came and, in his anxiety to obtain alms, almost put his leprous hand upon mine. At the entrance of the town the roads were again overrun with the cactus or prickly pear. We saw it utilised in a way we had not before seen or expected. A hungry camel was munching its juicy, prickly fronds, and apparently enjoying its evening meal. Ramleh is snpposed to be the Arimathea of the New Testament. It contains about 3,001 inhabitants, chiefly Moslems, and, from its position as an easy march from the sea coast, has had an eventful history. Our hostelry was the Latin convent, built in the style of our old baronial halls. As we dismounted and passed through the orchard gate into the first court yard,a three or four Monks were sitting in earnest conversation, and surrounded by the usual amount of Eastern filth. Passing through a second arched way we came into an open and spacious quad- rangle, around three sides of which were ranged the sleep- ing apartments, into which we stepped from the rough pavement. On the fourth side was the large dining hall, at whose capacious table—late on that evening and early next morning—we had our physical wants attended to in a way that left us little to wish for. To be served at table by Franciscan Monks with shaven heads, attired in their rough brown habits, with cowl and rope-girdle complete, was a new sensation. It showed what immense gulfs of religious differences could be bridged over to meet the corporeal wants of poor, frail, humanity. Some of us, who had often denounced the apostasy in no sparing terms, little thought we should ever have to depend on these sons of the " old mother" for shelter and sustenance. It was some consolation to know that their hospitality was more frequently a source of gain than otherwise, although, in cases of poverty and real need, I believe the wayfarer can always gain admittance and find bread provided for him, and his water made sure. As we walked out in the cool of the evening, we saw three or four camels lying beneath the shadow of the convent walls, evidently enjoying rest and shelter, with such entertainment as they could procure. While we stood looking for a moment on this truly Eastern picture, our ears were saluted with a noise like that of a hundred watchmen's rattles. It came from the throats of the multitudinous frogs in the adjoining marshes, and was something tremendous. We were in the saddle next morn- ing by half-past seven, with eight or nine hours of heavy ' travelling before us. They profess to have converted the old rocky way to Jerusalem into a carriage road. I pity the man who attempts to travel over it in a wheeled con- veyance of any kind. The hill country of Judea is rugged and bare to a far greater extent than I had anticipated. After leaving the maritime plain, the region, with the ex- ception of three or four miles, in which the terraced mountain sides are luxuriant with the fig tree and the olive, the whole way up to Jerusalem is bleak hill and stone-bestrewed valley. Some parts of the road are extremely rough and precipitous. The poor ponies, full of life when they set out from Jaffa, found it hard work to climb the bills, and harder still to go down. Once or twice I dismounted and led mine down the steep and stony declivities, for which he seemed truly thankful, pulling up the opposite hills with increased vivacity. After scaling the first mountain range we pro- ceeded along the valley of Ajalon, the most beautiful part of the journey. Leaving Ajalon behind, and wending round the high mountain tracks leading to Kirjath-jearim, we had the heights of Gibeon before us in the far distance with the valley of Beth-boron running from it to the left. How much I should like to have travelled, either on foot or horse- back, the distance thus spread out before us in the distant landscape! No day in this world's history, apart from Calvary's unapproachable scenes, is inure memorable than that which gave Gibeon and Beth-boron their bloody but celestial fame. Over yon lofty hill, sloping gently doWp On all sides, the, sun, in his meridian, stood stock still; over this beautiful valley, behind us the pale crescent moon stopped in her silent march until yonder valley of Beth- boron had received its last victim of the unsparing wrath, both of God and man. Shall I be pardoned if I introduce here an attempt to embody the scene in verse?— THE BATTLE OF BETH-HORON. Under the shade of night. Girded with strength and might. Strode the rude Israelite, Agile and eager. Fires on the distant height. Flashing their lurid light. Showed where the Amorite Lay to beleaguer. Creeping around the hill, Stealthily, solemn, still— Shadowed by gorge and ghill— Israel's bold warriors Waited the day's first peep, Down on their foes to sweep Ere they awoke from sleep, Leaping all barriers. Wild was the cry that rose Breaking the night's repose, All through the camp there flows Panic, disorder. Trumpets remain unblown ; Swords on the sward are strewn; Tents in the rush o'erthrown— Wild the disorder! Vainly their leaders cried— Nothing could stem the tide; Right down the mountain side Fled that great army. Deaf to the loud command— No man would lilt his hand, Who should the Lord withstand Of that great army. Down in the morning light— Down in his wild affright Fled the dark Amorite Far as Beth-horon ! Havock and slaughter reigned; Hearts of their blood were drained Far as Beth-horon ! Joshua trod that day Azekah, Makkedah— Urging his men to slay Fiercer and faster. " Follow with purpose felt! Naught must the tempest quell— Leave not a soul to tall Hamor's disaster !" Turning him round, he said, " Sun ! let thy wheels be stayed," And the bright sun obeyed— Resting o'er Gibeon. "Moon! stand thou still, upon Beautiful Ajalon." And the fair moon, anon, Stood till the day was won. Onward the stricken host, Yelling, the valley crossed. Like the huge billows test, Far as Beth-horon. There, in the narrow pass, God, with His thunder bass. Met the dark heaving mass Shut in Beth heron. Then, in His anger dread, Down came the hail like lead Crushing the thousands dead Fast in Beth-horan. Battered anti black they fell; Horrors no tongue can tell Filling that narrow dell Down in Beth-boron. As we sweep round the hill overlooking an extensive range of "'ultra', we have Kirjath Jearim to the right, about a qaarter of a mile from the road. We were pointed to a a building, a little hiher than the village, as the house of Abinadab, to which the and where after its recovery from the Philistines, was brought, to it Jerusalem,re m ai n d Tfohretwheonnteye Years—until David removed t may indeed be on the site of Abinadab's or it may not. We know the latter was on the side of the hill, but time can scarcely have dealt so gently with it, preserve it in that state for nearly 3,000 years! Further ° they oat, as well, the house of Obededom, to which the Liken before it reached Jerusalem, after Uzzah had been s s' tin for touching it. In this case, also, we are satisfied to know that we are within vision range of the place made lered by this interesting circumstance. And, now, we are travelling along the side of the mountain on which th,

armies of Israel were encamped, when the Philistines on the opposite hill, with Goliah at their head, defied and overawed them. The mountains are much nearer to each other than I had pictured to myself. It is difficult to understand how two armies could have stsod so closely together for forty days without coming into conflict. They must have been relying upon some strategy not apparent in the record, or, both armies must have been greatly demoralised. That a single individual, however prodigious in size, should have kept a whole army in mortal fear, and at bay, for forty days, and, that his own host, moreover, the moment he was slain, should turn their backs and fly from the foe, are facts which present a picture as humiliating as can well be con- ceived. But in this slough of cowardice—in this dark depth of Israel's dishonour,—how gloriously the God of their fathers appears to redeem His name in the person of the ruddy stripling from Bethlehem! What clouds of infamy are dispelled from the standards of Israel, as David, relying upon the God of battles, and proclaiming His authority, sends the boasting Philistine rolling in the dust. Well ! there babbles the brook, and before us spreads the valley of Elah ! Along the foot of the hill there the giant would probably stride each morning to the blare of the trumpet, clanking his mail, and with his huge spear waved aloft, give his terrible challenge. And, down here in the valley, we can see the craven-hearted monarch of Israel almost smothering the son of Jesse with armour, until the youth lays it quietly aside, sarcastically observing that 'as it has not been tried he prefers to go forth in his shepherd's coat with staff in hand. We need not pursue the tale, so thrilling in its sublime trust, its unconquerable zeal, its lion-hearted force. Pursu- ing our journey, so rich in historic scenes and memories, we keep Bethel and Beeroth to the left, and then, seven or eight miles from Jerusalem, looking still to the left, we have Kulonia, the supposed site of Emmaus, very pretty in the distance, but like all other villages in Palestine, miserably dirty when you come near—so lam told. From this point, therefore, we pass through scenes over which the feet of the risen Saysour and His two Disciples must have trod as He talked with them, and made "their hearts burn within them by the way." How little we dream, in reading the history of Christ's life' of the hilliness and ruggednessof the roads over which he had to pass. Between Emmaus and Jerusalem, the way is as steep and rough as the most of I the hill country, and is a fair sample of the roads the I Saviour had to travel during his earthly life. But as we drew near to Jerusalem the road is considerably improved, taking advantage of which the rest of the party rode quickly forward, and left me, oppressed with sickness and headache, to find my way alone. The approach to the city by the Joima road is tame compared with every other. I confess to a feeling of disappointment as the dull grey walls of the city came in view, on a level with the road, without any valley between, and surrounded by a greatnumber of modern suburban residences, convents, dm. The Russian Hospice and Consulate stand out very conspicuously, and beyond their extensive range of buildings is the Armenian convent, and, further on, the long row of neat alms-houses recently erected by Sir Moses Montefiore for destitute Jews. Leav- ing these on the right. I passed under the walls of the city towards the Damascus Gate, near to which our tents had been pitched. From previous study of the topography of Jerusalem, I felt convinced I drew nigh to the place where the Redeemer had been crucified, and in spite of my physical suffering, I felt my soul intensely moved. It was with diffi- culty I dismounted from my horse, and, staggering into the tent, threw myself upon the little iron bed prepared for me. I do not know that I ever felt more thankful than as I lay there recalling God's mercies to us through the journey, and adoring Him for the kindness that had brought us all in safety to this sacred spot. (To be continued next week.)

THE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT WARRINGTON. The Rev. Peter Mackenzie, the popular Wesleyan preacher, visited Warrington on Monday, and preached in Bewsey- road Wesleyan Chapel in the afternoon, to a large congrega- tion, the subject of his discourse being Paul's thorn in the flesh, and his vision of Heaven. In the evening, the rev, gentleman lectured in the Public Hall, on "Solomon, his Wealth, his Wisdom, and his Folly," when there was a large attendance, the lecturer being sup- ported on the platform by the Revs. E. 0. Coleman, F. S. Hagen, and T. Brackenbury, and other gentlemen. The LECTURER said he could not say of King Solomon what he had often said of Queen Esther, that she was a diamond without a flaw, a rose without a thorn, a luminary without any spot on her disc. While they were speaking with reference to his wealth and his wisdom, they had also to refer to his weakness and his folly. Still we had to be thankful that Solomon ever lived and moved and breathed and had his being amongst Cs. The songs which he com- posed were beautiful along with those of his father. There was The Song of Solomon, a marvellous production of its class. The Proverbs of Solomon were unparalleled and un- approachable, apart altogether from any religious feeling. Solomon was the third king of Israel, but was as unlike his predecessors as they were totally different the one to the other. Saul, the son of Kish, went out a commoner and came back a king; be was the first king of Israel. The father of Solomon was entirely different to him. In the early part of his history he kept sheep on the downs of Bethlehem; and when he came into possession of his kingdom he fought faithfully to hold his own, for the nations of the earth com- passed him about. But Solomon was born a prince. He came into power whzn the kingdom was established. He came into possession of his farm when the ditches were dug, the hedges planted, and the crops waving, and had nothing to do but to draw the rent. (Laughter.) And there was also this difference, that of all the men of Scripture there was not one who had less said about him with respect to persottal incident. But they had a thorough analysis of his household and of the usages of the time. The times and seasons and figures were laid before us with great...exactness, though three thousand years had passed away since he was amongst us. The footprints of other kings and queens had been swept away in that time, but wherever there was litera- ture or religion, a memorial to Solomon survived, and his name was a household word. In many a distant part men of dusky skins were found to gather together to talk of the wealth and the greatness and the grandeur and the glory of Solomon. One volume would hold all that had been written about his father, but 80 volumes were filled with information about Solomon. Throughout Europe the name of Solomon gathered around it the strangest and most fantas- tic tales. His name was known among the Ara- bians, the Ethiopians, the Greeks, and the Jews. Solomon had a vast income derived from his taxes, and he took care to conserve it. It was certain that the ships of Solomon called at Penzance for tin and copper which they made into bronze for the temple. Solomon's features were cast in the finest mould and his countenance was like Lebanon, and fairer than any of the earth-bore race. His turnout consisted of 1,400 chariots. His footmen had golden helmets and golden powdered wigs. It was the opinion of some that Solomon had buried a good deal of the treasure left him beside his father, and that if David's body could be found there would be as much found near it as would reduce every Englishman's income tax to 1 one penny in the pound. (Laughter.) Referring to the 1 Temple of Solomon, he said it was small compared to ; structures which stcod at the present day; but no temple that ever stood in Egypt, Greece, or Rome had so many 1 attractions as that of Solomon. The Lord consecrated the site 1 and superintended its erection, and when it was finished He ' filled it with His glory. Solomon's wisdom was very great. The ancients said he had a thorough kno Arledge of the language of beasts and birds; he had also a thorough knowledge of the virtue of plants and the value of pearls, and he had great curative powers. His wisdom was seen in the fact that he built a temple for God before he built a house for himself. That was an evidence of piety. Although he was thirteen years in building his own house, he built the house of God in seven. He also showed his wis- dom in the management of his empire; for while the mili- tary chiets were too many for his father to manage, Solomon did that which was necessary, and a firm hand. Solomon's wis- I dom was also seen in his songs and in his proverbs. How beautifully Solomon, in his Proverbs, had recommended filial affection, and love and loyalty to parents! How beauti- fully he recommended the advantage of having good com- pany—not to join with the base and the unprincipled. How beautifully he recommended truth ! "Cling to the truth, cleave to the truth." How (beautifully be recommended sobriety! tie tried the other thing, and he found that there was nothing like cold water for keeping one clear in the cranium. (Laughter.) How beautifully he recommended the "soft answer that turneth away wrath," and not " grie- vious words that stir up anger." They could not read a verse in the Proverbs without finding some pithy sentence in it. After briefly referrine, to Solomon's great knowledge of natural history, the lecturer said Solomon had his weak side. He had his 700 wives and his 300 concubines, and his was not what a religious existence ought to be. His excellence was marred by defect, and he fell so fearfully low that the-most charitable man now could scarcely say that he ever got up again. There was a worldliness in his occu- pation. Every one knew what a difficult thing it was to keep spiritual in a carnal region, and it was difficult to keep the spiritual stream flowing and the mind fixed on things above when there was so much to attract one's attention. The love of God and the love of the world were two affec- tions not only in a state of rivalry but enmity, and so utterly irreconcilable that they could not by any possibility dwell together in the same bosom. (Applause.) How could Solomon swim with 700 heathens dragging him down? Would they like to try ;t ? (Laughter.) How did he get on with his grandeur? It was all vanity and vexation of spirit. Solomon did not say that. He said it was vanity of vanity—the small end of nothing whittled to a point. (Loud laughter.) It was said that in his old age Solomon was whirled by the mazy dance of strange women into the hands of demon worship. He did not regard him as an old man. He died at the age of 58. He forgot the God who had honoured him, and he was whirled into the arms of demon worship. He advised them to look, and if they did so God's blessing would rest upon them, to the kingdom to which they were hastening, to the land of felicity and bles- sedness. He did not think that any king of Israel did so much harm to Israel as Solomon, and the taxes were increazed ; the people were taxed till they could not bear it. But their Solomon had not come to increase their taxes. "He who was rich for our sake became poor, that we through His poverty might become rich." RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND NR. CLIFF'S CONTRACT. On Thursday afternoon a special meeting of the Runcorn 4. of Commissioners was held, for the purpose of con" sidering the street cleansing contract with Mr. Cliff and the memorial from the ratepayers in respect to it. Previous to the meeting the Highway Committee met and fully dis- cussed the question at a most interminable length. Dr. Steele took the chair at the Board meeting, and there were also present Messrs. Frith, Norman, McDougall, J. J. Speak. man, Taylor, Handley, Marshall, Linaker (law clerk), and Brookes (secretary). Dr. McDo-maid, was of opinion that the memorial from the ratepayers had not received that careful consideration at previous meetings of the Commissioners which it ought to have done. He proposed that it be read. The CHAIRMAN then read the document, and remarked that it came before the Board at a rather late date, as Mr. Cliff had now been carrying on the work of cleansing the streets for about four months. It had been said that under the contraff -plan there would be no work for the old men who had previously been found work; but he found, on enquiry, that, with the difference of one or two new hands, Mr. Cliff was employing all the old men. The only one who had left was one of the age of 45 years. Mr. MARSHALL asked if all who had signed the memorial were r, tepayers. The CrUIRMAN then began to read an analysis of those who bad s. •ned the document, but no sooner had he said that 38 of 'hem were Sons of Temperance, than Dr. McDougall sa 1 he objected to such an analysis being given, for it might be said that many of the signatures were not those of persons who really paid rates, though they did so indirectly by compounding for them. , The Law CLERK: Do they pay poor rates? The SECRETARY: We have no knowledge that the people referred to do so. Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said that Mr. Curzon told them that if he had had time, he felt sure he could have obtained the names of 99 out of every 100 ratepayers in the town to the peti- `ion.

Mr. MARSHALL: Don't quote him. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN said he had been requested to read a letter, addressed to the Secretary, from Mr. W. H. Rogerson, stating that he should be glad to have his name erased from Mr. Curzon's memorial. The Secretary having read the memorial, Mr. HANDLEY said he was of opinion that it ought to receive a written reply. Dr. McDouGarl, believed that at the last meeting there was some disposition to take an adverse view of the matter, and he thought that Mr. Frith should say what he had to state in respect to it. Mr. FRITH had no desire to inflict upon the members of the Board a speech of half an hour's length, seeing that they had already been occupied with the question two hours in committee. (Laughter.) It was resolved, unanimously, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. FRITH, that the memorial be received, and that the secretary write to the gentleman who laid it before the Commissioners, stating that the Board re- gretted that owing to the contract having been already agreed to, and the fact of the contractor having worked under it for some time, the document was received too late for it to be of any avail. The SECRETARY then read the minutes of the meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, held that morning, at which it was resolved, on the proposition of Mr. Marshall, seconded by Mr. Frith, that the committee advise that the seal of the Board be affixed to the contract with Mr. Cliff, for street cleansing. Mr. Nonmaar, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he was just in the same position as every one else—he was very sorry the memorial did not come before them sooner. He was of opinion that if the ratepayers had taken the mat- ter up when they saw the advertisement relating to the matter in the newspapers, some arrangement might have been come to. Mr. MARSHALL seconded the resolution, and thought they ought not to lose eight of the fact that the Board were not a benevolent institution whose work it was to discharge the duty which belonged to the guardians in the case of two old men. The real question which they had to decide was as to whether the letting of the street cleansing contract to Mr. Cliff would be for the benefit of the ratepayers, both from a financial and sanitary point of view. He stated, without fear of contradiction, that the scheme financially would prove a great benefit to the town, as it would save the ratepayers from £lOO to £l5O per annum. But for the dilly-dallying policy pursued on the question by some of the members, the town would that day have been quite prepared to do without one of the officials they now employed, whose salary alone would have been a clear gain of about LSO a year. Mr. Cliff, by accepting the contract, would render himself respon- sible for seeing it was properly carried out. They were, how- ever, well acquainted with the question, and knew that he had always faithfully discharged whatever contract he had accepted in past years. He wished to say a word with re- ference to the gentleman who presented the memorial to them. This person told the contractor that he did not mean to do him any harm, but the action he had taken was simply against certain of the Commissioners. Now, this was quite contrary to what the gentleman in question said at the Board meeting. (Considerable interruption.) The com- missioners had made an arrangement with Mr. Cliff, and they ought to carry it out in a straightforward and honour- able manner. He was of opinion that if the Board were to be put off from doing what was their duty by such moves as had been practiced upon them, then the members must have arrived at their dotage, and the sooner they were disbanded and the better. (Laughter.) In conclusion, he hoped they would not be deterred from acting straightforwardly, or led to entertain any proposition in favour of cancelling the con- tract. Mr. PHILIP SPEAKMAN said he should move that the con- tract be not signed, but he was told that he could not do this, as it was merely proposing a negative. He then pro- ceeded to say that he deeply regretted the surveyor was not able to be present that day, owing to the death of his daughter, for if he had been, he should have asked for the correspondence which had passed with Mr. Cliff since he commenced to work under the contract. When he first brought this matter before the Board, he took good care to make all necepsary enquiries as to whether he was upon firm ground or not. He asked Mr. Linaker whether the Com- missioners were bound by the action Mr. Cliff had taken, and he found that gentleman had distinctly told the Board they were not. Dr. McDouctALL, said he did not wish to give a silent vote on the question. He had always held that the memorial should receive that consideration at the hands of the Board which it justly merited. It seemed to him, after all, that they were honourably bound to carry out the contract they had made with Mr. Cliff, and affix the seal of the Board to it. He must express his regret that it was not provided by theagreement that the work should only be let for 12 months. There could be no doubt that it was a matter of regret to every one of them that the memorial did not arrive in time to prevent the Board letting the work. He did not, personally, think it was wise for any public body to hand themselves over to a private contractor for a period of four years. They had had an interview with Mr. Cliff, who had expressed his unwillingness to deviate from the agreement, and the re- sponsibility rested with him. The resolution for the confirmation of the minutes of the committee was then passed. Only two members—Messrs. J. J. Speakman, and Philip Speakman—voted against them. The proceedings then terminated.

THE EDUCATION QUESTION AT WARRINGTON. The School Board Chronicle says t—We report this week some remarkable speeches made at a Town Council meeting at Warrington on School Board and education questions, the result of what took place at the somewhat memorable in- terview with the Lord President and Vice-President of the Council, on the payment of school fees, three or four weeks I ago. Mr. Mundella, we are rather glad to say, made quite an impression upon the Warrington contingent of that depu- tation. They are never tired of telling one another of the right hon. gentleman's vigorous and determined manner of encountering the naive and extraordinary suggestions which they innocently and seriously laid before him. Warrington evidently does not care very much about what goes on in other parts of the country. It wants Acts of Parliament for doing its own business in its own way, and it seems very difficult indeed to make the leaders of public affairs in that borough understand that Warrington is not to make laws for itself, whatever may be the legislative genius of its Alder- ' men, its Town Councillors, and its Poor Law Guardians. It is not alone the functions of Westminster Palace that the public men of Warrington seem anxious to monopolise. Warrington public bodies are in the constant habit of tres- passing upon each other's grounds. We referred a few weeks ago to the high-handed proceedings of the Town Council in discussing and confirming proceedings of the School Attendance Committee with which the Town Coun- cil hat nothing whatever to do. The matter in hand at that time was an application to the Education Department to lower the standard of half-time exemption from the third to the second, and we pointed out that while this was a matter within the exclusive province of the Attendance Committee, and not at all subject to the revision of the aldermen and councillors, both Town Council and School Attendance Committee would probably very soon learn that the Lords of the Education Committee were of the opinion that the circumstances of Warrington are not such as to render necessary an exceptionally low standard of half-time exemp- tion. Our anticipation has proved correct. The aldermen and town councillors at their quarterly meeting, minding as usual the business of the Attendance Committee instead of their own, had under consideration, in addition to the matter of the truculent attitude of Mr. Mundella at Whitehall, the refusal of the Education Department to permit the committee to lower the standard of half-time exemption from the third to the second. The Town Council is in the habit of :boasting of the"superior educational position and advantages of the town, and of its own high qualifications for performing School Board functions, but neither Alderman nor Town Couneillor be- trayed any sense of the discredit which attaches to a place like Warrington in consequence of asking. after all these years of the establishment of the education system, for an exemption standard below the third for euabing its young children to be employed. By way, we suppose, of demon- strating the capacity of the Town Council to administer edu- cation law, Councillor Platt observed that the difficulty be got over by giving instructions to their officers that w'Aen children are in school half-time, and are in beneficial

employment, there shall not be any prosecution. Mr. Councillor Platt's notion evidently is that, if the Lords of the Committee of Council refuse to sanction a proposal made to them by the local authority of Warrington, all the local authority has to do is to violate the law and proceed ex- actly as if their Lordships had said yes when they said no. There are two things which Mr. Councillor Platt does not appear to know—and nobody at the Town Council meeting offered to set him right. In the first place, if the Atten- dance Committee permits children to work half-time without passing the half-time standard the committee will have forfeited its position, and be liable to be declared a committee "in default" and to be suspended by the Department; and in the second place, those children so allowed to be unlawfully employed half- time will not be permitted to earn grants in the schools by making 150 attendances; wherefore we fancy, from what we hear from time to time of the voluntary schools of War- rington, that there will not be found any school managers in the borough to admit those children as half-timers into their schools.

But the great event of the day at that Warrington Town Council meeting was the formal proposal, by Mr. Councillor Jeans, of a short Act of Parliament intended to set aside Mr. Mundella's difficulty about granting the changes which the Warrington members of the deputation asked. Mr. Mun- della intimated that he could not undertake to legislate for Warrington to the extent of investing the Town Council with the powers of a School Board, and that he could not, for reasons which he gave, make provisions for allowing Town Councils, Attendance Committees, and School Boards to pay the fees of indigent children in denominational schools. Mr. Councillor Jeans appears to have misunder- stood the nature of Mr. Mundella's difficulty. He seems to have thought that the Vice-President of the Council found himself deficient of the literary capacity necessary to enable him to draft a clause, or a short Act of Parliament, for enacting what Warrington wishes. Now Mr. Councillor Jeans was not conscious of any 'snch literary deficiency. He drew up a short draft of an Act of Parliament, and laid it before the Town Council for preliminary approval, with a view to sending it to Whitehall to be put through the formality of being read three times in the two houses and sanctioned by the Sovereign. Having read his resolution and draft Bill for giving Town Councils the powers of School Boards and for enabling Town Councils, Attendance Committees, and School Boards to pay fees his speech consisted mainly in explaining that Mr. Mundella's difficulty was entirely solved by this form of words. The performance reminds us of some of the exercises of the

;‘ corner men" of the Christy Minstrels. Mr. Jeans, having put his words together and framed his Act of Parliament, was utterly incapable of seeing—what everybody out of Warrington sees—that the whole proposal is ridiculous, and that as a matter of policy it is not likely that three men in the House of Commons could be found to vote for it. After what we have reported of the Warrington Town Council from time to time, our readers will not be surprised that Mr. Jeans's proposal met with a good deal of approval. But it was not adopted, because even those who approved of it saw that it would be nothing more than going before Mr. Mun- della a second time with the old and rejected prayer, in a new set of words.

FOREIGN TARIFFS AND BOUNTIES. There was a good attendance at the Warrington Public Hall, on Wednesday, to hear an address from Mr. Robert G. Web- ster, on" Foreign tariffs and bounties and their effect on British industries." The chair was taken by the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and there were also on the platform Alderman Davies, Alderman Webster, Alderman Chandlev, Mr. Artingstall, Rev. W. H. Williams, Mr. Bowes, Coun- cillor Francomb, Mr. A. Mackie Councillor Litton, Councillor Jeans, Councillor Burgess, G. Y. Bolton, die. His WORSHIP, who was received with applause, said they were met that evening to hear a lecture from Mr. Webster, a gentleman pretty well known in Warrington, and also in London, and other parts, as the author of Several works. (Hear, hear.) There were there to listen to a lecture on " Foreign tariffs and bounties and their results on British industries." He understood that Mr. Webster had given a very great deal of thought to this subject, and he had not the slightest doubt that he would give them a most in- teresting description of what the effect of Free Trade had been in this country for the last 20 years. It was a question that was stirring the thoughtful minds of a great many men in the country—not only of the manufacturers and trades- men, but also of those gentlemen who were at the head of the House of Commons. It was not political. It was stir- ring the minds of men on both sides—Conservatives and Liberals. It was a question that affects the future of this country, and he was sure that whatever had been the result of Free Trade, whether it was proved to be good for the future, or whether they have to give it up, both Conserva- tives and Liberals would do that which they thought was best for the general welfare of old England. (Ap. plause). For his own part, for some years it had seemed rather a strange thing to him that British industries which were sent over to foreign countries—to Belgium or France, for instance—should have placed upon them a heavy duty which, in effect, amounted to a pre- scription, when, on the other hand, they could make their machines and send their silk and cotton goods over here, and we received them free of duty. Therefore he thought, looking at the question in a straighforward manner, they had the advantage of us, (Hear, hear.) No doubt those gentlemen who argued that Free Trade in the abstract was good for all, would say it was a very one-sided question if England itself was on one side and all other countries against it. There was no doubt it would be a very good thing if England and all other countries accepted the Free Trade principle, but when we found that every country in Europe and America was against us we ought to look at home and see what we could do to mend matters. (Hear, hear.) He then introduced Mr. WEBSTER, who said the question appeared to be one of very deep and pressing importance, for, whatever be the true answer to the question agitating the public mind in regard to trade, there could be no doubt that in a great many industries in this country there was serious room for anxiety. In speaking to that meeting, in which there was represented nearly every class of the community, he would state his views with perfect frankness. They need not look at the matter from a narrow but a broad point of view; and he thought in discussing the matter they should give up calling one another protectionists and free traders, but dis- cuss the matter from a Free Trade standpoint. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that the best state of things would be for every country to be an open market for all the countries of the world. (Hear, hear.) That was not the case, and the only manner to arrive at it seemed to him to be a problem which English statesmen ought to unroll. Competition was keener now than when we held the undoubted supremacy by our commercial interests. When that competition succeeded in beating us solely because the foreigner bad greater ad- vantages he did not think anyone would wish to protect, but when it arose from protection or bounties imposed upon the goods he contended that a different question arose. The question how, to preserve and increase trade affected not merely iron masters, cotton spinners, and those engaged in manufacture, but every class of the community. Competition must reduce profits, but the question was, was it fair competition ? He believed that no country, least of all a country situated as England now is, could afford to loose their export trade. It would appear certain that no country could permanently maintain the position of being a great commercial country unless it had natural advantages. He maintained we had in England great natural advantages. We had excellent communication by water to our shores, we had good navi- gable rinrs, we had the handmaidens of commerce in the shape of iron and coal easily " get-at-able "; and with all these advantages we ought to be able to beat the world as a manufacturing nation. He proceeded to give the initiation of our present so-called Free Trade, and remarked that our statesmen at that time inaugurated what they described as unrestricted trade, but the way in which they set about it was to his mind not a very business-like way and defeated the object they had in view. Mr. Cobden'a platform was that all duty for protection should be removed, and free and unfettered intercourse established with all the nations of the earth. The first part of that platform had been carried out. We had taken off the duty for protection, but we had done it in such a way that we had made it impossible to have unfettered intercourse with all nations of the earth. Now that we were arranging a commercial treaty with France and the affairs of our commercial life were forced upon us, he thought it was our dnty to examine what Free Trade really was. He thought two questions forced themselves on their attention, one was the new French treaty, and the other the bounties given to foreign labour in English markets. (Hear, hear.) Having explained how differently treaties were previously made to the one we were now making, he said Mr. Chamberlain said in transacting this treaty with France we were not to take what we wished, but what we could get. He (Mr. Webster) thought we should be firmer in transacting the treaty with France. (Hear, hear.) The whole export trade with France in 1869 was 126 millions, and of that amount 34 millions were exported to Great Britain, or one third, whereas on the other hand, only 1-13th of our export trade was sent to France. Therefore in transacting this treaty we had the power in our own hands. He contended English statesmen should not take what they could get, but France must give us what we would have. (Applause.) He granted, with Mr. Chamberlain, that the silk trade was a decaying in- dustry, and having referred to the falling off in the woollen exports, said he was told the leather industry would be greatly affected by specific duties. He adverted to the sugar bounties, and said that in 1864 our imports of sugar were insignificant, but at the present moment we imported 150,000 tons, and the result had been that 10,000 British labourers had been thrown out of employment, and 30 or 40 sugar refineries closed. The Government, by allowing this bounty system to go on had entered into a real connivance with a most unfair system of protection. This question it was in the power of our legislators to amend if they only put on an intercepting duty. But he did not think we should have any reason to put on this countervailing duty if the French and other nations knew we were really in earnest. Sugar was not the sole industry which had been attacked by the new French bounty system. A most important industry had lately been attacked by the protection bounty given by the French—the shipping interest. A bill had been passed in the French Senate, by 265 votes to five, giving a bounty on ships built in France, and also on the running of ships from French ports, and the only emendation that was made was one slightly more detrimental to this country—that any vessel built on the Clyde should only have half the bounty. He thought we should look ahead. He did not deny that while the French were protecting their merchant marine they might be going to Greenock and Newcastle, and might be buying vessels from us. But would that continue? This bounty question was a question that had not only been mooted in France, but also in the United States. In regard to this French treaty, we should put our foot firmly down, and refuse to make a treaty which would not give us the power of putting on a countervailing duty, and which we could not terminate if we found it advantageous to us, in one year. We found in the year 1880 half our exports went from these shores to our colonial possessions, and Mr. Farrar Ecroyd, the member for Preston—(applause)—calculated the result of our trade in 1877. He found that every Australian in that year was as good a customer to us as 16 Americans, and every Canadian was a great deal better than 35 Russians. (Applause.) But the time might come when the question of having a great federal union of the whole of our colonies might enter into the minds of our statesmen. If that time did arrive he be- lieved it would be to the benefit both to the mother country and the colonies. (Applause.) The doctrines that had been preached by these doctrinaires had been falsified, and they had not the moral courage to own it. It was calculated in America that in the next 5 years 500,000 of our best workingmen would emigrate to their shores, and he considered it was the duty of all to combine and insist that their birthright should not be traded away for a miser- able mess of pottage. He feared when the French treaty was settled we should find ourselves with isolated free trade, and it appeared to him that our industries would be placed during the next ten years in a very precarious position. If a man came before them and called himself a Conservative tell him not only to conserve the honour and integrity of the empire, tell him not only to conserve the institutions of this country, but tell him to conserve the commercial and mari- time position of Great Britain. (Hear, hear, and applause.) If a man came before them and called himself a Liberal, tell him not to be liberal in his promises at election times— (applause)—and forget them when he was in power, tell him not to be liberal in giving away the Queen's territory to rebels (applause)—tell him not to be liberal in granting one sided commercial treaties to foreign countries to the detri- ment of British labour. (Applause.) He confessed he en- tertained great sympathy with the foreigner and the alien race, still he did not entertain the same simpathy that Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Chamberlain. (Applause.) His motto was " England before all." (Applause.) That 'Might not be a cosmopolitan idea, but it was the idea of great states- men in past years. (Applause.) Mr. ARTINGSTALL, in proposing a vote IR thanks to Mr. Webster, said this was one of the best lectures upon this sub- ject he had heard in Warrington. It was a subject upon which there was a great variety of opinions, and a short time ago people would not listen to an expression of opinion such as they had heard that evening. (Hear, bear.) The people were now beginning to find that their pockets were touched. (Applause.) Man'irfacturers' profits were going down—(hear, hear)—and mrkpeople's wages were as a natural consequence being reduced. Everything was re- duced. Railway dividends were reduced. Free Trade was a fine thing. What we wanted was real Free Trade, but we had never had Free Trade. (Hear, bear.) We bad given Free Trade to France and to America, and they had profit- ted and became rich at our expense. (Hear, hear, and i.ap- plause). They send their goods here without let orohf hind- the "nee, and they take the bread out of the mouth o ought People of this country—(hear, hear) —who to be. employed in manufacturing gooda, It was a
people would belie-ve it as time went on. Councillor BURGESS seconded the motion, Which carried. and A similar compliment was passed to the Mayor, proceedings terminated.

div.head: WIDYES SEWERAGE SCHEME.
div.p: THE WIDYES SEWERAGE SCHEME.
Board

On Tuesday, a spec:al meeting of the Widnes Local Board was held, for the porpose of hearing an explanation of the two schemes of sewerage submitted to the considera- tion of the Joint Highway And Health Committee. Mr. Eustace Carey presided, in the absence of Major Cross, and there were also present Messrs. town, Pankhurst, Heyes, Handley, Sadler, Shuttleworth, Kershaw, O'Keeffe, Allen (accountant), Higginson (surveyor), and Copland (sewerage scheme surveyor). h The CHAIRMAN said they. were met that afternoon to hes.' from Mr. Kershaw, the Chairman of the Joint II ighway and Health Committee, the reason why the gentlemen composing that committee had come to the decision that the :;cheme submitted by Major Cross was the best which had been s,ub- mitted for their consideration. Mr. KERSHAW said the members of the Board were aware that the scheme brought forward by the chairman of their body ha'.d some time ago been adopted by themselves, and also approved by the Local Government Board; but another proposal for the drainage of the district had been brought before them by Mr. Higginson, their surveyor. On analyzing the latter scheme they found it to be 200 yards longer that that of Major Cross, and, this being the case, it must consequently cost more money. In the first instance, the surveyor suggested that a cheaper material than was proposed by the Board's Chairman should be used. The committee had, however, no hesitation in asking the Board to adopt the Major's scheme, which, if the best material were used, would cost £14,800 against Mr. Higginson's £19,000 in the best material. If they only used the commonest materials, the Chairman's scheme would cost £lO,OOO and Mr. Higginson's nearly £13,000. All they required to do in order to be convinced of the undoubted superiority of the Chairman's scheme, was to traverse the course proposed to be taken by the two different plans. If Mr. Higginson's scheme was decided upen, there would be many difficulties to surmount in it which did not exist in that of the Major's. In fact, he (the speaker) was at a loss to know what decided the surveyor to choose the route be had. If they left out of the question the plan submitted by Major Cross, he was prepared to maintain that 'a better scheme than the one sug- gested by Mr. Higginson would be to proce2d from the police station and down Hutchinson-street, as the work would then only have to be carried out along roads belong- ing to the Board, and there would be no railways to pass under or other difficulties to contend with which were met with in the surveyor's plans. Such a plan could be executed for between £lB,OOO and £19,000. Then he might, if necessary, speak to them of another sewerage scheme which could, pass through his own timber yard, and would cost £20,000. This plan he believed to be a far preferable one to Mr. Higginson's. Much might be said against using inferior materials in carrying out any plan of sewerage in a town like Widnes, as the particular manufacture for which it was known generated gas, the effects of which could not be resisted by inferior materials. The committee, therefore, thought that the better course would be to go in for the scheme which would cost £14,000. It had been suggested that the size of the sewer might be reduced from 4ft. Gin, with advantage, but he did not consider it would be prudent to do so as it would have to be the main outlet for the dis- trict, even though, as he said, they could thus effect a saving of 3,365 yards in the excavation, which would reduce the cost pretty nearly £6OO. By a still greater reduction in the size of the sewer, they might make a difference of about £792. Mr. BROWN understood that Major Cross's proposal would cost some thing like £4,000 less than the surveyor's, but he should like to ask if it would drain as great an acreage as Mr. Higginson's. He had been told that the surveyor's plan would drain all the West Bank property, whilst the Chairman's did no do that satisfactorily. What would the expense of sewering the West Bank property be if the drain at present in use were removed and made good. Personally, ' he must say he considered the route laid out by Major Cross the preferable one. What they must guard against was that they did not accept a sewerage scheme estimated to cost £14,000 and then find that they had a great amount of addi- tional work to carry out. He was willing to admit that though he at first was of opinion that it would be a wise plan to reduce the size of the sewer, he was not now of that opinion. Mr. KERSHAW said that an expenditure of £5OO on the West Bank drainage, at a point between the railway arch and the outlet, would put it in capital order. In answer to a question, the CHAIRMAN said that Major Cross's scheme would drain 1,600 acres. It had always been admitted by the committee that one advantage in connec- tion with the surveyor's scheme was the course Mr. Hig- ginson's proposed to take as to repairing the drain at West Bank. They, however, found that the cost of repairing would be so comparatively small, that it would be better to carry out the work separately. 1 Mr. KERSHAW said he was willing to admit that at first he had an interest in Mr. Higginson's scheme, but he found it was not practicable. He moved that the recommendation of the joint committee in favour of carrying out Major Cross's scheme be adopted. Mr. BROWN remarked that he was quite willing to second the proposition, as since the last meeting he had made enquiries which had satisfied him that the Major's scheme was decidedly the preferable one. The resolution was put and carried unanimously, after which the members left the Board-room for the purpose of inspecting the route.

div.head: EDUCATION AT WIDNES,
div.p: EDUCATION AT WIDNES,
NEW CATHOLIC SCHOOLS.

Probably there is no town of the same size in the United Kingdom which has done more towards supplying educa- tional facilities for the people, since the passing of the Elementary Education Act, than Widnes. Its Board Schools are an honour to the body under whose direction they have I been built, and such buildings, complete in every put, would be pointed to with pride even in some of the first cities of the Empire. The great stride which has been made by the country in making education compulsory, so that even the poorest child may become possessed of a capital intellectual training, has put the managers of denomina- tional schools upon their mettle, in order to prevent their being outstripped in the race for the Government grant ; and the appeal made by that part of the public who have a firm belief in the importance of religions training being always carried on in conjunction with intellectual development, have nobly responded to the calls made upon them.

- - The Catholics of Widnes are, without doubt, a very strong body in the chemical metropolis, and their priests are men quite abreast of the age, and quick to notice the signs of the times. For some period the acommodation afforded to the children of this faith at the Hutchinson-street, and the girls' and infants' school at Newtown, has not been found at all commensurate with the calls made upon the manage- ment, and it has been decided to meet the difficulty by the erection of a new and thoroughly commodious building. The first step towards this commendable object was the purchase of a piece of ground upon which two cottages, until lately, stood, and which adjoins the existing New- town schools. Plans were then drawn up for the alteration of the old and the erection of the new building, which was commenced some three months ago, and is now rapidly nearing completion. The architect of the structure, which will form an ornament to the neighbourhood, is Mr. Edmund Kirby, Cook-street, Liverpool, and the contractors are Messrs. James Yearsley and Thomas Yearsley, St. Helens. The building stands at the corner of Margaret and George-streets, and joins the old schools. It is two storeys in height, and the height of the first is 15 feet, and the second 12 feet. The height of the schools from the base. ment to the roof is 27 feet. On the first storey will be a room measuring 65 feet by 25 feet, and a class room the dimensions of which will be 20 feet by 15 feet. The room on the upper storey will measure 70 feet by 25 feet, with a class room of the same size as the one upon the ether storey just &scribed. In the basement storey will be four windows, measuring 9 feet 9 inches by 4 feet 6 inches, and on the Margaret-st. side of the building, six windows, each 6 feet 6 inches long by 4 feet broad. At the back of the school the windows will number four, and the size of them will be 4 feet 8 inches by 6 feet 6 inches. The schools will be approached by an entrance measuring 5 feet by 6 feet, and out of this will run a winding staircase which will lead to I the class rooms. The building will be of red brick, and on each floor will be accommodation for about 300 children. The lower storey will be used for infants and the upper for boys. By the erection of the new schools those at New- town can be used entirely for girls. The total cost of the new buildings will be about .£1,300, and they are expected to be ready for occupation by the 20th September next.

div.head: ...-.....i.p....
div.p: GOOD TEMPLLEY.—The "Henry Oldfiold " Lodge, 2,220, Wigan, recently held its quarterly meeting, therel being a good attendance. The reports of the various officers were mad and adopted. That of the W. secretary and the W. treasurer were of a most cheeringcharacter, and refl^cted very great credit upon those officers. The W.C.T. reported the receipt of 100 pledge cards, as also a quantity of tracts as a gift. The W. treasurer reported the receipt of over £1 for initiation fees, as also a donation to the funds of the Lodge of £2 from our esteemed Bro. A. E. Eccles, of Chorley. The officers were installed by Bro. C. F. Haddy, ' H.D. (of St. Helens), who takes a lively interest in this Lodge, having assisted at its re-opening a short time ago. This Lodge, although resuscitated but a short time, and the I only Lodge in the town, has had the courage to invite the S. W. Lancashire District Lodge to bold its next meeting at Wigan, when Bro. Joseph Wins, G.W.C.T., will preside, and members from all parts of the district will be present. The Lodge again assembled on the 15th inst., and the fol- lowing visitors were announced and took part in the pro- ceedings :—Beo. the Rev. James Mackenzie, P.G.Ch. and D.0.T., of North Durham; the Rev. Enoch Franks, P.G.Ch. (recently appointed to the Presbyterian Chapel. Wigan) ; Bro. R. Williams, D.C.T., and Bro. R. W. Kirkus, W. D. Sec.. both of Liverpool; and Bro. C. F. Haddy, P. W. D. Sec., of St. Helens. Fourteen new members were initiated, and seven received the second degree, or Degree of , Fidelity. The Rev. J. Mackenzie gave a most interesting and stirring address on Good Ternplary, which was very attentively listened to and highly appreciated, and which will have a beneScial influence on the members of the Lodge and others who were present. A very enjoyable evening was spent.
