div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS, WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr: Artingstall, and Mr. Samuel
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS, WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr: Artingstall, and Mr. Samuel
Rigby.

THEFT FROM AN ORCHARD—.:—Thomas Clare (14), Edward Robert Brown (13), and Edward Allen (12), were charged with stealing a quantity of pears, valued at is. 6d., from the orchard of Mr. William Beamont, Orford Hall.—On Sunday afternoon the prisoners were seen in the garden by the gardener, who had set an alarum, and subsequently ap- prehended. A boy named Lingard said Clare and Brown were not in the garden ; they were with him on the bridge.—Mr. Rigby: Did you go to get some apples?— Witness: Yes. (Laughter.)—The prisoners were each fined ss.
.--- KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT A LICENSE.—A young man named John Golding, of Penketh, was charged wieh keeping a dog without a license on the nth July, and he was fined ss. and costs. _

STRAY Cows.—Thomas Owen, farmer, Penketh, was charged with allowing two cows to stray on the hichway on the 9th inst.—P.S. Batersey found the cows grazing on the highway in charge of defendant's daughter.—Defendant was fined in the costs.

BICYCLISTS ON THE FOOTPATH—TWO youths, named Robert Eatough and Wm. Flaharty, were charged with ob- structing the footpath on the Liverpool-road, at Sankey, by riding a bicycle thereon on the sth inst.—Defendants were ordered to pay G. costs. DAMAGE TO POTATO FIELDS.—Peter Ford (14), Seth Wood (13), and Thomas McCannon (14) were charged with trespassing on the grounds of James Isaac Ashcroft, at Orford on the 12th inst., doing damage to the grass and potatoes to the extent of Is. 61—Complainant said the boys were " old practitioners," and he had a great many pota- toes pulled up.—Ford and McCannon had previously been up for a theft, and they were each fined 23. and Os. costs, Wood was ordered to pay 63. 6d. costs. EXTENSIVE THEFT OF Funiv.--,-James Walsh (15), John Griffiths (14), John Griffin (15), Wm. Summerseat (14), Edward Butler (9), Alfred Glover (14), and Thos. Chadwick (13) were charged with having on the 7th August, at Mid- dleton, stolen a quantity of fruit from the orchard of Hugh Holt, doing damage to the amount of 10s. The four first- named defendants were seen in the garden pulling apples and pears from the trees and sending them into the lane to the other defendants, who were picking them up. A large basket of apples and pears taken from the defendants was produced.—Butler was ordered to pay 6s. 6d. costs ; Walsh, Griffiths, and Chadwick, who had been previously before the court, were fined 10s. and costs; Griffin, Summerseat, and Glover were each fined ss. and costs. UNJUST SCALES.—Evan Cross, grocer, Penketh, was sum- moned for having unjust scales.—Superintendent Jackson visited the defendant's shop on the sth inst., and found a pair of flour scales half an ounce out of balance against the purchaser, and a pair of counter scales quarter of an ounce against the purchaser.—Defendant was fined 10s., and 10s. costs.—Charles Cooper, grocer, Sankey-bridges, was charged with a similar offence, his flour scales having been found three quarters of an ounce out of balance against the purchaser. Defendant was fined 10s. and COSI& BREACHES OF THE EDUCATION ACT. Mary Wood and John Gill Feddar were summoned for breaches of the Education Act.—The former was fined 23. 6d., and the latter ss. _ . .

... NECESSARY TO RESIST. John Milton, a young man, wale charged with assaulting Thomas Ury. On the 21st of July, the complainant went to the defendant's house to execute a warrant for rent. Defendant was away from home, and the complainant waited for him. When be arrived defendant seized the person who was assisting the complainant and pushed him out of the house, and return- ing, he similarly dealt with the complainant, striking him twice in the scuffle. The police were informed of the occur- rence, and an officer returned with the complainant, who with difficulty effected an entrance and seized two articles. —Defendant said he had a dispute with the landlord, and he thought it was necessary to resist in order to maintain an action. He pushed complainant from the house, but did not strike him.—He was ordered to pay costs.

BREACH OF THE SANITARY AUTHORITY'S BYE-LAWS For not complying with the bye-laws of the Warrington Rural Sinitary Authority, by neglecting to cleanse his ash. pits, &c., Wm. Isherwood, of Winwick-road, Orford, was fined 2s. 6d. and Bs. 6d. Mts. ROBBERY FROISI THE PENKETIC CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—A boy nine years of age, named Elijah Fisher, was charged with having, on the 10th inst., stolen 3d. from the cash box of the Conservative Club at Penketh.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. _ _

THE BT:ROLXRY AT SlNKEY.—Patrick Connor, who is said to have only recently been released from Dartmoor prison, where he had undergone ten years penal servitude, was charged with having, on the night of the Bth instant or the morning of the 9th instant, feloniously entered the house of Joseph Gill, Liverpool-road, Little Sankey, and stolen therefrom a shawl and vase valued at 6s. 6d. the property of Mary Gill. On Tuesday morning about four o'clock a man named Samuel Nichol was returning home from the forge, along Liverpool-road, when he discovered the bottom portion of prosecutor's parlour window to be open. He knocked at the door and awakened Mrs. Gill, whose husband was away from home, and told her what he had seen. She went into the parlour, finding footprints on the window sill, and also on a chair near by. The curtain was on the floor, which was marked with the footprints of muddy shoes. Further examination showed that a shawl, and a vase from the'mantel shelf had been abstracted. At 11 o'clock the same morning the prisoner pawned the shawl at Mr. Morton's, pawnbroker, Latchford, where it was found by P.C. Phillips, who apprehended the prisoner at a lodging house in Stanley-street at 5 p.m. on Tuesday, the 9th inst. When charged, he replied " I found the shawl and went and pawned it."—The prisoner was committed to the Liverpool assizes.

THE CHESHIRE, SHROPSHIRE, AND NORTH WALES FARMERS' SUPPLY ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting was held at the Royal Hotel, Crewe, on Wednesday, Mr. G. W. Latham, of Bradwell Hall, presiding. There was a large attendance of members. The report stated that the financial position of the association was better by £1,500 than last year. The directors stated that they had instituted a series of comparative trials of the Manchester city manure and other manures, with a view of ascertaining the real value agriculturally of a manure manufactured close at hand, and by so public-spirited a body as the Manchester Corporation ; but in consequence of the season being advanced when the experimept began they had not arrived at any definite re- sult. The average of profit on capital per cent. had been this year 21.4, while the average for the last ten years had been 21i. On the whole, in spite of the unfavourable year for agriculture, the outlook was most hopeful, and directors believed that the association was now ready to meet the de. mands which more prosperous times and more bountiful harvests would probably make on its enterprise and re- sources.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the re- port, said he hoped that the agriculturists of England were about to see better times. He trusted that with a good harvest they would obtain better p ices, and that farmers would soon emerge from the terrible depths of misfortune into into which they had been plunged.—After some discussion regarding the business of the association, the report statement of accounts were agreed to, and a vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceedingq,

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.—ELEMENTARY EDUCA- TION ACTS, 1870, to 1879. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a SPECIAL MEETING of the COUNCIL of the Borough of War- rington, will be held in the Could= CIIAMBER within the Town Hall, on TUESDAY, the 6th day of SEPTEMBER, 1881, at half-past five in the evening in pursuance of the Elementary Education (Industrial Schools) Act, 1879, and all other statu- tory provisions in that behalf, to take into consideration the making of a contribution towards the maintenance in a Certi- fied Industrial School, of three boys ordered by the magistrates upon complaint made by the School Attendance Committee, of the Borough of Warrington, to be sent to such Certified In- dustrial School. Dated this 19th day of August, 1881. W. H. BROOK, Town Clerk.

NO VISITOR TO SOUTHPORT SHOULD MISS SEEING TIE BOTANIC GARDENS, CHURCHTOWN, SOUTHPORT. Acknowledged to be one of the most charming spots in the North of England. SPLENDID GROUNDS AND SHRUBBERIES. The Unique Fernery, with its Mirrors, Grottoes, Waterfalls, Fountain, and Fishpools, forms a lovely Pantomimic Fairy Scene. THE GRAND CONSERVATORY, With its mass of rich ever-varying Bloom, and large central Fountain, is indeed a "thing of beauty." Fine Ranges of VINERIES AND PLANT HOUSES. Excellent MUSEUM of Natural History, Geology, Coins, Medals, and Curiosities. (The Natural History Section contains a complete Entomological Collection of Southport.) Spacious and well-appointed first and second-class public and private Refreshment Rooms. Admission to the Gardens (in- cluding Conservatory, Fernery, and Museum), 4d; children under 12 years of age. 2d each. Street tramway cars run between the Botanic Gardens, Southport, and Birkdale, every seven minutes in summer.

LIVERPOOL TO YORK. The revival of the Stage Coach, with its bounding steeds and far-sounding bugle, was a pleasant reminder of the good old days when railways were not, although there are few who would care to recall the times when "George the the Third was Ring ; " yet the remembrance of bye-gone days, with slow means of transit, and difficulty in reaching distant towns; no penny post; no gas; no telegraph, has a charm for the busy people of the latter half of the nine- teenth century. In those days the existence of large firms like THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY would have been an impossibility. A Coat purchased at a very large outlay had to last a man's lifetime, and descend from father to son, as a valued acquisition. With the Introductioß of railways and machinery, commercial enterprise in the manufacture of Clothing, as in other branches of trade, effected a complete revolution. "Our Boys" of the present day are clothed In a manner our grandfathers would not have dreamed of. Talented artists are engaged in designing, and thousands of specially trained workpeople in making up, dress for the Boys. A quarter of a century ago THE GRAND CLOTMNG HALL COMPANY com- menced their operations, starting with a thorough know- ledge of the trade, and large capital at command. They soon became known in the commercial world for the uni- form excellence of their Men's, Youths, and Boys' Clothing; and probably at the present time they are the largest Manufacturers of Clothing in the World. They reject all but the most reliable material in their manufacture; and, by constant supervision in the minutest details, maintain the pre-eminence they have obtained as producers of Clothing for all Classes. THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY, 28, 30, & 32, BBIDGE-STBEET, WARRINGTON; ROCHDALE, PRESTON, SHEFFIELD, DERBY.
